item.title: [SCMP] Why US chip controls took a back seat at the Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
There is little question that Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, the heads of US semiconductor chip giants Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), had secured two of the best seats in the house at the White House state dinner on Thursday evening: at the head table alongside the two presidents and their wives.

But what remains unclear is how much progress they were able to make on their primary goal of restoring access to the Chinese market, amid entrenched opposition to that happening in both China and the US.

That is because US semiconductor chip export controls do not seem to have been a major sticking point during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic state visit to Washington this week, despite most of the restrictions still being in place.
item.content:encoded:
There is little question that Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, the heads of US semiconductor chip giants Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), had secured two of the best seats in the house at the White House state dinner on Thursday evening: at the head table alongside the two presidents and their wives.

But what remains unclear is how much progress they were able to make on their primary goal of restoring access to the Chinese market, amid entrenched opposition to that happening in both China and the US.

That is because US semiconductor chip export controls do not seem to have been a major sticking point during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic state visit to Washington this week, despite most of the restrictions still being in place.

Early indications suggest that export controls were not a significant topic of debate during the talks, with no direct mention of them in the readouts so far from both Beijing and Washington summarising the achievements of the Xi–Trump summit.

“This is especially strange considering that export controls were brought up regularly by Xi during his talks with [President Joe] Biden,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Washington think tank Brookings specialising in Chinese technology.

On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the US side had taken “off the table” all the export controls “that are national security issues” during trade talks this week. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Saturday did not mention export controls or Beijing’s usual references to US tech restrictions in its announcement of eight deliverables from the summit, including the launch of a China-US dialogue on AI risks.

But if export controls have become less of a sticking point, it is not because they have gone away. The Trump administration has largely kept intact restrictions first introduced by the Biden administration in October 2022 on China’s ability to obtain advanced chips and chipmaking equipment.

Some areas were even tightened at the start of Trump’s second term, including a ban on exporting Nvidia’s H20 chip to China, which the company had developed specifically to comply with US rules.

According to Chan, Beijing has likely grown more comfortable with the export controls already in place as it looks to deepen its technological self-reliance campaign to reduce its reliance on US tech.

“The biggest thing that’s changed is China’s growing confidence in its chip self-reliance efforts,” he said. “While the 2022 export controls may have surprised Beijing at the time, China has made real progress on building a domestic supply chain for advanced semiconductors in the years since”.

A temporary stalemate

When Washington first imposed sweeping export controls on China in 2022, Beijing treated them as a direct attack on China’s technological and economic rise and began regularly calling for their removal in talks with the US.

The controls became a wedge issue in US-China relations. At China-US talks on AI safety in Geneva in May 2024, Chinese officials tied progress on AI safety to the US unwinding those controls, former Biden administration officials have said.

This was not an issue this time around. Export controls were not brought up during the AI safety related talks between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last Sunday in New York, according to Greer, who also attended the meeting.

The AI talks, which also resulted in the launch of a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents, were “candid, in-depth and constructive”, Beijing said.

Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said Beijing is likely “pleased with progress that the domestic semiconductor industry has made despite the [US] controls”.

Chinese chip manufacturers are taking a greater share of the domestic market. According to TrendForce, Chinese chip suppliers led by Huawei Technologies and Cambricon Technologies are set to capture nearly 80 per cent of the domestic AI server market this year.

Nvidia, AMD and other foreign suppliers’ share is set to fall to 21 per cent in 2026 from 34 per cent last year, according to the Taipei-based research firm.

Domestic chip substitution is expected to further ramp up in the coming years as tech self-reliance remains a central pillar of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. Earlier this year, Beijing resisted efforts by both President Donald Trump and Nvidia’s Huang to push for the US chip giant’s less powerful H200 chips to be allowed back into the Chinese market.

Beijing has since allowed a small number of Chinese tech companies to purchase the chip with the quantities capped, as it continues to promote domestic chip adoption instead. Meanwhile, the delayed approval caused Nvidia to take a US$400 million charge due to excess H200 inventory in the first half of the year.

Spanner in the works

Still, talk of an export control impasse might still be premature. That is because Beijing is likely to push back forcefully against any new restrictions the US introduces, with some already on the horizon, according to Triolo.

A major area of concern is US congressional efforts to bolster its export controls regime. One of these is the Match Act, which would require US allies such as Japan and the Netherlands to more closely align with US restrictions on selling advanced semiconductor equipment to China, such as Dutch firm ASML’s deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography machines.

The bill has been folded into the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA) in the US Senate, improving its chances of becoming law.

“Chinese officials view any new controls as a violation of the Busan agreement, and [would] retaliate strongly via expanded controls on rare earths and related production equipment,” said Triolo, referring to the economic detente reached in October 2025 between the two countries that paused escalating tit-for-tat tariffs and export controls, which the two leaders agreed to extend to January.

“Beijing likely sought assurances on this [this week],” he said.

Even as the official readouts of the two presidents’ meeting have largely focused on trade and investment, senior Chinese officials have referenced US technological restrictions on China in statements elsewhere.

On Saturday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a post-meeting statement that China and the US should not “adopt a defensive posture towards each other” in the emerging field of AI.

The relative quiet on export controls this week might therefore reflect strong domestic pressure on both sides not to concede ground, Triolo said, with powerful contingents in the US pushing for tighter controls and those in China for greater self-reliance.

“Neither side will acknowledge progress on any of these issues, given domestic sensitivities around anything that could be perceived as a concession,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] 3 top reasons Trump will face a stronger Xi Jinping at November Apec forum in China
item.description:
When Donald Trump arrives in Shenzhen for the November Apec summit, he will face a Chinese leader even more confident than the one who left Washington this week after a state visit heavy on pageantry but light on concrete deliverables.

Experts attributed this confidence to three key factors – a newly upgraded bilateral framework seeking a “constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, the warmer tone during Xi’s three-day visit, and – crucially – the significant leverage of host diplomacy.

In southern China’s Shenzhen – home to technological giants Huawei, BYD and Tencent – President Xi Jinping will have greater control over the agenda and showcase Beijing’s growing diplomatic clout in ways impossible during a bilateral summit.
item.content:encoded:
When Donald Trump arrives in Shenzhen for the November Apec summit, he will face a Chinese leader even more confident than the one who left Washington this week after a state visit heavy on pageantry but light on concrete deliverables.

Experts attributed this confidence to three key factors – a newly upgraded bilateral framework seeking a “constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, the warmer tone during Xi’s three-day visit, and – crucially – the significant leverage of host diplomacy.

In southern China’s Shenzhen – home to technological giants Huawei, BYD and Tencent – President Xi Jinping will have greater control over the agenda and showcase Beijing’s growing diplomatic clout in ways impossible during a bilateral summit.

Meanwhile, the Washington spectacle will reverberate with US allies and middle powers, who experts said would need to reassess their China strategies.

“As the Apec host, China will clearly possess far more autonomy in agenda-setting, topic selection, and preparatory work than it did during the Washington summit, where the US controlled the choreography while China held only participation and discussion rights,” said Chen Qi, director of the Centre for US-China Relations at Tsinghua University.

The shift in leverage would be particularly evident in the multilateral setting, he added.

“Beijing could also showcase its diplomatic influence and leadership far more effectively than in bilateral encounters.”

Statements released by both countries on Saturday confirmed that Trump intended to travel to Shenzhen in November to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, setting up a third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting would help Xi highlight “China’s growing economic and diplomatic sway – including with several US allies and partners” shortly after midterm elections likely to be bruising for Trump’s Republican Party.

“Xi appreciates how greatly Trump values opportunities to convey that the two leaders enjoy a strong rapport … Their Washington summit this week demonstrated his willingness to reverse or weaken US measures that might risk his meetings with Xi,” Wyne added.

Zhang Chi, senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World (CCCW), called the upgraded relationship “a very successful strategic convergence” that placed Beijing and Washington on a fairer footing.

“Equally important is that China has demonstrated that attempts by Washington to reshape the bilateral power balance through ‘maximum pressure’ are ineffective and create uncontrollable problems,” he said.

Marking his second state visit to the US since 2015, Xi arrived to a rare tarmac greeting from President Donald Trump – a courtesy usually delegated to lower-level officials.

The 42 hours of summitry that followed saw both leaders hold up China as an equal or near-equal power to the United States. Trump spoke warmly of an emerging “great friendship”, while Xi portrayed the bilateral bond as a “river that never stops flowing” as its leaders work to “steer the giant ship” of relations forward.

Saturday’s statements by both countries further indicated a fourth Xi-Trump meeting this year, at the December Group of 20 summit in Miami. The pair last met in May, when Trump travelled to Beijing on a state visit.

Just ahead of the Washington summit, the two sides agreed to extend the bilateral trade truce set to expire in November by two months. As part of the truce, Washington has pledged to pause new tariffs while Beijing will suspend some rare earth export controls.

The unprecedented frequency of head-of-state interaction – four summits in eight months – signals a window of relative stability, according to Chinese experts.

The high-frequency meetings this year make policy continuity “both a promise and an inertia”, said Zhang Zhizhou, from the school of international relations and diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University.

This would potentially help to shield Beijing from disruptive unilateral actions by Washington in the interim, he said, while identifying several factors contributing to China’s increased confidence heading into the Apec summit. These include China’s rising technological strength, growing influence in the Global South and Belt and Road Initiative partner nations.

All of this would make the Chinese side – which excels at host diplomacy – “more confident and bolster their negotiating position”, Zhang in Beijing said.

Shortly after Trump and Xi wrapped up their Washington summit, the White House announced that both sides had recommended reciprocal tariff relief covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive trade moving in each direction.

US exports slated for preferential treatment under the proposed framework include agricultural produce, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical equipment.

The reciprocal Chinese list covers consumer goods such as small household appliances, toys, festive decorations and children’s car seats.

But experts also urged caution on long-term predictability, noting that the present strategy remained tied to Trump personally and domestic pressures and geopolitics could test the diplomatic momentum.

“Going forward, there are two key factors to watch: whether Trump can still honour his commitments once his hands are free, as upcoming midterm elections and the quagmire in Iran are currently draining his attention; and second, any provocative moves on Taiwan arms sales,” Zhang from CCCW said.

Trump, who has described arms sales to Taiwan as a negotiating tool with Beijing, postponed a planned US$14 billion package following his May summit with Xi.

The South China Morning Post reported this month that the US was considering postponing the announcement of arms sales to Taiwan until the end of the year, pointing to the potential Apec and G20 summits.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. But Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Ma Bo, associate professor at Nanjing University, said Washington was operating on two parallel tracks. While the White House projects cordiality at the top, the US security apparatus – aligning with its allies – continues to press ahead.

“Detente at the leader level does not bind Congress, technological export controls, or the actions of America’s regional allies,” Ma warned.

The current equilibrium is also seen as likely to prompt uneasy recalibration among middle powers and traditional US allies who watched Xi’s visit with a mix of relief and trepidation.

Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for US Studies at Fudan University, noted that Washington’s regional partners – from Tokyo to Manila – were increasingly anxious about the potential erosion of US strategic support.

“As [US-China] ties stabilise, the backing these countries can extract from Washington will inevitably erode,” Xin said.

“If they attempt to use America to confront Beijing, they may find themselves without US endorsement, or even risk being left out in the cold.”

According to Zhang from CCCW, Europe is in an “embarrassing” position, as the progress in US-China ties will make Europe’s own escalation of trade pressure on Beijing look increasingly discordant.

Meanwhile, countries that recognise Beijing’s playbook in handling Washington – “those convinced that caving in to Trump brings no tangible benefit, will be the first to pivot towards Beijing with a more proactive and pragmatic posture”, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump, Takaichi reaffirm US-Japan ties in phone call after Xi state visit
item.description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday.

The call followed the US president’s nostalgic invocation of the World War II alliance with China during his summit with Xi Jinping, remarks that sent shock waves through Tokyo.

Trump made the references as he welcomed the Chinese president to the White House on Thursday for his first state visit to Washington in over a decade.
item.content:encoded:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday.

The call followed the US president’s nostalgic invocation of the World War II alliance with China during his summit with Xi Jinping, remarks that sent shock waves through Tokyo.

Trump made the references as he welcomed the Chinese president to the White House on Thursday for his first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

In a social media post on Saturday, Takaichi said Trump provided detailed explanations regarding the recent US-China summit during the call starting at 9pm Tokyo time. They exchanged views centred on various issues surrounding China, including the economy and security, and confirmed the Japan-US collaboration, she wrote.

Takaichi met Trump in person on Tuesday in New York, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Two exchanges with the US leader within one week “truly demonstrates the strength of the Japan-US alliance”, her post read.

“Japan and the United States have now become the most trusted allied nations, and we confirmed our commitment to jointly contribute to peace and stability in the region and the world.

“In order to elevate our unwavering Japan-US alliance to even greater heights, I will closely collaborate with President Trump,” she pledged.

Both Trump and Xi repeatedly invoked their nations’ wartime alliance against Japan in their remarks in Washington – an unusual historical reference that immediately unsettled Tokyo.

Such bonds were also reflected in statements released by the two countries following Xi’s visit.

“The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” both statements said.

However, the White House statement added a paragraph to justify US presence in the region.

“Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” it said.

Takaichi said on Friday that Tokyo and Washington were “allies bound by very strong ties” based on mutual trust. But she pointedly declined to comment on the Trump-Xi summit.

To avoid being sidelined completely, Takaichi had rescheduled her address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, moving it up by two days to secure a 35-minute meeting with Trump on Tuesday.

Japanese analysts warned that the wartime nostalgia boded poorly for Japan, though they cautioned against reading too much into the rhetoric.

Chinese observers, meanwhile, argued that the moment should prompt Tokyo to rethink its approach towards Beijing.

Shin Kawashima, professor of international relations at the University of Tokyo, said the main question was why Washington was embracing the wartime framing now.

“Trump’s remarks could easily be interpreted by China as indicating that the US and China are in agreement on issues of historical perception and that the US supports China’s rhetoric condemning the [Takaichi] administration as a form of ‘new militarism’,” Kawashima said.

Hotaka Machida, a visiting senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said Japan would find Trump’s historical references “surprising and awkward”, but noted that the remarks were made in the context of the US-China relationship.

Still, he cautioned: “Japan needs to be careful about the possibility of the Chinese side taking advantage of the amicable atmosphere presented this time as a propaganda tool.”

Kenichi Doi, senior research fellow at the same institute, called Trump’s description of wartime China as an ally “striking”.

But the bigger question was whether that shared history would be used to cast doubt on present-day Japan. It would be a mistake to assume that Trump had endorsed Beijing’s criticism of Tokyo, he said.

Rintaro Nishimura, a senior associate at The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said that though worrying, the single statement was unlikely to weaken the US-Japan alliance.

Tokyo was also less concerned because Takaichi coordinated with Trump on issues related to China ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, he added.

“[But] it does not bode well for Tokyo that Washington and Beijing are both emphasising the fact that the two countries were wartime allies,” Nishimura said.

Beijing and Tokyo have remained largely out of official contact since November, when Takaichi suggested that a blockade of Taiwan would be a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

Official relations went into a tailspin but Japanese business and legislative delegations have made sustained efforts to visit Beijing to gauge Chinese thinking.

Another business delegation, led by former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya, will go to China on Sunday in the latest attempt to bridge the diplomatic impasse.

Nishimura expected Tokyo to “stay the course” when engaging with Beijing, using legislative and commercial dialogue to tease out potential openings for government-level talks, with an end goal of securing a Takaichi-Xi meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November.

“Japan will be looking to see if there are any signs that Washington is ready to compromise regional security for a deal, perhaps economic, with Beijing.”

Meanwhile, Tokyo’s discomfort is seen as an inevitable consequence of stabilising US-China ties, with analysts saying the warm tone from the summit should prompt Tokyo to reassess its own approach to Beijing.

Kawashima noted that Japan-China relations would “grow more tenuous” if US-China ministerial engagement deepened and might prompt Tokyo to conclude that it was better to improve relations with China to some extent.

Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, said Japan’s anxiety was an inevitable result of further stabilisation between Beijing and Washington.

“The sheer fact that Chinese and American leaders can have such frequent interactions this year should serve as a prompt for Tokyo to change its perceptions towards China and rethink its posture,” Wang said.

Zhang Yun, professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Tokyo harboured deep concern about the prospect of another 1972 “Nixon shock”, when the US normalised ties with China without consulting its closest East Asian ally.

Takaichi’s push to meet Trump ahead of his talks with Xi reflected this anxiety, he said.

“Compounded by Trump’s transactional approach towards its traditional alliances and tariff actions, these dynamics are fuelling deep-seated anxieties in Tokyo over Washington’s reliability, leaving Japan’s position adrift,” Zhang said.

According to Cho Sung-min, associate professor of international relations at Sungkyunkwan University in Seoul, the memory of US-China military cooperation against Japan has long been a Chinese talking point.

“Trump’s reference to America’s past partnership with China against Japan, a US ally in the present, suggests how far he was willing to go to maintain a cordial relationship with Xi,” Cho said.

item.title: [SCMP] China-based Brics bank set for lead role in hunger alliance this year, Brazil says
item.description:
The Brics-founded New Development Bank could help launch a fund by the end of the year to guarantee cheap loans for poor families in Africa and Latin America, Brazil’s social development minister said.

The scheme would be the Shanghai-based lender’s first financial commitment to Brazil’s global anti-hunger alliance, an initiative sidelined by Washington’s presidency of the G20 this year.

Wellington Dias told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the chances of a first pilot programme, worth as little as US$200 million, getting off the ground by December were “very big”. The bank is designing the scheme with four other development lenders, he added, and each still has to run its compliance checks.
item.content:encoded:
The Brics-founded New Development Bank could help launch a fund by the end of the year to guarantee cheap loans for poor families in Africa and Latin America, Brazil’s social development minister said.

The scheme would be the Shanghai-based lender’s first financial commitment to Brazil’s global anti-hunger alliance, an initiative sidelined by Washington’s presidency of the G20 this year.

Wellington Dias told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the chances of a first pilot programme, worth as little as US$200 million, getting off the ground by December were “very big”. The bank is designing the scheme with four other development lenders, he added, and each still has to run its compliance checks.

The money would go to Brazil’s Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, launched at the G20 summit Brazil hosted in Rio de Janeiro in November 2024 but dropped from the group’s agenda after the United States took over the rotating presidency in December last year.

The Trump administration, which boycotted last year’s summit in Johannesburg, has narrowed the G20 agenda to deregulation, energy, technology and trade, leaving out priorities of Brazil’s 2024 presidency such as inequality and hunger.

Dias, who co-chairs the alliance, said Washington had become “somewhat isolated” on hunger, but admitted that its reduction in aid was a “hard problem” for the group’s objective.

This is because even though it has 215 members (including over 107 countries and 14 international financial institutions), the alliance has no money of its own and relies on members to fund the programmes it brokers.

Much of the money so far has come from the Inter-American Development Bank, which pledged up to US$25 billion between 2025 and 2030. It approved US$4.1 billion in alliance-aligned operations last year and expects to approve US$5.8 billion this year.

Dias acknowledged that neither the New Development Bank nor the Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank had financed any alliance programme so far, but added that the Brics’ bank contribution would come through the guarantee fund.

That would be new territory for a lender set up in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa to finance mostly infrastructure. When it joined the alliance in October 2024, the bank offered help with water, sanitation, housing and irrigation projects, without naming a funding figure.

In the model he described, local banks would lend to poor borrowers and the guarantee fund would absorb any defaults.

“This will allow a poor person in the country being supported to walk into a bank and get financing,” Dias said.

“The poorest are seen by banks as high risk, and the interest is very high. With the guarantee fund, that goes away. The rate collapses, and that matters for financing in both rural and urban areas.”

The idea draws on Brazil’s Acredita programme, which offers microcredit to low-income families backed by a one billion reais (US$194 million) government guarantee fund. By October last year it had lent 1.7 billion reais, with a default rate of 0.36 per cent, according to the social development ministry.

China steps up global anti-hunger alliance involvement

The fund would also add a financial dimension to China’s involvement in the alliance, which it has lacked so far.

When President Xi Jinping announced China would join the Rio summit in November 2024, Beijing’s statement of commitment covered domestic policy and knowledge sharing but left out the section on financial support that members can choose to sign.

Its pledges were largely domestic, including a 50-million tonne increase in grain production capacity by 2030.

Abroad, China offered advice on 13 types of policy, among them microcredit for poverty alleviation through the International Poverty Reduction Centre in China.

That state-backed centre says it has trained nearly 15,000 officials from 140 countries and runs a poverty reduction forum with the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States. Its deputy director general, Li Xin, sits on the alliance’s Board of Champions as one of its vice-chairs.

Asked what Beijing had contributed since joining the alliance, Dias began with China’s success in reducing poverty at home before turning to its investment in developing countries.

“China is also one of the countries investing the most in Africa and South America, and with that it contributes, even if in a traditional way, to opening up opportunities for jobs and work,” he said. “It invests in infrastructure and so on.”

On the alliance itself, Dias said Chinese financial support has been focused on family farming in African countries, alongside other donors.

The minister also cited larger Chinese purchases from small producers’ cooperatives in Brazil, Africa and South America, including organic honey from Brazil’s north and northeast.

Countries contribute “with knowledge, with money, but also with investment”, he said, and “in this field, China is a prominent partner”.

Dias said Beijing could help fill the space left by US aid cuts, though as part of “a pact among several countries” rather than alone. But talks on that between the Brics bloc, the European Union and other forums were disrupted by the Iran war early this year, according to the minister.

Cuba’s isolation and armed conflicts worldwide

Alliance members have sent food to Cuba, mainly milk, and are backing better seeds, irrigation and fishing projects to help the island produce more of its own, Dias said.

Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts since Venezuelan oil shipments stopped after US forces captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, and Washington has since blocked tankers bound for the island.

Dias described the positions of China, Brazil, Mexico and Spain on Cuba as “very firm”, and mentioned a Cuban target of 3.5 gigawatts of solar power.

With 42 countries at war or in armed conflict by his count, Dias asked richer economies, China among them, to avoid further aid cuts or to compensate where they had happened. He framed it as self-interest.

“When wars proliferate, when hunger and poverty are not dealt with, the richest also pay,” he said.

“Look at disorderly migration. All countries pay, whether it is the United States, countries in Europe or Brazil.”

item.title: [SCMP] Xi-Trump Washington summit aimed at putting US-China ties on equal footing: Wang Yi
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States was crucial to maintaining the overall stability of China-US relations and aimed at putting the relationship on an equal footing.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who accompanied Xi on the three-day trip to Washington, gave the assessment on Saturday, expanding on relations between the two countries.

According to state news agency Xinhua, Wang said Xi’s visit “maintained the overall stability of Sino-US relations” and “will have a deep impact on the world’s peace and development”.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States was crucial to maintaining the overall stability of China-US relations and aimed at putting the relationship on an equal footing.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who accompanied Xi on the three-day trip to Washington, gave the assessment on Saturday, expanding on relations between the two countries.

According to state news agency Xinhua, Wang said Xi’s visit “maintained the overall stability of Sino-US relations” and “will have a deep impact on the world’s peace and development”.

The Chinese foreign minister also expanded on one of the eight outcomes of the trip – an agreement between the two leaders to build a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

“It means the two countries have equal sovereignty and no one is more superior than the other. None is domineering or abusive and they should resolve their own concerns on an equal footing,” Wang said.

“Respect” referred to respect for each other’s sovereignty, territory and core interests, while “fairness” meant rejection of the “zero-sum mindset”, he added.

Wang said the exceptional reception given to Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, including the personal welcome US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania gave on the tarmac on arrival, reflected respect for Xi and the importance of China-US relations to the United States.

After the trip, China and the United States issued separate statements about the outcomes, saying they had agreed to improve cooperation on artificial intelligence, tariffs and chemical precursor control.

The two countries agreed that their leaders would also support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and Group of 20 summits later this year, signalling their intent to attend the meetings in person.

The agreement means that Trump plans to travel to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen in November, while Xi is scheduled to go to Miami in December, making this year unusual in terms of the number of face-to-face meetings between the two men.

Also unusual was the mention in both statements about the leaders’ references to the US-China alliance during World War II, a partnership that Xi and Trump highlighted several times during the trip.

Xi, also accompanied by chief of staff Cai Qi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, left Beijing for Washington on Wednesday and returned to the Chinese capital on Saturday afternoon.

The Chinese statement about the trip said both sides agreed to open a communication channel on incidents involving “artificial intelligence”. The US statement said they agreed to rename AI as “super intelligence”, a campaign Trump has been pushing in recent weeks.

The two leaders also formally endorsed a US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement reached earlier by the Chinese and US trade teams, as well as an extension of their trade truce.

The two countries affirmed the establishment of the Board of Investment. The US said the board would discuss “potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments”.

On geopolitics, both countries said they agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons and that no country or institution should impose tolls on international waterways.

They also lauded the arrest in August of 21 Chinese citizens for making and distributing precursor chemicals for illicit drug producers in North America, saying the action was the fruit of China-US cooperation on fentanyl.

While neither statement mentioned Taiwan, a sticking point of bilateral relations, Wang said the issue was brought up during the meetings.

“President Xi Jinping set out China’s principled position on the Taiwan issue, stressing that China is firmly committed to safeguarding national reunification and territorial integrity,” Wang said.

“[Xi] urged the US side to maintain the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’, handle the Taiwan issue prudently, and remove obstacles to China-US strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations.”

In a veiled reference to Japan, Wang said Xi also urged the US to share the “responsibility to uphold the post-war international order and prevent the revival of militarism”, with this year marking the 80th anniversary of the start of the Tokyo war crimes trials.

There were also differences between the statements from the two countries, which has become the norm in recent years since they stopped issuing joint statements.

The US said China had agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the United States next year and again in 2028 – a commitment that Beijing did not refer to.

The US also said the two sides would “continue to work on” US concerns about China’s exports of rare earths and critical minerals to the US, “with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels”. Again, the Chinese statement was silent on the issue.

In addition, the White House said the next meeting of the newly formed US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue would take place by November.

China’s Ministry of Commerce confirmed on Thursday that its senior trade negotiators had already held their first talks with the US on artificial intelligence.

One of the biggest differences was over the American presence in Asia.

Although the US highlighted its alliance with China during WWII, it nevertheless implied that it would remain a force in the region, which Beijing has repeatedly condemned as US hegemony.

“Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” the US statement said.

The Chinese statement instead highlighted potential improvements in military-to-military communication.

“The Chinese and US militaries agreed to sign as soon as possible a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communication and prevention,” it said.

In the meantime, Iran continued to wait for an official US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US ending its sanctions.

The proposal was made at the UN General Assembly and conveyed to the Americans via Qatari mediators, Iran said.

Trump and Xi also discussed concerns about Russia and North Korea, saying the US “advocated” for trilateral arms-control negotiations between the US, Russia, and China.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the affirmation of the investment board exceeded expectations as differences within the US had stalled progress.

“The US statement said specifically that the investment board will discuss potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments, and that is going towards the direction that China has hoped for. And the work of this board is one thing we need to look out for,” Wu said.

He said the historical alliances during WWII mentioned by both sides was particularly interesting and it was not expected, especially as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke to Trump in New York before Xi’s visit.

“Trump is different from [his predecessor Joe] Biden. Biden has a strong ideological orientation and when he talked about these things, he would certainly talk about the shared values of the United States and its allies – things like democracy,” Wu said.

“Trump is a nationalist, so he has a strong memory of Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbour. You can see that he likes to bring up Pearl Harbour from time to time. So for him, as a nationalist, there is nothing unusual about talking about World War II.”

Chen Qi, professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, said there was room for further discussion on trade and hopes for trade relations to stabilise with the Apec and G20 meetings later this year.

“The trade truce extension until January will [also] give more room for imagination for the rest of the world,” Chen said.

“When they are meeting so frequently, in November and December, do you think it is possible to upend the trade relationship and reopen the door to additional tariffs? I don’t think there is any room for that,” he said.

Daniel Kritenbrink, a former US assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, said the frequent meetings between the two leaders this year meant there was less pressure for deliverables during this trip.

“I think we have to keep in mind that we are in this extraordinary period right now where two presidents are meeting so frequently that I think the amount of pressure on each interaction is slightly less than would traditionally be the case,” said Kritenbrink, now a partner at Washington-based strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.

Additional reporting by Alyssa Chen

item.title: [SCMP] Xi-Trump atmospherics welcomed but mask structural rifts: analysts
item.description:
During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables.

But the fact that the two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability ahead, certainly relative to last year’s all-out trade war, chest-thumping and market turmoil, said analysts, companies and former US officials.

“Both countries are demonstrating some degree of restraint,” said Sara Schuman, managing director at consultancy Beacon Global Strategies and a former US diplomat in Beijing. “The optics that President Xi is travelling to Washington and he’s receiving a full state visit with a state dinner, this is in itself the core deliverable.”
item.content:encoded:
During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables.

But the fact that the two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability ahead, certainly relative to last year’s all-out trade war, chest-thumping and market turmoil, said analysts, companies and former US officials.

“Both countries are demonstrating some degree of restraint,” said Sara Schuman, managing director at consultancy Beacon Global Strategies and a former US diplomat in Beijing. “The optics that President Xi is travelling to Washington and he’s receiving a full state visit with a state dinner, this is in itself the core deliverable.”

By that definition, the visit was chock full.

Xi said the two leaders were “making history” with two summits in four months and two more meet-ups planned, one in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and another the following month at the G20 Trump is hosting in Miami.

And Xi spent the Mid-Autumn Festival outside China, only the second time during his near 14-year administration he has done so.

Trump, for his part, greeted Xi in person when he arrived at the airport, a role usually reserved for lower-level officials and a courtesy that the Chinese president did not extend to Trump when he landed in Beijing in May.

Both leaders also spent the 42-hour visit implicitly or explicitly framing China as an equal or near-equal global power, outlining the “great promise” of the bilateral relationship built on “mutual trust”, foreshadowing “a truly great friendship” like a “river that never stops flowing” as they “steer the giant ship of China-US relations steadily forward towards the future”.

No mention of rare earth minerals stand-off

Unspoken was the hugely consequential cudgel China has unsheathed: its global grip on rare earth minerals, which has fundamentally shifted the power balance after Trump pushed Beijing to the wall, threatening tariffs in excess of 125 per cent during last year’s “Liberation Day”.

Add China’s accelerated bid to diversify its trade dependence on US markets, its increasingly competitive artificial intelligence industry and its dominant position in electric vehicles, lithium batteries and renewable technologies, and it is not difficult to understand Beijing’s growing confidence.

Since then, Beijing has negotiated a trade truce with the US, which was extended this week until January 10; seen the transactional US president reframe Taiwan and high-end semiconductors as negotiable; forestalled a planned US$14 billion arms package to Taipei; pushed away US threats to sanction Chinese banks and refineries for bypassing Washington’s Iran sanctions and watched as greater distance opened between Washington and such long-time allies as Japan and South Korea.

“This is Xi Jinping’s world, and we’re all living in it,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). “The administration’s China strategy was poorly designed from the beginning. They thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, and that did not occur. In fact, the opposite did.”

Time and relative stability afford China more time to develop its increasingly successful trade strategy, allow Beijing to focus on its domestic economy rather than respond to erratic tariff gyrations, and see Washington increasingly distracted by Trump’s war of choice in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and his record-low popularity leading into the November midterm election.

Missing Chinese holidays, travelling repeatedly to the US by a president whose trips are carefully calibrated, displaying keen interest in Trump’s new helipad and supporting his bid to rebrand AI as “Super Intelligence”, expressing warmth hardly instinctual in China’s more austere political culture and making favourable references to Trump’s “make America great again” mantra may be a small price to pay.

“China has flexed its muscle, established its ability to counterstrike and the credibility of its retaliation,” said Yun Sun, China director at the Simson Centre. “Xi Jinping will visit Washington any day to be the peer of his US counterpart.”

In addition to the two-month trade truce extension, the week’s modest, more conventional deliverables included a likely Board of Trade deal involving reciprocal trade carve-outs subject to reduced tariffs that is likely to include some combination of “non-strategic” farm products, apparel, consumer electronics and other manufactured goods. Details are due out on Monday.

But analysts also said the increasingly frequent meetings between Xi and Trump, who favours in-person negotiations unencumbered by extensive planning or expert input, make it difficult to expect the sort of big-dollar deals and structural reforms that often took years of intensive negotiation under past US administrations.

Warm “friendship” at the very top also masks underlying seams, analysts said. Hawks on both sides quietly resist ostensibly closer ties. Important lower-level channels across the Pacific have winnowed as both presidents pared down officials in the military and broader bureaucracy. And growing competition and rivalry leave deep reservoirs of distrust. The lack of written agreements also lays the groundwork for misunderstanding.

“There’s been so much miscommunication or differing perceptions from both sides coming out of these summits,” said Emily Kilcrease, senior fellow at the Centre for a New American Security and a former senior US Trade Representative negotiator.

“Given how low the trust is between these two countries, it’s really important that people know who their counterparts are and can call them when there’s a crisis.”

US visit helps Xi-Trump bromance to blossom

Framing the budding Trump-Xi bromance are more than a few similarities, analysts said. Both believe they are battling “deep state” bureaucratic resistance. Both enjoy the pomp and pageantry of their power.

Both believe their economic model is superior, that their AI and technology will win out. And both face domestic economic challenges.

“When you see Xi Jinping and Donald Trump together, each of them believes that time is on their side,” said Edgard Kagen, a CSIS senior adviser and former political chief with the US Embassy in Beijing. “The US [believes it] will develop alternative sources of critical minerals and rare earths, and so time is on the US side. When Xi Jinping sits down with Donald Trump, he very much believes the US is in a hurtling decline and the time is on China’s side.”

“Neither of them has an interest, at least at this point, in an escalation on trade issues.”

Two more presidential meetings this year are likely to help maintain bilateral stability. They are also likely to push off any Taiwan arms package.

But the prospect of Trump alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at both – Moscow’s representative attended the two-day G20 Finance Ministers meeting in North Carolina starting August 31, and Putin is expected in Shenzhen – could further weaken traditional US alliances, some said.

“Trump continues to berate many of our closest allies, from Canada to Europe to Korea to Japan. At the same time, when he meets with US adversaries, usually he says relatively nice things,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and a former National Security Council official.

“That message would be heard loud and clear, and it will just further accelerate the drive from a lot of US allies to decrease their reliance on the United States. And it may embolden Russia and China to test those alliances even more.”

With so much at stake, experts say, the test will be whether this week’s atmospherics lead to longer-term equilibrium or a return to instability.

“You can have a state visit, respectful rhetoric, a very good dinner, while both governments continue to build tools to compete with each other the next day,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Federation for the Defence of Democracies and a former US diplomat.

“I don’t expect a reset in US-China relations. I do not expect a grand bargain on trade. I don’t expect Washington and Beijing to resolve their technology competition, economic security disputes, or any fundamental disagreement over Taiwan.”

“It’s a summit about managing stalemate, not resolving it.”

item.title: [SCMP] The porcupine dilemma: why US-China diplomacy is about distance, not deals
item.description:
Arthur Schopenhauer’s classic parable of relationships may help us understand today’s China-US ties.

The reclusive German philosopher famously described how wintering porcupines need to cluster together to survive the biting cold, but hurt one another with their quills if they get too close. In the end, the porcupines must learn to balance the need for shared warmth against the pain of pricking each other.

Chinese President Xi Jinping received an unprecedentedly lavish reception from Donald Trump this week – one that would make America’s staunchest allies envious. On his second state visit to the US, a first for a Chinese president, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan schmoozed with the American first couple like old friends. Both presidents heaped praise on one another and pledged to do more to further the friendship of the two peoples.
item.content:encoded:
Arthur Schopenhauer’s classic parable of relationships may help us understand today’s China-US ties.

The reclusive German philosopher famously described how wintering porcupines need to cluster together to survive the biting cold, but hurt one another with their quills if they get too close. In the end, the porcupines must learn to balance the need for shared warmth against the pain of pricking each other.

Chinese President Xi Jinping received an unprecedentedly lavish reception from Donald Trump this week – one that would make America’s staunchest allies envious. On his second state visit to the US, a first for a Chinese president, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan schmoozed with the American first couple like old friends. Both presidents heaped praise on one another and pledged to do more to further the friendship of the two peoples.

They will meet again in Shenzhen and Miami before the year is out: three presidential summits in four months set another record.

Yet the warmth between the two leaders could not conceal the tensions sizzling beneath.

The fact that the two sides only agreed to extend the truce in their costly trade war by two more months, after an unscheduled, eleventh-hour negotiation ahead of the summit, is telling.

Expectations for any breakthrough on critical minerals or chip controls are low. Observers also doubt whether Washington is willing to fundamentally shift its policy on Taiwan, even though Trump did postpone an approved arms sale and was careful about public comments on the issue, mindful of Beijing’s sensitivities.

To some, the three-day summit seemed heavy on pageantry but light on substance. One former US diplomat called it “theatrical pageantry” that “papered over real problems”.

Yet often in diplomacy – and especially in this case – form is substance. Protocols and rituals function in human society as a way of setting the right distance.

It is unrealistic to expect the two sides to reach any substantial breakthrough, given the sharp spikes these two “porcupines” carry on their backs.

While Xi was given the highest honours by his host, the trip was overshadowed by domestic American political turmoil and Trump’s feud with the mainstream media.

Most Americans saw little footage of the actual summit, as major television networks did not provide live coverage – a consequence of Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

When the visit was covered, the narrative was often coloured by the networks’ anger at the president. Trump was relentlessly criticised by liberal media for warming up to Communist China, and the tirades against Beijing often bordered on hysteria.

We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other

The underlying sentiment seems to be that Washington simply needs to “act tough” to strong-arm Beijing into submission.

That script has been tried before, and it has never worked. Before this week’s meeting, the US and China had already settled into nine years of intense rivalry, fighting trade wars, tech wars, financial wars and narrative wars.

We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other.

It is fitting, if ironic, that it’s Marco Rubio – still on Beijing’s sanctions list – who offers the sharpest rebuttal to that view, now wearing his Secretary of State hat.

“The United States and China are the two largest economies in the world. The United States and China are probably the two most powerful militaries in the world. The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Secretary Rubio said. “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to. That doesn’t mean we don’t have strong disagreements. Of course, we do.”

The present entente between China and the US is hardly, as some commentators believe, the result of Trump’s tendency to cosy up to authoritarian strongmen. The two sides are being driven together by the need for “shared warmth” in the face of pressing internal and external urgencies.

Unlike the Soviet Union and the US during the Cold War, there is no Iron Curtain separating the two sides in today’s globalised world. For all the efforts to decouple or de-risk, Chinese and American national interests remain deeply intertwined.

A study released by the Peterson Institute for International Economics last month found that despite all the tariffs and trade restrictions imposed on Beijing by Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden, China’s share of total value added in American imports dropped by only 2 per cent. Chinese supply chains remain deeply embedded in the American economy.

At the same time, the need for cooperation on issues like the regulation of artificial intelligence – or “superintelligence” in President Trump’s terminology – is real and pressing.

The danger of artificial intelligence lies not so much in machines replacing humans, but in the disproportionate power it hands to those with access to advanced AI over those without. That imbalance opens the door to every kind of abuse and misuse.

It also sharply raises the risk of miscalculated nuclear warfare.

During the Cold War, a strategic missile launched from Soviet or American soil would take roughly an hour to hit its target. Today, hypersonic technology has cut that window to under 20 minutes, and sophisticated stealth technology makes early detection far harder.

Cold War-era generals had time to assess intelligence and call each other for clarification in an extreme emergency. Today, no human being can do all of that in 8 to 20 minutes.

Inevitably, this may mean ceding control of the nuclear button to AI – unless the two sides can reach some comprehensive agreement first.

These are just some of the cold realities both sides must face. No matter how much you dislike the “spiky porcupine” across the room, you have to learn how to get close enough to survive the winter.

This, in a roundabout way, is my explanation of what Xi means by “strategic stability” between the two sides. The term, first raised last October when the two leaders met in Busan, South Korea, describes how China and the US might find the “Goldilocks distance” – close enough to cooperate, far enough to compete, without risking bringing down the house.

Seen this way, the success of this week’s summit should not be measured by the deals signed or missed, but by whether the two sides have established the right distance to contain their differences and allow controlled cooperation – one step at a time.

item.title: [SCMP] China set to decide if Costa Rican or Guyanese diplomat becomes first woman UN chief
item.description:
China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite.

Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN.

The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei.
item.content:encoded:
China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite.

Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN.

The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei.

China has kept cordial but cooler relations with Milei since his 2023 presidential campaign, when he called the Chinese government “assassins” and promised to cut ties in favour of the “civilised side of life”.

Under UN rules, the 193-member General Assembly appoints the secretary general on the recommendation of the 15-member Security Council. The winner will succeed current UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31. The assembly has never rejected a name put forward by the council.

A candidate needs at least nine votes in the council and no veto from any of the five permanent members, which are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Before a formal vote, the council holds secret straw polls in which members mark each candidate “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion”. Colour-coded ballots, used in later rounds, show whether a discourage vote came from a permanent member, though not which one.

Both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett travelled to Beijing this year to meet Foreign Minister Wang Yi, but China has not publicly endorsed either of them.

Grynspan led the first straw poll in July with 10 encourage votes, and Rodrigues-Birkett came first in the second round in August.

In the third poll a week ago, Grynspan received nine encourage votes, five discourage votes and one no opinion, according to diplomats with knowledge of the tally sheets. Rodrigues-Birkett received eight encourage votes, and her discourage votes rose from three to six.

Grossi, Ugandan diplomat and former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu and Senegal’s former president Macky Sall received five encourage votes each. Former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa received three, and Ecuador’s Ivonne A-Baki received none.

The results do not show whether any of Grynspan’s five discourage votes came from a permanent member. In the 2016 race, which took six straw polls, Guterres did not fall below 11 encourage votes.

China has not said publicly which candidate it prefers, but the Brics summit in New Delhi earlier this month could serve as a hint of what Beijing thinks of the contest.

During the summit, the Brics leaders adopted a joint declaration noting that “no woman has ever been elected for the role of Secretary-General” and that only one national from Latin America and the Caribbean had held the post.

Also, China’s ambassador to the UN, Fu Cong, reportedly said in May that Beijing supported regional rotation for the organisation’s top job and would be “pleased to see a woman in the post”, according to Costa Rican news site El Observador. Grynspan thanked him for the remarks at the time.

Bachelet’s withdrawal

While the choice between the leading female candidates appears wide open, another contender has categorically failed to win China’s favour.

While there is no confirmation on its position on Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett, three sources familiar with the matter told the SCMP that the Chinese delegation “decisively voted against” Michelle Bachelet, the former Chilean president.

Bachelet withdrew from the race last Saturday, a day after she received one encourage vote and 11 discourage votes in the third poll. Her withdrawal left seven officially nominated candidates in the race.

Chile’s government under President Jose Antonio Kast withdrew her nomination earlier in the year, and her candidacy continued with the backing of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Mexico. Conservative US lawmakers had also urged Washington to veto her over her support for abortion rights, Reuters reported.

Bachelet’s relationship with Beijing deteriorated during her term as UN high commissioner for human rights. She visited Xinjiang in May 2022 and Western governments criticised the trip as too soft on China.

Then, minutes before her UN term ended in August that year, her office published an assessment of Xinjiang. It said abuses against Uygurs and other mostly Muslim minorities in the region “may amount to crimes against humanity”.

China’s mission in Geneva rejected the report as disinformation serving the US and other Western countries.

Meetings with Wang Yi

Grynspan met Wang in Beijing in June and, according to the Chinese foreign ministry, reaffirmed her commitment to the one-China principle. She also praised China’s support for multilateralism and the UN Charter.

Wang told her that her remarks showed an understanding of the concerns of Global South countries.

He said the next secretary general should uphold the UN Charter and be capable, fair and responsible, and that China would take part in the selection with a “constructive attitude”.

Grynspan has led UN Trade and Development since 2021. In 2022 she helped broker the Istanbul agreements, which reopened Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea and eased Russian food and fertiliser shipments.

Rodrigues-Birkett also met Wang in Beijing, although a month later. The ministry said she “expressed support for UN General Assembly Resolution 2758”, which Beijing cites as the basis of its claim to represent China at the UN, and “reaffirmed the one-China principle”.

She also praised Chinese President Xi Jinping’s four global initiatives and China’s proposal for a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. The Chinese-language readout quoted her as calling China “a leader on development issues”.

After the meeting, Guyana’s Department of Public Information reported that China supported her candidacy. It later apologised and said the report had “mischaracterised Beijing’s position”.

In February 2021, Guyana cancelled an agreement for a Taiwan office less than 24 hours after it was announced, following a public objection from the Chinese foreign ministry.

Yet, two sources from countries represented at the Security Council told the SCMP that Grynspan had a slight advantage with Beijing. But they said the Chinese delegation was wary of her because of her ties to Israel and her perceived closeness to Washington.

Chinese commentators have also pointed to Grynspan’s Jewish background and relatives in Israel. She would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.

Meanwhile, the New York Times reported this week that the US had indicated it would block Rodrigues-Birkett. The newspaper said the objection related to her statement to the Security Council in 2024 that “a veritable genocide” was taking place in Gaza.

A State Department official told the newspaper that the US wanted a candidate who would pursue substantial reform and streamline the organisation. The Guyanese government has not commented publicly on the report.

China’s mission to the UN and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Tuesday, Rodrigues-Birkett joined Guyanese President Irfaan Ali in New York as he signed the Shield of the Americas security communique with US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

Next steps

The sources heard by SCMP said they expected the race to be discussed during Xi’s visit to Washington this week. They said it was not clear whether Xi would raise it with Trump or leave it to a meeting between Wang and Rubio.

Xi met Trump at the White House on Thursday but did not travel to New York for the General Assembly’s high-level week.

The race remains open, and diplomats said new compromise candidates who are acceptable to all five permanent members could still emerge if the deadlock persists. Some rumoured names could include Emirati diplomat and former UAE permanent representative to the UN Lana Nusseibeh , former Dutch minister Sigrid Kaag, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. None of them has said they would run.

The split among the permanent members has no precedent in recent UN selections, and it risks disrupting the organisation’s leadership if no successor is chosen by the end of the year.

Guterres has made clear he does not intend to stay on in an interim capacity while the council searches for a successor. He has already begun arranging his permanent return to Portugal, according to a UN source.

A fourth straw poll could be held after the high-level week ends on Monday. In 2006 and 2016, the council held its final straw polls in early October.

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong firms are future-proofing business in challenging times
item.description:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.

Swire Coca-Cola’s mainland plants are also using AI-powered robots that can make decisions and adapt to changing operating conditions as they pick and sort heavy, shrink-wrapped loads of drinks from pallets at high speed – a breakthrough in the labour-intensive industry.

These were some of the cutting-edge technologies Swire Coca-Cola had piloted on the mainland to transform its business, while looking to scale them to other provinces and even to Southeast Asia through and in Hong Kong, chief executive Karen So told the South China Morning Post.

“Due to our geographic coverage, we’re exposed to many geopolitical risk factors which we have to manage,” So said, adding that one of the most obvious recent impacts had been rising raw material costs, including those of aluminium and sugar.

“We have to stay very vigilant. Overall, we’ve had to make sure our brand and operations stay relevant in the past few decades to mitigate our external risks,” she said.

The company, which started business in 1965, is now the fifth-largest Coca-Cola bottling partner in the world.

As Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan sets out the blueprint for the city’s economic upgrade, businesses like Swire Coca-Cola are working to future-proof themselves against geopolitical headwinds and compete in an increasingly challenging environment.

City leader John Lee Ka-chiu last week urged Hongkongers and businesses to adopt a long-term vision, saying enterprises had to stay competitive even as the government rolled out measures to cultivate new growth drivers for the city.

“While the government works hard, business operators need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said.

An uneven economic recovery

Hong Kong’s economy has powered ahead in recent months, with merchandise exports hitting record highs on the back of overseas demand for AI-related products.

The government has consequently upgraded its 2026 full-year economic forecast to 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent, from an earlier projection of 2.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent.

Despite the stronger overall performance, streets are dotted with shuttered shops while retailers and restaurant operators continue to struggle.

In a high-profile warning, real estate advocacy group Momentum 107 said the sharp decline in shop values in recent years had rapidly eroded the pool of available capital, undermining confidence in investment and consumption.

It noted that shop prices had fallen by more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, while the overall vacancy rate had reached a 40-year high of 12.5 per cent in late 2025.

The retail and food and catering sectors have also been hit by the continuing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border to spend their leisure time and money.

Meanwhile, inflation has been on the rise.

After war broke out in the Middle East on February 28 and triggered a global oil crisis, the city’s inflation rate jumped from 1.1 per cent year on year in January to 1.7 per cent in February and has hovered above 1.7 per cent as of August.

‘Companies are forced to change’

Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that looking solely at struggling high-street shops overlooked the bigger picture, as high-value sectors such as professional services and finance continued to drive the economy.

However, consumer-facing sectors are undergoing structural shifts as mainland competitors catch up and local consumers spend more elsewhere.

“Hong Kong’s local consumption market is relatively small, so retail and catering suffer from northbound spending and changing habits,” Yuen said.

“Conversely, high-end services, technology and finance are holding up strong. But across the board, businesses rely heavily on international trade and foreign clients, leaving them exposed to global geopolitical frictions.”

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank and executive director of its Public Policy Institute, said companies faced three main challenges – high operating costs, disruption to global supply chains and geopolitical risks and barriers to technological transformation caused by shortages of funding and skilled workers.

He said Hong Kong’s rents, wages and logistics costs were relatively high, placing pressure on companies’ cash flow, while AI was creating another divide.

Large corporations often had money to invest but struggled to integrate new technology with legacy systems and secure cooperation across departments. While smaller businesses could be more agile, they frequently lacked capital and technical expertise.

Shui cited a Productivity Council survey suggesting about 90 per cent of responding companies intended to increase their use of AI.

The problem, he said, was not a lack of interest but uncertainty over how to turn that intention into practical transformation.

“Many people think of technology or AI as something that can help companies reduce costs and save money,” he said.

“But what is more important is how they can use AI to upgrade and transform themselves, innovate their business models or open up new markets.”

Hong Kong appeared to be performing relatively well in adoption.

Shui cited a survey by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology that found that about 72 to 73 per cent of respondents used AI at work daily or weekly, compared with a global average of around 30 per cent.

Another study put AI adoption among Hong Kong firms at about 41 per cent compared with less than 30 per cent in Singapore, he said.

But widespread use did not mean that companies were applying the technology effectively.

Shui said the ideal outcome was “human-machine collaboration,” in which AI performed repetitive research, data processing and preliminary analysis, while employees devoted more time to decision-making and setting the company’s direction.

“If your competitor is already doing this while you are making very limited use of AI, it will be very difficult to catch up,” he said. “This is something that many companies and employees will need to learn.”

Yuen echoed this view, saying that true AI adoption required a complete overhaul of corporate workflows rather than superficial daily tasks.

“The real productivity boost from AI isn’t just using it to write an email or draft a report – it comes when companies reshape their entire workflow from top to bottom,” Yuen said, comparing the current transition with earlier technological shifts such as the invention of the printing press, personal computers and the internet.

“Legacy businesses face a dilemma because changing established processes while serving existing clients carries risk. It could take eight to 10 years for industries to truly integrate AI into their bottom line,” she added.

Shui said Hong Kong needed a coherent AI development blueprint and stronger cooperation between the government, universities and industry.

The planned Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute could provide a platform through which companies test applications, academics provide expertise and the government coordinates resources.

Transform, transform and transform

In Swire Coca-Cola’s case, So said transformation was robust across mindsets, strategies and business practices, pointing out that the 61-year-old business had in recent years embarked on a sweeping revolution.

“The future of our business lies in moving from reactive, manual operations towards proactive, data-driven ecosystems that respond to modern consumer habits,” she said.

The company’s “suggested order” system in Jiangsu province produced 20 per cent higher monthly sales volumes during a year-long pilot that ended earlier this year.

She said it would be gradually rolled out to other markets, but conceded that it would take time for staff to get used to the AI tool.

“Our employees need time to adapt to tools designed to change how they make decisions and approach customers,” So said.

The project forms a key part of a transformation at Swire Coca-Cola, whose franchise bottling and distribution operations reach more than 940 million consumers across the western United States, 11 mainland Chinese provinces and Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taiwan and four Southeast Asian countries.

The company’s transformation became more complicated as it expanded beyond its two main markets – Greater China and the US – into Southeast Asia.

It acquired Coca-Cola bottling businesses in Cambodia in 2022, in Vietnam in 2023 and in Thailand and Laos the following year.

“When we acquired businesses from local operators of Coca-Cola in Southeast Asia, they had their respective enterprise resource planning systems,” So said. “We faced a challenge but also an opportunity to form a consistent operating system.”

Even basic data definitions varied among markets, including what constituted a home market sales channel and how revenue was calculated.

The company had to clean up and standardise the information before it could perform reliable analysis to improve the decision-making process and help salespeople make more targeted calls.

“The data alignment will take two to three years,” So said.

Another tool transferred from the mainland to Southeast Asia was the smart cooler – a drinks refrigerator which customers unlock using an electronic payment code.

Scales and cameras identify which drinks are removed and customers are charged accordingly.

“The solution adapts technology and operating concepts proven in mainland China to the Hong Kong market, which combines digital payment and product-recognition capabilities to offer a seamless cashless purchasing experience,” So said.

In Hong Kong, the group has deployed 120 coolers across a broad mix of locations including sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings.

So said the company aimed to replace traditional vending machines with these smart coolers.

Swire Coca-Cola’s regional expansion has also helped Chinese suppliers go global.
