Baosteel, China’s biggest listed steelmaker and a supplier of aluminium cans to Swire Coca-Cola on the mainland, established a factory in Ho Chi Minh City as the company expanded its presence there.

“It is a win-win situation – we have a stable supply of aluminium cans while Baosteel expands out of China for the first time,” So said.

“Hong Kong is where our ambition is set and our global system is run. A purpose-built solution developed in the Chinese mainland, and now ready to scale across the global markets we serve, shows the super value-added, superconnector role Hong Kong is positioned to play.”

Shui said Hong Kong could also turn the technological rivalry between China and the West into an opportunity by developing a “dual-model” environment in which businesses could access systems from both sides.

“Hong Kong has always been a bridge connecting mainland China with the rest of the world,” he said. “If both systems can be used here, companies coming to Hong Kong can choose the tools that best meet their needs or potentially use both.”

To raise efficiency and reduce manpower, Swire Coca-Cola has teamed up with a Hangzhou-based tech company, Seth Robotics, to develop its own AI-powered solution for its bottling plant in Zhengzhou, Henan province.

The plants boasts the world’s first AI-powered intelligent picking-and-sorting robot, according to So.

Capable of picking 600 pallets of drinks an hour with 100 per cent accuracy in executing orders, and handling loads as heavy as 40kg, the robot works at twice the speed of manual labour.

“Normally after the first hour of work, workers need to take a rest. The robotic deployment will enhance efficiency and minimise any work-related injuries of workers, too,” So said.

She added that Swire Coca-Cola’s technology development also showed what a Hong Kong-headquartered company could contribute to embodied intelligence.

Against the backdrop of these operational investments, the group reported solid financial results for the first half of the year – net profit rose 5.35 per cent to HK$846 million (US$107.9 million) while revenue increased 8.36 per cent to HK$23.3 billion, compared with the same period last year.

Yet, as economist Vera Yuen noted, the rising cost of uncertainty left businesses with little choice but to adapt their models or risk falling behind.

Ultimately, she said, the question was no longer simply whether companies adopted new technology, but whether they could restructure their core operations to deliver genuine value to consumers.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump hails WWII ‘ally’ China as Xi tells of bonds ‘forged in blood and fire’
item.description:
In a surprise nod to shared history, US President Donald Trump called China a World War II ally as he welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday ahead of summit talks.

But the historical reference was far from one-sided, with both leaders repeatedly referring to the joint fight against Japanese aggression as they sought to emphasise the long history of US-China friendship and the need to seek common ground.

“If we focus on our common interests, I’m confident there is much we can achieve,” Trump said in the White House foyer during the state welcome ceremony ahead of formal talks with the Chinese president.
item.content:encoded:
In a surprise nod to shared history, US President Donald Trump called China a World War II ally as he welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday ahead of summit talks.

But the historical reference was far from one-sided, with both leaders repeatedly referring to the joint fight against Japanese aggression as they sought to emphasise the long history of US-China friendship and the need to seek common ground.

“If we focus on our common interests, I’m confident there is much we can achieve,” Trump said in the White House foyer during the state welcome ceremony ahead of formal talks with the Chinese president.

“The pursuit of those common interests has connected our people across the vast oceans, across big tremendous distances, and many differences, and even made us allies in World War II,” he noted.

Trump went on to praise the “brave American pilots” of the Flying Tigers who had volunteered to “fight for China’s survival”, and said that he was happy to work with Xi in the same way.

“Just as our people worked together to win that war, President Xi and I will continue working together to forge a better future for both of our nations,” he said.

The Flying Tigers were American volunteer pilots who came to China in 1941 to fight Japanese forces alongside Chinese troops, before the US formally entered the second world war. They flew fighter missions against Japanese aircraft and helped to defend Chinese cities and supply routes during the conflict.

“They were just unbelievable,” Trump said.

His remarks came days after Japan – now a US treaty ally – renewed its call to remove the “former enemy state” clause from the UN Charter, and after Trump’s talks in New York with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

The clause “must be deleted”, Takaichi told the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22, pointing to a 2005 consensus resolution where world leaders had “resolved” to remove it.

The clause allowed allied states to act against defeated World War II enemy states without UN Security Council approval, but has been declared obsolete by the world body twice - in 1995 and 2005.

While Trump made no direct reference to Japan, Xi was more forthcoming – explicitly naming the country as he underlined China-US friendship forged in “blood and fire” during the war.

“During the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Chinese soldiers and civilians rescued hundreds of American pilots at the cost of hundreds of thousands of Chinese lives,” he said during Thursday’s state dinner.

“Such a friendship, forged in blood and fire, will surely live on through the generations.”

Xi also recalled the wartime “Hump” aerial resupply route over the Himalayas, citing the perilous joint operation as a testament to how the two countries united to sustain Chinese resistance against Japan.

The Hump became a vital lifeline for China after Japanese forces severed the Burma Road in 1942, cutting off military and humanitarian supplies, while Chinese soldiers and civilians helped to rescue hundreds of American pilots forced down along the route.

That cooperation came at a heavy cost for China, which suffered enormous civilian losses during the war, Xi noted.

It was the second time Xi had drawn on their shared history within hours. During the state welcome ceremony in the morning, he noted how soldiers on both sides had “fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression”

“[The] Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people,” he asserted.

The timing of the remark was particularly sensitive, given Japan’s stepped-up calls to remove the UN “enemy state” clause following its recent invocation by Chinese and Russian officials as tensions with Tokyo escalate.

Reacting to Takaichi’s speech at the General Assembly, the Chinese foreign ministry said on Wednesday that the clauses were “a legal mechanism in the UN Charter. For 81 years, these clauses have served to prevent the resurgence of fascism and militarism and defend the post-war international order. They are still relevant today.”

Trump’s use of the word “allies” in describing past US-China cooperation against Japan caused unease among Japanese media.

The Japan Times, for example, said the remarks were “likely to raise eyebrows in Tokyo, a US ally currently embroiled in a festering dispute with Beijing and facing pressure from Trump on both trade and defence issues”.

China-Japan ties have been marked by recurring tensions over Japan’s wartime occupation and atrocities in China, as well as disputes over Tokyo’s handling of that history.

Relations sharply deteriorated last year after Takaichi said that a Taiwan contingency could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan, justifying a military response. Beijing demanded an apology and imposed a slew of retaliatory measures, including curbs on rare earth exports.

Takaichi met Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 22, just ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington. According to NHK News, she told Trump that she wanted to “seize the opportunity to demonstrate to the world” the strength of the US-Japan alliance.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

In Washington, Xi also highlighted the shared economic and cultural history of the two nations, tracing the relationship to America’s earliest years.

After the US gained independence, it “turned its eyes to China”, Xi said in his dinner address. The two countries began trading, he said, “exchanging goods to meet each other’s needs and draw on our complementary strengths”.

George Washington, he noted, had personally acquired a large collection of Chinese porcelain.

Xi then fast-forwarded to 1971, when “ping pong diplomacy” and the “political wisdom embodied in a small ball moving the globe” helped Mao Zedong, founder of the People’s Republic of China, and then-US president Richard Nixon open the door to rapprochement.

The redwoods Nixon later sent as a state gift “took root in Zhejiang province, where I worked for several years”, Xi added.

Trump’s speech was similarly filled with historical references to US-China friendship, as the gala dinner capped a day of pageantry, politics and protocol.

“President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.

“Together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations.”

Trump invoked figures and events ranging from Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of modern China, to America’s declaration of freedom 250 years ago.

“Long ago, European explorers first discovered the American continent as they searched for a new way to reach China in the East,” Trump said, as he spoke about the first formal Chinese delegation to travel to the US and China’s first state dinner in Washington.

Despite the early historical reflections, including one about the first trade ships arriving on the banks of the Pearl River from New York, Trump took a midpoint detour to focus on the White House ballroom renovations – a frequent talking point for the president.

Going admittedly “off script”, Trump invited guests in the East Room to take a look at the new White House ballroom “in honour of President Xi and Madame Peng”, despite the project still being under construction.

The new ballroom would host more than 1,000 people, substantially more than the East Room, Trump said, claiming US presidents had wanted this for more than 150 years.

Trump then returned to the symbolism, gifting Xi a sculpture of a bald eagle that he said was made by an American artist and designed by him and the first lady, Melania Trump.

“The bald eagle is a national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America, and we hope it will find a nice place, a wonderful place in Beijing,” Trump added.

The bald eagle has been featured on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. It was officially designated the national bird of the US when Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden signed an act of Congress into law in December 2024.

In his closing remarks, Trump returned to history, referencing America’s 250th anniversary, marked on July 4 this year.

He raised a toast to his Chinese counterpart and his wife, as well as the long relationship between China and America that had bridged “thousands of miles and spanned hundreds of years”.

“May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace, and success,” Trump said.

The speeches were made to a packed room of invitees, including Chinese and US government officials, American business leaders and some Supreme Court justices.

Several prominent American CEOs made the guest list, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk, but no Chinese business leaders were present.

This stood in stark contrast to the Beijing summit in May, when Trump brought a delegation of nearly 20 top executives, many of whom were spotted at the state banquet hosted by Xi.

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
item.description:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.
item.content:encoded:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.

Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya.

The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.

The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism.

Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record.

Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia.

Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin.

Misbehaving tourists

Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners.

But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them.

Each post gets shared and reshared until the obvious disrespect for a proud local culture starts to sour public opinion on the costs of welcoming millions of strangers every year.

“Thai people are pragmatic. We do like the money [tourism brings],” said Voranai Vanijaka, a prominent political and social commentator. “But at the same time, we are highly nationalistic and we don’t like tourists acting the fool.”

This year alone, tourists have been caught performing sex acts in public, assaulting locals, trespassing on private property and vandalising local landmarks. Recent crackdowns have also revealed dozens of bars and restaurants run by foreigners but masquerading as Thai-owned enterprises.

Other crimes are far more grave. In June, Australian national Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested on suspicion of murdering a teenage Thai girl, stuffing her body into a suitcase and disposing of it in the undergrowth near Pattaya.

Authorities have separately uncovered Chinese and Korean cyberscam operators holed up in luxury villas, an Indian national flaunting firearms on social media and a steady stream of British cannabis mules.

All the while, public attitudes against foreigners have been hardening – a sentiment Voranai said had also been fuelled by global nativist trends, nationalism stirred up by the recent border conflict with Cambodia and grievances over foreign nationals buying up land and businesses.

“There is an anti-foreigner, anti-immigrant feeling sweeping the world; it’s not just in Thailand,” he said, describing a “mood and tone” within which every viral episode of misbehaviour now played out, and a “lower tolerance” for such actions.

The steady drumbeat of bad news pushed Thailand to end its 60-day visa-free stays for tourists from September 15. Days later, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters he thought misbehaving foreigners had “gone too far”.

Not for the first time, Thailand has said it will step back from playing the numbers game to focus on attracting fewer, higher-spending tourists instead.

Officials describe 2027 as “the year of transformation”, aiming to attract wealthier travellers willing to stay a week or two at a time.

A proposed flat fee of 450 baht (US$13.50) on all foreign visitors to fund tourism infrastructure upgrades is also being actively considered.

But this soul-searching over who Thailand wants to welcome, and for how long, comes as hotel bookings during the current low season have disappointed and as travellers appear to be waiting until the last minute to book their stays in the crucial high season that begins in November.

On the upside, Thai tourism authorities are anticipating 200,000 Chinese tourist arrivals during next month’s “golden week” holiday from October 1 to 7, just as a the baht’s recent retreat is offering travellers better value.

Against this uncertain backdrop, Charoon’s crocodile farm has enjoyed something of social media-spurred revival.

In its 1980s heyday, when his father welcomed dignitaries including Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, the business made headlines for encounters with reptiles that visitors elsewhere might only see behind glass.

But as the novelty of live-animal shows began to wear off and tastes changed, the zoo’s weekday crowds thinned to a trickle.

Then, in late August, a TikTok video showing a single visitor sitting alone in the stands at one of the zoo’s elephant shows found an audience all of its own, garnering more than 1 million likes and sending a flood of visitors streaming back through gates.

“I was shocked. I didn’t expect that. I never thought one video could communicate to so many people,” Charoon said.

“People are coming in their thousands. I just hope they keep coming.”

Show respect, or go

Thailand is far from alone in pausing to reconsider its relationship with visitors.

In Indonesia’s Bali, a foreign-led running club accused of barring locals from taking part suspended operations this summer; in Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks held a violent protest outside a newly opened Jewish community centre known as a Chabad house last month, questioning its legality; and in Vietnam, authorities have vowed zero tolerance for foreign misconduct after recent drunken rampages and a deadly shooting linked to foreign nationals.

Social media, as ever, amplifies both the insults delivered and how they are received.

One Phuket business owner, who asked not to be named to protect his livelihood, told This Week in Asia that the types of tourists now visiting Thailand were more entitled, demanding unreasonable discounts and firing off insults at the slightest whiff of not getting their own way.

“I don’t think Thais are xenophobic,” he said. “But my mindset has changed, like a lot of people on Phuket. Customers are customers, but if they’re not nice and don’t respect the culture and the people, we are happy to see them go.”

This change in public sentiment appears to have influenced the government’s decision to halve the 60-day visa free-entry. It has also produced unusually blunt warnings from ministers who normally pull their punches when addressing foreign embassies.

In August, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told the Chinese ambassador to “come out and explain” when sensitive issues arise “instead of speaking only to protect Chinese interests” – remarks that followed a viral confrontation between Chinese passengers and Thai officials at Bangkok’s main airport.

His comments also came amid mounting evidence of Chinese nationals illegally owning land and companies in Thailand, in some cases via officials bribed with as little as 500 baht to issue fraudulent birth certificates conferring land-ownership rights.

A small but vocal protest movement against official corruption and the influence of so-called grey money has since emerged, fronted by veteran conservative agitator Sondhi Limthongkul, who has rallied tens of thousands to take to the streets in the past.

Prime Minister Anutin, who himself rode a wave of nationalist sentiment to victory in February’s election, has responded to the backlash by fast-tracking deportations of foreign criminals and opening a wider investigation into “nominee” arrangements that allow foreign business owners to hide behind Thais.

Chinese, French, British, Indian and Russian nationals have all come under scrutiny, but it has been Israeli nationals – many of them military-aged and arriving in the wake of the war in Gaza – who have attracted the most intense attention, accused of building extensive “nominee”-business networks across southern Thai islands and of operating an illegal cemetery in Chachoengsao province.

“This has gone too far,” Anutin told officials on September 17 in response to the outrage.

“If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that. We have no objection whatsoever,” he said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here.”

Anutin’s point man on the “nominee” scandal, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee, has since said he is investigating several Chabad houses across the country, warning that any found to have been built unlawfully could be torn down.

Following a meeting with Thailand’s foreign minister earlier this month, Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm told local media that bad behaviour was not unique to citizens of her country, adding that Hebrew-language pre-departure awareness campaigns were being introduced outlining Thai laws and cultural norms.

Nationalist commentators with large online followings have seized upon the anti-Israeli rhetoric, some veering into outright antisemitism.

“There is a risk of this getting out of hand,” Voranai said, referring to growing anti-Israeli “paranoia” stoked by hardline conservatives chasing clicks and the political spotlight.

Yet he doubts the swirling public anger will cost Anutin’s government much in the long run.

“There is no risk to the government at all – except for bad press, which they don’t care about,” Voranai said. “Nor should they, they hold all the power and they can just ride it out.”

Meet the neighbours

Amid the blizzard of bad publicity, some are determined to build bridges between foreigners and their Thai hosts.

John Ho, who was born and raised in Hong Kong but swapped a career in hospitality for a new life in Chiang Mai with his Thai wife a decade ago, this month launched CosmoLocal CNX – a government-backed “pop-up village” offering workshops, talks and communal meals to draw the Thai city’s digital-nomad population into closer contact with their Thai neighbours.

“There’s a transitional period where you’re travelling as a tourist, when you may not care that much about the local culture and language,” Ho said.

“But then, if you want to stay longer and set up a base, it naturally comes to a question of: ‘OK, let’s make friends’. It’s better to learn some Thai, and learn some of the laws around business and work.”

His pop-up, which offers discounted tickets for Thai attendees to keep it accessible, trades on Chiang Mai’s slower pace of life, distinctive northern Lanna culture and small-town feel – qualities that have attracted legions of remote workers since the pandemic.

It is a world away from the raucous party scene of Thailand’s southern islands, where many of the recent cultural clashes have occurred.

“We see the tensions,” Ho said. “But the majority of nomads do care – maybe they need more facilitation to meet the locals. This is the first attempt to do that.”

As for the seemingly endless churn of viral confrontations between Thais and foreigners?

“News cycles are news cycles,” Ho said. “I think a lot of it is out of proportion. Everyone in Thailand welcomes foreigners.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Pakistan’s endless war on militants fails to break the cycle
item.description:
For over two decades, Pakistan has waged countless counterterrorism campaigns against Taliban and Baloch insurgents in its western regions bordering Afghanistan and Iran, yet remains mired in a cycle of violence it cannot break.

Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility.

Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings.
item.content:encoded:
For over two decades, Pakistan has waged countless counterterrorism campaigns against Taliban and Baloch insurgents in its western regions bordering Afghanistan and Iran, yet remains mired in a cycle of violence it cannot break.

Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility.

Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings.

Pakistan’s military regularly hails the success of its counterterrorism operations, touting the eradication of hundreds of perpetrators each month. Its press releases often read like scoreboards, listing the number of insurgents “sent to hell” – with only a handful surviving to be interrogated.

Yet these tactical victories have not translated into the strategic success Islamabad has long yearned for, analysts say.

“Force alone won’t help in curbing security issues long term,” said Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “Force will continue to meet force, keeping the loop alive. There has to be some political solution and dialogue.”

Such a solution would not appear overnight, she said, but without one – or at least a viable strategy to combat insurgency – Pakistan faced the prospect of continued instability deterring foreign investment, not least in its critical minerals sector.

Border escalations

Armed groups have long exploited the porous Pakistan-Afghanistan border to seek sanctuary, smuggle goods and provide logistical support.

In recent years, months-long terrorist campaigns have driven up casualty numbers and prompted Pakistan to launch retaliatory air strikes against insurgents based in eastern Afghanistan.

The latest came on Monday, when military jets struck Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) “terrorist camps and safe havens” in Afghanistan’s Paktika and Kunar provinces, killing 28 militants, Pakistan’s information ministry said, including what it said were suicide bombers in training.

Monday’s air strikes followed an assault on a mosque on September 18 that left at least 31 people dead and more than 100 injured at a police compound in the northwestern town of Kohat, Pakistan.

Zabihullah Mujahid, chief spokesman for Afghanistan’s Taliban regime, has repeatedly denied the existence of terrorist camps in his country and claimed in a statement that Pakistan’s air strikes killed three civilians.

After he vowed revenge, border skirmishes intensified, culminating on Thursday in eight “rudimentary” drones being launched from Afghan territory into Pakistani airspace, security officials said. All were shot down, four of them near Kohat.

Mujahid again denied responsibility for the drone incursions, though Pakistani officials view them as further evidence that Kabul is actively supporting the TTP, not merely tolerating its presence.

Pakistan retaliated in the early hours of Thursday with “precision aerial and drone strikes” on 10 locations in Afghanistan “used for launching and storing these drones”, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar announced in a social media post.

Officials in Islamabad have made clear they believe the Taliban government in Kabul has been feigning interest in recent diplomatic efforts by China, Turkey and Qatar to de-escalate tensions, following a previous cycle of insurgent violence that ended with Pakistan carrying out cross-border air strikes in June.

At a meeting in Belarus this summer, officials discussed potential compromises, including a joint mechanism to monitor the cross-border movement of TTP militants, according to Islamabad-based security analyst Iftikhar Firdous, who disclosed details of the talks in a social media post on September 16.

The meeting reportedly failed to produce a breakthrough because Kabul refused to compel the TTP to halt its attacks on Pakistan or relocate militants away from the border.

The day before the Kohat attack, Qatar’s National Security Council deputy secretary general Hamad Khamis al-Kubaisi and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın had visited Kabul in a renewed attempt to broker further talks between Afghan and Pakistani officials.

Analysts see the repeated cycles of violence as proof that Islamabad’s largely reactive approach to counterterrorism, built around retaliatory counter-attacks, is not working.

Riccardo Valle, a researcher tracking militancy across South and Central Asia, called the strategy “incomplete and limited”.

Local grievances and poor governance constrained the effectiveness of counterterrorism operations in violence-hit areas, he said, adding that local security forces in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan – especially the police – were ill-equipped to confront “full-fledged insurgencies”.

The reactive, rather than preventive, nature of intelligence-based operations is another limiting factor, according to Valle.

“Thus, tactical success cannot compensate for a broader strategic deficiency, which fuels a circle of instability” in the affected provinces, he said, with the twin insurgencies becoming a “multigenerational issue”, drawing in new cohorts of young militants.

As such, Valle said a holistic approach that accounted for both Pakistan’s domestic concerns and the wider conflict’s international dimensions would be essential.

Converging insurgencies

Signs have also emerged of increasing collaboration between the radical Islamist TTP and ethno-nationalist Baloch separatist groups in Balochistan.

The vast and sparsely populated province, bordering southern Afghanistan and eastern Iran, recorded a marked rise in attacks over the summer. In one instance this July, the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army carried out separate attacks in the province’s Pishin and Ziarat districts within hours of each other.

Muhammad Faisal, a South Asia security researcher based at the University of Technology Sydney, said tactical coordination between the TTP and Baloch insurgents was “increasingly documented”, including reports of joint training and logistical links.

However, he doubts this will amount to a “durable strategic coalition” given the two groups’ different ideologies and aims – the TTP seeks to overthrow the government of Pakistan and establish an Islamist political order, while Baloch groups are more concerned with achieving independence.

Linguistic, cultural and geographic differences further limit each group’s ability to operate in the other’s core territory, likely confining cooperation to an exchange of tactics and targets, according to Faisal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan’s ties with Iran have improved since the two countries exchanged air strikes against militants based on the other’s soil in January 2024.

Islamabad helped broker talks earlier this year aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, but Faisal said that widening conflict and residual Pakistan-Iran mistrust would continue to hamstring relations.

Pakistan has also accused India, with which it fought a brief air war in May last year, of covertly supporting Baloch separatists as proxies.

However, Faisal said Islamabad would be better off closely monitoring the separatist networks involved instead of treating every one of their attacks as proof of foreign backing.

The more immediate danger was the effect the Iran conflict might have on border security if it created a power vacuum filled with more militancy and foreign intelligence operatives, he said.

“This is a serious security risk, but one best managed through intelligence cooperation and sustained diplomacy,” Faisal added.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia faces a false binary in US-China mineral trade
item.description:
Critical minerals have become a recurring source of friction in international diplomacy, with China’s dominance in the sector and US efforts to build alternative supply chains raising concerns that Southeast Asian countries may be forced to choose between the two powers.

But this is a false choice. As important exporters of rare earth elements, Southeast Asian countries have leverage of their own and can use intensifying competition to diversify partnerships and capture more of the value chain at home.

The recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States ended with a chairman’s declaration rather than a joint statement, underscoring the lack of unanimity. China objected to, among other things, calls to eliminate “non‑market policies” and ensure smooth global supply chains for vital goods, including critical minerals.
item.content:encoded:
Critical minerals have become a recurring source of friction in international diplomacy, with China’s dominance in the sector and US efforts to build alternative supply chains raising concerns that Southeast Asian countries may be forced to choose between the two powers.

But this is a false choice. As important exporters of rare earth elements, Southeast Asian countries have leverage of their own and can use intensifying competition to diversify partnerships and capture more of the value chain at home.

The recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States ended with a chairman’s declaration rather than a joint statement, underscoring the lack of unanimity. China objected to, among other things, calls to eliminate “non‑market policies” and ensure smooth global supply chains for vital goods, including critical minerals.

The disagreement comes amid China’s tightening controls over rare earth elements (REEs), first introduced in April 2025 in retaliation for US tariffs and export controls. In October it went further, extending licensing requirements to certain foreign-made products containing at least 0.1 per cent Chinese-origin controlled REEs or using specified Chinese rare earth technologies. These measures were subsequently suspended until November this year, while the April 2025 controls remain.

Although Beijing has sought to reassure non-US importers that normal commercial trade will continue, such controls inevitably increase costs and uncertainty for firms dependent on Chinese rare earths, processing and magnets.

At the same time, a number of East Asian economies have joined Pax Silica and other US-supported efforts to build more resilient critical-mineral and technology supply chains. Has this increased pressure on them to choose between China-centred and US-backed supply chains? Given the region’s economic geography and dense webs of trade, few can afford such a binary choice.

In the case of critical minerals, however, such concerns about being forced to choose need to be put into context.

First of all, China’s present dominance in REEs stems from a long process of industrial development, not a strategy originally conceived to give Beijing a geopolitical weapon. The industry dates to the late 1950s. As applications expanded across metallurgy, petrochemicals, glass and ceramics, agriculture and equipment manufacturing, REEs were incorporated into national research and development programmes in 1986. In January 1991, the State Council issued a circular to curb rampant illegal mining under a national licensing regime, strengthen regulation and consolidate a fragmented industry.

REEs were thus initially treated as industrial resources for domestic use and export; they were not designed to be used as geopolitical instruments. Yet decades of investment and capability-building have given China considerable leverage within global REE supply chains. Amid intensifying Sino-US competition, these accumulated advantages have acquired strategic significance – hence the observation by Belgian political scientist Victor de Decker that, over REEs and other minerals deemed critical by the US, “Beijing is now mirroring Washington’s own semiconductor export control regime almost to the letter”.

For Beijing and Washington, the legitimacy of their export controls relies partly on the military applications of dual‑use materials and technologies, but their effectiveness is also limited. Curbing supply incentivises investment in alternatives, eroding the restricting country’s credibility and long‑term competitiveness as a supplier. Neither side can fully control an interdependent supply chain – midstream producers rely on downstream consumers abroad, while end users can reduce dependence through alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling.

This interdependence is particularly relevant to Southeast Asia. Despite its dominance of REE extraction and processing, China is a net importer of raw REEs, including substantial supplies from the region. In 2024, Myanmar supplied 34.3 per cent of China’s REE imports, Malaysia contributed 10.6 per cent and Laos 8.3 per cent. Together, they accounted for over half of China’s total imports.

Southeast Asia will not remain a mere supplier of raw materials, however. Malaysia already hosts the most commercially significant rare earth separation facility outside China, with much of its feedstock supplied from Lynas’s Mount Weld mine in Western Australia. The facility’s outputs are used in products ranging from lamps to semiconductors, a sector where Malaysia has decades of experience. It is only a matter of time before other regional ore exporters move into separation and other downstream applications.

Indonesia is another case in point. In recent years, it has banned the export of unprocessed minerals like nickel, requiring producers to invest in processing facilities to add value before export. While this builds on earlier practices, its character also aligns with the industrial policies adopted by China, the US and others at comparable stages of technological development.

As such, the proverbial choice between aligning with China or joining the US‑led Pax Silica is largely rhetorical for Southeast Asia. Both countries are interested in accessing Southeast Asian supplies of raw REEs on the basis of cost, not for the lack of material availability elsewhere, including within their own countries.

The more consequential question for Southeast Asian exporters is how competition over critical minerals can help them diversify into more higher-value activities. The real measure of competing partnerships should therefore be what China, the US and other partners contribute to Southeast Asian efforts to move up the value chain. This includes investments in processing and refining, technology and skills transfer, and stronger linkages to downstream manufacturing.

Seen in this context, the emerging competition is not just over who secures Southeast Asia’s minerals, but over who offers a more credible pathway from resource supplier to higher-value producer. To address societal concerns that REE refining is detrimental to the environment, the challenge is committing to importing the most environmentally-friendly processing technologies and rigorously enforcing standards on foreign corporate practices.

In the final analysis, access to critical minerals is likely to remain high on the regional agenda. But this is also the area in which Southeast Asian REE exporters can exercise a certain level of agency.

China’s dominance of REE processing gives it considerable leverage, but this should also not be overstated. Excessive restrictions incentivise alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling. Between China and the US, the likely outcome is a shifting balance between interdependence and diversification, not a full decoupling.

For Southeast Asia, the perceived binary choice between the two powers is a false one: all countries face the same task of adjusting their policies within a shared set of mineral‑industry dynamics among producers, processors and consumers.

Zha Daojiong is a Visiting Senior Fellow with ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is also Professor of International Political Economy at the School of International Studies, Peking University. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] India’s ‘cockroach’ movement targets election chief in political pivot
item.description:
India’s “cockroach” youth movement is testing whether it can turn anger over education and jobs into a broader challenge to the country’s political establishment, two months after its protests helped force an education minister to resign over alleged entrance exam leaks.

Its latest target is another powerful institution: the country’s election watchdog. The shift marks a transition for the movement from high-profile demonstrations in New Delhi to a more diffuse campaign of school audits, meetings with authorities and demands for electoral reform.

Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Thursday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after a local newspaper reported allegations that his handling of voter-list revisions could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in India’s electoral process.
item.content:encoded:
India’s “cockroach” youth movement is testing whether it can turn anger over education and jobs into a broader challenge to the country’s political establishment, two months after its protests helped force an education minister to resign over alleged entrance exam leaks.

Its latest target is another powerful institution: the country’s election watchdog. The shift marks a transition for the movement from high-profile demonstrations in New Delhi to a more diffuse campaign of school audits, meetings with authorities and demands for electoral reform.

Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Thursday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after a local newspaper reported allegations that his handling of voter-list revisions could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in India’s electoral process.

The Indian Express reported on Wednesday that two election commissioners had raised questions or expressed concern to Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, mostly over the process of updating voter lists that began last year.

The report alleged that Kumar repeatedly bypassed the two other election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi – who had formally raised objections – making critical decisions regarding voter lists, registration and deletions without their knowledge or consent.

The dispute has heightened scrutiny of a large-scale exercise to revise electoral rolls, with critics questioning whether voters excluded from draft lists will have adequate safeguards and opportunities to challenge their removal.

“When millions of names can disappear from draft rolls, the burden is on the commission to establish that every exclusion is lawful, transparent and subject to meaningful reviews,” said CJP National Convenor Abhijeet Dipke.

If Kumar did not resign by Saturday, the CJP would launch a nationwide protest, Dipke said.

Anjali, a national executive member of the All India Students Association, said 300 to 400 young people representing different backgrounds had already launched protests demanding Kumar’s resignation.

“We believe this [the chief election commissioner’s actions] weakens democracy to the core. So along with civil society and concerned citizens, we have staged a protest at Jantar Mantar,” she said, referring to the venue in the capital that was the focal point for earlier demonstrations. She added that they had been detained by the police.

The CJP began in May as a satirical online campaign after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant referred to unemployed young people as “cockroaches”. It then turned its attention to alleged irregularities in the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) – a nationwide medical examination – and other grievances with the education system.

Its protests at Jantar Mantar in Delhi helped force the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July. But the movement has since shifted from high-decibel demonstrations in the capital to less prominent school audits and meetings with authorities across at least six states.

The non-political movement, which has given voice to middle-class anxieties over opportunities for young people, highlights a growing challenge for political leaders trying to respond to one of the largest sections of India’s electorate.

“There is a definite Generation Z factor coming up. That Generation Z factor is largely anti-establishment,” said Yashwant Deshmukh, an independent political commentator and founder of C-Voter, a public opinion research firm.

The younger generation’s grievances had exposed a cross-party challenge that all political parties were struggling with, Deshmukh said: connecting with young people’s hearts and minds.

India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is now in its third successive term – this time at the head of a multiparty coalition – has gradually recovered ground in state elections after losing its outright majority in 2024.

The BJP’s dominance has only grown amid a fragmented opposition led by the Congress party, which held sway for decades following India’s independence in 1947.

Analysts say it is too early to predict whether the cockroach movement could trigger broader political changes ahead of a string of elections next year in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat.

“It is going to create problems for anybody in power in those states. It is not one-way traffic,” Deshmukh said, referring to the BJP’s political fortunes.

On Friday, Congress was set to stage protest marches at state election offices across India to demand Kumar’s arrest.

“No matter what narrative is created by the opposition and Congress, eventually it will come down to what kind of party infrastructure they have to turn that traction from Gen Z into votes against the BJP,” Deshmukh added.

Young voters’ challenge

The cockroach movement’s expansion beyond education has coincided with what independent political commentator Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay described as a change in India’s “political drift”.

Demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner was likely to catalyse that change further, Mukhopadhyay said.

“What has happened is that the movement has triggered the erasure of fear from the minds of youngsters,” he said, pointing to a protest against the gang-rape of a 17-year-old girl on Thursday by students from Lady Shri Ram College for Women in Delhi as an example.

But Mukhopadhyay warned that the protests did not mean the BJP was facing an electoral rout, saying next year’s state elections would provide a clearer test of its popularity.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of Congress has also been seeking to connect with Gen Z voters through a nationwide student outreach programme called Chhatron Ki Goonj (Echo of Students), aimed at amplifying grievances over the education and examination systems.

The initiative had given Gandhi greater credibility among young people, Mukhopadhyay said.

Meanwhile, a high-powered panel led by technology entrepreneur Nandan Nilekani is examining structural reforms to the NEET.

The panel was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi after weeks of protests against alleged irregularities in the exam, which culminated in Pradhan’s resignation and the government agreeing to several of the movement’s demands. Its report is due by the end of this month.

Suhruda Dasyam, who graduated from the London School of Economics in December and currently works in London, said she took part in solidarity protests in the city in July to express her support for the movement.

“I think there is a larger issue that needs to be addressed. People are unemployed and struggling to get by. I sought education in a country that is not mine because I feel that I don’t have the same opportunities in India,” she said. “I feel so many people share the same sentiment. I just hope that we can get there some day.”

Dasyam said the movement had not lost momentum, although its focus had shifted since Pradhan’s resignation.

The cockroach movement had also been trying to build a presence beyond the capital, with its leaders personally inspecting facilities in government schools across different states, said Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator.

“Their network is growing well. What they have not been able to do is attract more people to do the job in a decentralised way,” he said, pointing out that visiting India’s roughly 1 million state schools would be physically impossible without support from other groups.

The audits had struggled to capture national attention, partly because the CJP’s founders had refused to align with any political party, reducing local media interest, Ramaswamy said.

Pradhan’s resignation also appeared to reduce the movement’s momentum, he added, as many young supporters felt the job was done.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ short-lived Discord ban exposes cracks in online safety strategy
item.description:
The Philippines’ decision to block messaging platform Discord for less than a day following a series of school shootings has raised questions about the government’s response to child safety online, with analysts describing the move as a show of regulatory muscle that did little to address underlying problems.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced on Thursday that it had lifted the ban after what officials described as successful negotiations with Discord over compliance with child safety measures.

The government’s action came days after a shooting on September 18 at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, where a student opened fire on classmates, killing two students and himself, and injuring eight others.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ decision to block messaging platform Discord for less than a day following a series of school shootings has raised questions about the government’s response to child safety online, with analysts describing the move as a show of regulatory muscle that did little to address underlying problems.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced on Thursday that it had lifted the ban after what officials described as successful negotiations with Discord over compliance with child safety measures.

The government’s action came days after a shooting on September 18 at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, where a student opened fire on classmates, killing two students and himself, and injuring eight others.

Authorities said they were investigating whether the student had been influenced by online conversations, while the government also raised concerns about online communities being used to groom or radicalise minors and potentially encourage real-world violence.

On Wednesday, the government gave Discord and Reddit 24 hours to establish a physical office or assign a resident agent, alongside detailed explanations of their safety protocols, rapid-response mechanisms and age-assurance systems.

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre (CICC) said Discord had servers associated with nihilistic violent extremism and grooming, but stopped short of blaming either Discord or Reddit for the recent shootings.

Reddit was given an extension to comply, while Discord was blocked after failing to meet the government’s deadline.

‘Performative’ governance?

The move drew widespread public criticism, as it disrupted communications for enterprises, workers and students who use the platform.

“People use Discord for work meetings, school and running small businesses. Block it and they all get hit, while bad actors just move to another app,” Filipino actor Paulo Avelino wrote on social media. “Child safety matters. So fix the actual problem, not just the easiest target.”

“We now live in a world of super powerful AI swarms,” said Carl Javier, executive director of ethics organisation Data and AI Ethics PH, describing their ability to “hack into government systems and cause catastrophic harm to key digital infrastructure”.

“And the department that wants to be at the head of dealing with these threats … does not know how Discord works?”

The CICC apologised for the inconvenience caused by the hours-long ban.

“Please don’t worry, as we are already working to resolve everything,” Renato Paraiso, undersecretary and executive director of the CICC, said at a press conference.

The CICC was also responsible for banning the video game GoreBox, which was part of officials’ investigation into a school shooting in Tacloban City in June.

Beyond the immediate disruption, digital rights and child safety advocates said the incident highlighted a lack of foresight in creating coherent and feasible regulatory systems.

“When access to a platform can disappear abruptly, the consequences reach far beyond a single app,” volunteer-led civic technology initiative BetterGov said in a petition to protect digital democracy. “Work can be interrupted, learning disrupted and communities cut off. People deserve to know who made the decision, what evidence supports it, how long it will last and how it can be challenged.”

The government likely banned Discord to flex its regulatory muscle and look like it was tackling online harm, but the decision ultimately proved to be “careless”, said Jason Torres, a tech consultant and founder of BetterGov.

“I don’t think they properly consulted the people affected. We use Discord to organise volunteers and get work done. Others depend on it for school and income. You can’t ignore that impact just because you want a platform’s attention,” Torres said.

Javier shared similar views regarding the government’s approach.

“Performative governance allows them to seem like they are taking steps to ‘protect us’, threatening bans on platforms when these don’t actually fix the root causes of the problems,” Javier said.

Torres added that the incident showed the Philippines’ lack of capacity to address online harm properly, despite rising cases.

Ysrael Diloy, a child protection specialist at the Manila-based non-profit organisation Stairway Foundation, said the “more useful way of looking at this is not whether a 24-hour directive by itself inspires trust, but whether we are developing a coherent, realistic and sustainable system for holding platforms accountable”.

The CICC’s requirement for platforms to designate local representation was legitimate, Diloy said.

“When there is an immediate threat to a child – sexual exploitation, grooming, a credible threat of violence or digital evidence that needs to be preserved – authorities should not have to spend critical time figuring out whom to contact in another jurisdiction,” he said. “However, regulatory demands also have to be realistic and feasible.”

Setting up in a new physical office within a 24-hour time frame was unrealistic, Diloy said, even with the alternative of appointing a local representative.

“That naturally raises an important question: why 24 hours, and what exactly is expected to be realistically accomplished within that period?”

Constitutional questions

Digital creators and advocates said targeting platforms such as Discord and Reddit also raised concerns over free and protected speech.

“Blanket blocking raises constitutional questions, especially when the legal basis and due process are unclear,” Torres said.

“When I was undersecretary of the DICT … pressures were coming in from Congress for us to block websites, apps, and even to take down critics’ posts,” former DICT Undersecretary Jeffrey Ian Dy told ABS-CBN News on Friday.

“But we didn’t do it because, number one, it is unconstitutional. There was already a ruling by the Supreme Court that there shouldn’t be unilateral blocking of any websites except those that are clearly defined to be blockable under the law,” Dy added. “Last time I checked, we’re still a democracy so they should work within the boundaries of the law.”

Speaking on a podcast hosted by tech founder Ann Cuisia on Thursday, Dy accused Congress of holding the DICT’s budget hostage in exchange for action against posts critical of public officials.

He said he suspected the issue of child safety was being “used” by congressmen as a smokescreen to get negative posts about themselves taken down.

“If you look at the transcripts of Congress hearings regarding DICT’s budget. Congressmen were asking why DICT was unable to take down posts negative to them … They’re talking about child safety and ‘fake news,’” Dy said.

“The real reason why our politicians want to regulate social media is that they can’t take the heat,” Carlo Ople, founder of Creators Against Corruption, posted on social media.

“They want the people who are talking about their alleged corruption and alleged illegal activities to be silenced. This is a question about free speech, more than anything else.”

While the intention of the Discord ban might not have been to stifle free expression, Javier said it ran counter to previous court rulings.

“It runs over due process, and whether they intended it or not, if allowed to stand it would’ve set a dangerous precedent,” Javier said. “At present, the DICT and CICC continue to invoke ‘protecting children’ as their motivation. But they need to balance that with defending our rights as well.”

Diloy said authorities could earn the public’s trust by carrying out reforms, not by how quickly they acted after an incident.

“It is whether we see a sustained, technically informed and evidence-based approach – one that invests in prevention, investigation, child protection services, regulatory capacity and meaningful engagement with technology companies,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Taiwan’s coastguard vessel transfer to the Philippines has sparked a double outcry
item.description:
Taiwan’s transfer of a former coastguard vessel to the Philippines has triggered a dual controversy – raising concerns over the interests of Taiwanese fishermen and prompting strong criticism from Beijing.

The matter centres on a 61-metre (200-foot) retired cutter handed over to the Philippine Coast Guard through a non-governmental organisation on Monday, as Taipei and Manila expand practical maritime cooperation despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties.

Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) has condemned the move, accusing the island’s ruling party of ignoring infringements by Japan and the Philippines as they pursue maritime delimitation talks.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan’s transfer of a former coastguard vessel to the Philippines has triggered a dual controversy – raising concerns over the interests of Taiwanese fishermen and prompting strong criticism from Beijing.

The matter centres on a 61-metre (200-foot) retired cutter handed over to the Philippine Coast Guard through a non-governmental organisation on Monday, as Taipei and Manila expand practical maritime cooperation despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties.

Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) has condemned the move, accusing the island’s ruling party of ignoring infringements by Japan and the Philippines as they pursue maritime delimitation talks.

The Democratic Progressive Party had failed to protect the interests of the people of Taiwan and was instead “helping an evildoer do evil”, TAO spokeswoman Zhu Fenglian said on Wednesday.

The authorities’ conduct had increased the risk of harm to the interests of Taiwanese fishermen, she warned, describing the DPP’s action as “despicable”.

On Thursday, Taiwan’s cabinet-level Ocean Affairs Council defended the donation, with minister Kuan Bi-ling saying it was intended to strengthen regional maritime safety.

“The donation agreement contains comprehensive safeguards, explicitly stipulating that the donated vessel must not be used for law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing boats,” she said.

Kuan also rejected Beijing’s criticism on the matter, arguing that Taiwanese fishermen faced more immediate risks from mainland China and citing the boarding and detention of Taiwanese vessels.

Taipei says such incidents have taken place at least three times since 2024.

The We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation, a Philippine non-profit organisation focused on maritime issues, said on Monday that it had formally donated the Taiwanese cutter, renamed Training Ship WPS, to the country’s coastguard.

The ship would be deployed to Mindanao for search and rescue, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, and marine environmental protection, WPS cited Philippine coastguard commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan as saying.

The foundation did not disclose the vessel’s origin or explain how it had acquired it.

However, a Philippine source confirmed to Taiwan’s official Central News Agency on Tuesday that the vessel was the decommissioned Taiwanese coastguard patrol ship Kinmen.

That corroborated earlier information obtained by the South China Morning Post that the retired cutter had been transferred to Manila from Taiwan.

The concerns over the donation reflect a long history of fisheries disputes between Taiwan and the Philippines.

In 2013, personnel aboard a Philippine coastguard vessel opened fire on the Taiwanese fishing boat Guang Da Xing No 28 in overlapping waters, killing one fisherman.

The shooting prompted Taipei to impose sanctions and step up fisheries-protection patrols, which subsequently led to a 2015 agreement to avoid the use of violence or unnecessary force in fisheries law enforcement.

Despite those efforts, tensions linger. Just last year, the Taiwanese fishing boat Sheng Yu Feng was boarded by Philippine personnel and taken to port.

The vessel and its crew were released without penalties the same day after a formal protest from Taipei, which said the boat had been fishing in waters where the two sides’ exclusive economic zones overlap.

Lawmakers from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang have also raised concerns about the Japan-Philippines maritime boundary talks, warning that the waters in question overlap directly with Taiwan’s claimed exclusive economic zone off its east coast.

KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun described the ship transfer as “rubbing salt into the wounds” of Taiwanese fishermen, while party legislator Hsu Yu-chen asked whether the vessel might ultimately be deployed in overlapping waters to board, pursue or expel Taiwanese fishing boats.

The DPP, however, has portrayed closer ties with Manila in a broader regional context.

Lawmaker Wang Ting-yu hailed the recent coastguard cooperation as a “historic breakthrough”, highlighting its strategic significance as both sides face growing grey-zone pressure from Beijing.

Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, a Taipei-based think tank, said geopolitics was the main reason Taipei was willing to proceed despite its history of fisheries disputes with Manila.

“The Philippines is part of the first island chain and an important link in constraining Beijing’s military expansion in the South China Sea,” Wang said, adding that the US had encouraged regional partners, including Japan and South Korea, to help strengthen Philippine capabilities.

“The United States is a major factor behind this,” Wang argued.

The transfer is unusual because previous recipients – including the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu – maintain diplomatic ties with Taipei, while the Philippines recognises Beijing and has no formal relations with Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and never ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States, Taiwan’s No 1 international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Taiwanese authorities have offered few details about the vessel transfer.

Marvin H. Bernardo, a Taiwan affairs researcher from the Philippines and PhD candidate at National Chengchi University, noted that the absence of formal diplomatic relations meant an intermediary was needed to facilitate the transfer.

“Given the sensitivity of Beijing to any form of engagement with Taiwan, which they interpret as a violation of the one-China policy, it was more politically expedient to go through an NGO,” he said.

The vessel transfer comes alongside other efforts by Taipei to expand contact with Manila.

Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung has confirmed plans to open a second representative office in Cebu – after Manila – to facilitate economic cooperation. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration has also pledged to send 100 personnel to the Philippines for a goodwill port visit in October next year.

Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, cautioned against interpreting the donation as evidence that relations had entered a fundamentally new phase.

“This is driven by geopolitical factors. It cannot really be described as Taiwan-Philippines friendship moving to a new stage,” Lo said.

He said Taipei was also seeking to show Washington that it was willing to contribute to broader regional security efforts.

At the same time, Lo said, Manila remained cautious about antagonising Beijing, making it unclear how far the Philippines would be prepared to cooperate with Taiwan in responding to pressure from mainland China.

Bernardo said the arrangement nevertheless indicated a willingness on the Philippine side to be more flexible in its engagement with Taiwan.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesian coal deal fuels doubts over production quota approvals
item.description:
A major coal deal in Indonesia is set to secure a powerful new partner for one of the country’s biggest miners, even as the industry worries a delay in the government’s approval of production quotas could have a severe impact on the business outlook.

Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, the biggest shareholders of Bayan Resources, agreed on September 16 to sell a 30 per cent stake in Indonesia’s third-largest coal producer to fellow tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam.

The deal comes at a sensitive moment for Bayan after the government delayed approval of additional coal quotas for three of its subsidiaries. The uncertainty sent Bayan’s shares sharply lower in the days before the deal announcement. It rose by about 20 per cent as soon as news broke about the stake deal, hitting the upper auto-reject limit.
item.content:encoded:
A major coal deal in Indonesia is set to secure a powerful new partner for one of the country’s biggest miners, even as the industry worries a delay in the government’s approval of production quotas could have a severe impact on the business outlook.

Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, the biggest shareholders of Bayan Resources, agreed on September 16 to sell a 30 per cent stake in Indonesia’s third-largest coal producer to fellow tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam.

The deal comes at a sensitive moment for Bayan after the government delayed approval of additional coal quotas for three of its subsidiaries. The uncertainty sent Bayan’s shares sharply lower in the days before the deal announcement. It rose by about 20 per cent as soon as news broke about the stake deal, hitting the upper auto-reject limit.

The timing has fuelled speculation that the quota hurdle might be linked to the deal, a suggestion that the government has rejected.

Under the conditional agreement, the Lows would sell 10 billion Bayan shares to Jhonlin Baratama, a subsidiary of Haji Isam’s Jhonlin Group, a commodities and logistics conglomerate.

The deal would give Jhonlin a substantial stake in a major Indonesian coal producer. Bayan produced 68 million tonnes of coal last year, compared with Jhonlin’s output of 24 million tonnes.

“Acquiring a major stake in a top-three coal producer like Bayan fundamentally rewires our energy landscape. The state must ensure this consolidation doesn’t birth a mega-cartel,” said Dipo Satria Ramli, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics.

Indonesian media have described Haji Isam as an ally of the president. In 2025, Prabowo awarded him the Bintang Mahaputera Utama, one of Indonesia’s highest state honours.

Haji Isam has set his sights on expanding Jhonlin’s coal output after having applied for a 60-million-tonne production quota, known as Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB) in Indonesia, for the rest of this year.

Ahmad Zuhdi Dwi Kusuma, principal at Energy Shift Institute, an independent energy finance think tank, said Jhonlin’s 30 per cent stake in Bayan would strengthen its market position.

“Haji Isam can connect the existing ecosystem he has under his group to Bayan,” he said.

Assuming Jhonlin was successful in acquiring its new 60-million-tonne quota, which was separate from the Bayan quota, its output combined with Bayan’s could account for about one-eighth of Indonesia’s coal market, Zuhdi said.

Details about the deal remain scant, pending further announcements from Bayan.

The Lows currently hold 62 per cent of Bayan’s shares. If the 30 per cent stake sold to Jhonlin comes entirely from their holdings, they would be left with about 32 per cent, potentially leaving control of the company uncertain.

But Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based Four Capital, a family office investment firm, said control of Bayan would likely remain with the Lows after the sale.

“Like most Indonesian conglomerate families, they have a lot of nominees in the rest of the 38 per cent stock.”

Under Indonesia’s RKAB system, mining companies must obtain government approval for their production volume. Without an approved quota, miners cannot legally produce beyond an amount authorised by the government.

On September 11, the three Bayan subsidiaries notified customers and invoked force majeure, citing the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources’ failure to issue additional production quota permits for the rest of 2026.

“The approval has not been issued to the company’s subsidiaries, although applications for approval to amend the RKAB have been submitted in accordance with applicable laws and regulations,” Bayan director Low Yi Ngo wrote in a statement.

Without the permits, Bayan’s production in 2026 is expected to total 39 million tonnes, 43 per cent lower than last year.

When Bayan announced the force majeure status to the Indonesian Stock Exchange on September 14, its shares fell by as much as 9.2 per cent that day.

The company eventually received approval for the subsidiaries’ quotas on Wednesday, a week after the deal was announced.

The episode highlighted how coal mining operations could be severely curtailed because of delays in government approval of production volumes, according to analysts.

Without the RKAB, Bayan would face difficulties in planning its production and budget, Zuhdi said. With its quota cut by almost half, it had no choice but to declare force majeure on its existing obligations to clients, he added.

“This serves as a reminder that the regulatory side of the industry in Indonesia is increasingly the be-all and end-all factor for a miner.”

According to a report by The Jakarta Post, the government has faced questions over whether Bayan’s permit delays were linked to Haji Isam’s acquisition. Other Indonesian media outlets highlighted that the quotas were approved shortly after the deal was signed.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Bayan and Jhonlin for comment.

Ho urged caution over drawing a link between the two developments.

When questioned by reporters in Jakarta on September 16 on why Bayan’s permits were not issued on the same day as the deal announcement on September 16, the director general of minerals and coal at the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, Tri Winarno, said: “It’s still being evaluated and examined in terms of technical aspects, so it will take time.”

He also pointed out that not all of Bayan’s permits were held up. “From all Bayan’s coal subsidiaries, only three are having their permits re-evaluated. So there’s no deliberate targeting here.”

Bayan Resources has 16 subsidiaries – all of which have separate permits to mine coal – covering 126,000 hectares in East and South Kalimantan.

Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia on Wednesday rejected any connection between Bayan’s quota crisis and its stake sale. “The two were separate processes with no link whatsoever,” he told reporters.

Nonetheless, the developments have left market participants worrying about uncertainty over regulatory decisions and their impact on the value of Indonesian mining assets.

Calling it an “unpalatable aftertaste” for investors, Ho said: “The optics remain remarkable because a regulatory approval becomes critical to production, the company declares force majeure, a major ownership transaction is signed, and the regulatory uncertainty clears almost immediately.”

Dipo said the developments would affect investors’ perceptions of official transparency. “Investors will be even more cautious about potential government intervention in the future,” he added.

Katherine Hasan, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, said that beyond the deal, Bayan and others in the coal industry would have to balance between staying competitive even as the Indonesian government sought to increase the proportion of energy production from green sources.

The Prabowo administration is seeking to phase out all coal and fossil fuel power plants by 2040 and increase solar energy production to 100 GW by 2029.

While Bayan and its peers were aiming to bolster their cash flows by increasing domestic coal production, they faced the “political reality” of Jakarta seeking to curb its fuel subsidies and enhance the country’s long-term energy security.

item.title: [SCMP] Ukraine’s POW transfer reveal deals North Korea a propaganda blow
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The disclosure – made during Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday – directly challenges Pyongyang’s narrative that its soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces would choose death over surrender.

North Korea is unlikely to acknowledge the transfer publicly, but may strengthen ideological controls over its troops deployed to Russia to prevent further defections, observers say.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The disclosure – made during Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday – directly challenges Pyongyang’s narrative that its soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces would choose death over surrender.

North Korea is unlikely to acknowledge the transfer publicly, but may strengthen ideological controls over its troops deployed to Russia to prevent further defections, observers say.

“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” Zelensky said during his UN address, using South Korea’s official name.

“These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself and he was shocked that fate didn’t let him die.”

The two soldiers were reportedly captured by Ukrainian forces in January 2025 after being deployed to Russia’s Kursk region to support Moscow’s war effort. Zelensky said they subsequently expressed a desire to travel to South Korea, as indicated in interviews and handwritten letters sent to organisations representing North Korean defectors.
