South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to confirm any specific details regarding the POWs, citing concerns for the safety of the men and their families in the North.

But it did say in a statement that the issue should be resolved in a manner that “respects the free will of the individuals concerned and is consistent with international law and humanitarian principles”.

“In line with this position, the government has been engaged in necessary consultations with Ukraine and other relevant countries and organisations,” the ministry said, adding that this was “a sensitive matter” and it could not divulge details about bilateral consultations.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung expressed regret about the disclosure in a social media post on Thursday, calling it “a highly sensitive matter” that could have serious implications for diplomacy and security on the Korean peninsula.

“Considering the various issues that could arise from making the matter public, keeping it confidential was the reasonable course of action in every respect, and that was what we agreed upon,” Lee wrote in Korean.

“While I do not know the specific circumstances that led the Ukrainian side to break the agreement and go public, the situation is deeply regrettable.”

South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said on Thursday that the two prisoners had left Ukraine last weekend, travelled via a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days earlier, likely under the protection of South Korean intelligence agencies.

In July, Lee and Zelensky agreed on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara to handle the North Korean POW issue based on humanitarian principles while respecting the prisoners’ wishes.

‘Propaganda nightmare’

Zelensky raised the POW issue while accusing Russian President Vladimir Putin of recruiting foreign fighters to prosecute his war on Ukraine.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory … instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Zelensky said, adding that Moscow had recruited citizens from 47 countries, including Ghana, Nepal and India.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said Pyongyang would likely remain silent to protect the narrative of absolute loyalty and self-sacrifice among its troops.

“North Korea is likely to ignore the issue or show little interest, given the potential burden of allowing it to become a major political issue,” Yang said. “At the same time, Pyongyang is expected to strengthen ideological education and internal controls over North Korean troops in Russia to prevent similar defections.”

Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, described the situation as a “propaganda nightmare” for Pyongyang, as it had consistently eulogised its soldiers as heroes who take their own lives rather than surrender.

“For North Korean soldiers in Russia, this news opens a different option that is not death when they risk being captured,” Oh said, adding that Ukraine was likely to use the defection in psychological warfare targeting North Korean troops.

Questions of trust

Yang said that Zelensky’s decision to go public with the POW transfer could have broader geopolitical implications – potentially driving a wedge between Seoul and Kyiv.

“Bringing such a sensitive humanitarian issue directly into the international spotlight at the United Nations could undermine trust in relations between South Korea and Ukraine,” Yang said. “The Ukrainian president could also face criticism that a sensitive humanitarian issue is being politicised.”

Respecting prisoners’ free will should have included getting their consent before revealing their transfer, Yang added, given the risk of retaliation against their families remaining in North Korea.

“Announcing their defection without first securing their consent would constitute an inhumane act,” he said. “Zelensky himself should make clear whether the prisoners’ consent to the public disclosure was explicitly obtained.”

Yang dismissed speculation of a secret deal between Kyiv and Seoul, pointing to President Lee’s stated preference for diplomatic transparency.

Oh said the disclosure could also serve Ukraine’s broader strategy of highlighting the deepening military relationship between Russia and North Korea as Kyiv sought continued international support for its war effort.

While Seoul has provided humanitarian aid to Ukraine, it maintains a strict policy against supplying lethal weapons to any country at war.

Asian Games defections?

Zelensky’s disclosure coincided with an unconfirmed report that two members of North Korea’s delegation to this year’s Asian Games in Japan were seeking asylum.

South Korea’s Monthly Chosun magazine reported on Tuesday that the pair – part of an estimated 180-member North Korean delegation – had approached Japanese authorities expressing a desire to seek asylum in Japan rather than South Korea.

Citing a source linked to Japan’s Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office and the pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, known as Chongryon, the magazine said the individuals’ identities and roles had not been disclosed.

Japanese authorities have not publicly confirmed the report and it is unclear whether any defections have occurred at the Games.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws fail to meet modern demands, experts say
item.description:
Hong Kong’s existing animal welfare laws are no longer “fit for purpose” to deal with issues around pet abandonment and strays, legal experts have said, urging authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms to the city’s ordinances following a spate of dog attacks.

The calls echo comments by Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan, who said on Wednesday that authorities would look at whether existing penalties for pet abandonment should be strengthened and bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of the year.

Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have drawn intense public scrutiny following a string of recent incidents, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman by stray dogs in Yuen Long last Saturday night.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s existing animal welfare laws are no longer “fit for purpose” to deal with issues around pet abandonment and strays, legal experts have said, urging authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms to the city’s ordinances following a spate of dog attacks.

The calls echo comments by Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan, who said on Wednesday that authorities would look at whether existing penalties for pet abandonment should be strengthened and bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of the year.

Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have drawn intense public scrutiny following a string of recent incidents, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman by stray dogs in Yuen Long last Saturday night.

“Hong Kong’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance … remains fundamentally focused on prohibiting acts of cruelty,” said Kim McCoy, a practising barrister and founder of the Hong Kong Animal Law and Protection Organisation.

“It is an outdated and fundamentally flawed framework, no longer fit for purpose and wholly incapable of meeting the demands of modern society.”

Stray dogs have caused increasing concern as land clearance for the Northern Metropolis megaproject has led to a surge in abandoned animals.

Preparatory land resumption for the megaproject in the New Territories has triggered a growing animal welfare crisis, as many residents and business operators abandon pets or guard dogs ahead of government clearance deadlines.

Despite these concerns, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) previously told the South China Morning Post that no prosecutions had been brought against people for abandoning animals under the Rabies Ordinance – the law governing such matters – between 2023 and 2025.

In his recent policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government would amend the city’s laws on animal care by the end of 2027 while also reviewing pet ownership and control regulations.

Speaking to lawmakers on Wednesday, Tse said authorities would bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of 2026.

But animal law reform has been an ongoing discussion in the city for years, with the government submitting a paper to the Legislative Council in 2022 outlining proposed amendments to the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance.

The proposals, which received support from 88 per cent of respondents during a public consultation exercise in 2019, included increasing the maximum penalties for animal cruelty offences and strengthening rules around animal abandonment.

They also introduced a positive “duty of care” provision, long sought by animal welfare advocates and legal experts, requiring owners to ensure their pets’ safety and fulfil basic care obligations.

Such requirements would include ensuring animals have a suitable diet and living environment, exhibit normal behaviour patterns, and are protected from pain, suffering and injury.

While the 2022 paper suggested the bill amendments would be put before lawmakers that year, it was never formally introduced. In subsequent responses to lawmakers’ questions on the lack of progress, the government as recently as this February cited “divergent views” among stakeholders on the need for “duty of care” provisions and the extent of penalties.

It is not yet clear whether the government’s new round of proposed amendments will match those introduced in 2022.

Animal welfare advocates have argued that existing laws make it difficult to prosecute owners who fail to microchip or properly secure their pets, while allowing them to deny that an abandoned animal belongs to them.

McCoy said introducing “duty of care” rules would define responsible ownership, and a person who acquired an animal would need to accept the responsibilities that came with their decision.

“In the context of these recent incidents, a properly drafted ‘duty of care’ could help prevent neglect and abandonment, improve standards of supervision and enable earlier intervention where an animal’s welfare is being compromised,” he said.

He also called for a comprehensive review of the city’s Rabies Ordinance.

“While rabies prevention remains important, we should not be relying on disease-control legislation to address fundamental issues such as animal abandonment, irresponsible ownership and the humane management of stray animals,” he said.

Amanda Whitfort, an associate professor at the University of Hong Kong specialising in animal law, said there was a need to introduce welfare standards for animals, prosecute abandonment, and introduce humane population control of strays in certain areas.

Whitfort co-wrote a landmark animal law reform report in 2010 which, among a number of recommendations, called for the implementation of a new Animal Welfare Ordinance containing “duty of care” provisions.

“Rather than take a holistic view of solving these problems, the [AFCD’s] policy has been to collect and pass on their responsibility for unwanted dogs to overburdened shelters. This policy has not been sustainable for some time,” she said.

She noted that the department had not brought any prosecutions for animal abandonment in recent years, which she argued “sends the public the message that they may give up their responsibilities to their pets without significant repercussions”.

Whitfort said it was too easy for people to keep dogs without obtaining licences under existing rules, and suggested that laws could be altered to reward those who spay or neuter their dogs with lower licence fees.

She also called on authorities to follow Macau’s example, where failing to report the loss of a dog within a specific time period was an offence.

In a reply to the SCMP, the AFCD said that pet owners had a responsibility not only to care for their pets but also to control them.

“While ‘duty of care’ focuses primarily on the animal’s welfare needs, the concept of ‘pet owner responsibility’ encompasses welfare, safety, environmental considerations and public health,” it said.

“We will encourage pet owners to understand and fulfil their responsibilities through reviewing regulations and conducting public education and publicity campaigns.”

The department also reiterated that the government would consult the Legislative Council on proposals to step up efforts to combat cruelty to animals, and that it would work to complete the amendment exercise in 2027.

item.title: [SCMP] Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

On Wednesday, Amodei pushed further for a slowdown when he addressed the UN Security Council by video link, warning that mismanaged AI posed an existential threat to humanity and urging nations to unite on global safety standards.

These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety, among other issues.

Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight.

These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

“Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.”

It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability.

This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders.

The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share

Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI

What is driving calls to slow down?

There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate.

While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”.

While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China.

“Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”.

Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader.

Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls.

China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week.

Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power.

“The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said.

Existential risks, practical realities

Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week.

Huang dismissed such “doomerism” while on a New York Times podcast on Wednesday , arguing that fearmongering only slowed down industry adoption.

There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies.

As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely.

Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety.

Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards.

Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down.

According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers.

China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels.

Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week.

“I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said.

With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources.

In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month.

Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement.

According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries.

Genuine safety fears

While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks.

Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development.

Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely.

Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.”

According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead.

“At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.”

Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”.

Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development.

Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration.

“Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said.

As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped.

A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun.

There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues.

He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries.

“Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Bangkok’s World Gourmet Festival, where top chefs share the kitchen
item.description:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration
item.content:encoded:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration

Beyond now commonplace four-hands dinners and chef residencies, the World Gourmet Festival presents a unique set of challenges. Chefs must traverse language barriers, unfamiliar ingredients, and sky-high expectations from some of the industry’s most trained palates. For many, this tests more than culinary skill; it also challenges adaptability and creativity.

Josiah Citrin, chef-owner of restaurants Mélisse and Citrin in Los Angeles, acknowledges the pressure this event brings. “The expectation is always high, but that’s what makes these events exciting,” he explains. “In the kitchen, food becomes its own language quickly. Once you start cooking together, you find a rhythm, and that’s part of the fun of doing these events around the world.”

This balancing act – maintaining one’s gastronomic identity while embracing the unknown – is central to the festival’s spirit.

Pastry chef Puyachart “Boy” Puttawong of Saneh Jaan in Bangkok frames the goal precisely. “A successful collaborative menu should allow guests to recognise each chef’s individual personality while still experiencing a clear and harmonious connection from the first course to the last.”

Weaving a comprehensive throughline that connects each course, rather than jockeying for attention, helps diners understand the interplay between both cuisines and each chef’s culinary ethos. “Our intention is not to make every dish taste Thai, but to allow Thai culinary knowledge and ingredients to become part of the creative conversation,” Puttawong stresses.

Creating a cohesive dining experience amid such diversity can be daunting. Chefs must develop a menu together that reflects their individual styles while maintaining culinary continuity across courses. “Menu development begins with understanding each chef’s strengths,” remarks chef Pilaipon “Toi” Kamnag of Saneh Jaan. “Compromise doesn’t mean weakening anyone’s culinary identity; it’s about making thoughtful adjustments.”

Clavijo stresses the importance of listening rather than competing for space on the same plate: “I wouldn’t really call it ‘compromise’. If both chefs are trying to prove their identity in every single course, the guest feels that tension. A good partnership requires enough confidence to know when to speak and when to let the other person speak.”

Communicating can be a challenge in itself, with chefs from so many different countries taking part. But for many involved, food serves as a universal tongue, reducing friction.

Thanh Vuong Vo, executive chef of Coco Dining in Ho Chi Minh City, shares his perspective: “In a professional kitchen, communication goes beyond spoken language. You communicate through technique, timing, gestures, tasting and repetition,” he says. “If there is a difference in interpretation, we taste together and use the food itself as the common vernacular.” This fluidity allows chefs to communicate through actions and shared experiences rather than relying solely on verbal exchanges.

Zee Zheng, chef-owner of Fabula in Shanghai, observes, “I believe a chef is simply a messenger of nature. My role is to act as a bridge – connecting dishes while weaving in subtle local touches that add a sense of discovery.

“It’s all about both chefs working together to allow the ingredients to speak for themselves; that is what defines high-level cuisine.” This synergy cultivates an environment where innovation thrives despite the pressures of the event.

Ingredient-led approaches

Despite the challenges, one of the event’s most exciting aspects is the opportunity to experiment with niche Thai ingredients, from produce to proteins. For the chefs involved, these ingredients offer both inspiration and a challenge. Says Vo, “I want to understand the Thai ingredients and techniques first, then see how they can enter my own culinary language naturally.”

His goal is to create something that feels like a genuine conversation between Vietnam and Thailand, rather than simply combining ingredients from both countries. “Understanding their role in Thai cooking allows me to incorporate them into my own cuisine in a meaningful way while keeping the Vietnamese perspective at the heart of my cooking.”

This mindset of exploration is essential for chefs seeking to create dishes that resonate with both their own background and the local culture.

Clavijo’s approach at his restaurant, El Chato, is deeply rooted in Colombia’s ecological variety, and he sees Thailand as a mirror rather than a contrast. “Even though Colombia and Thailand are far apart, there are many similarities in our ingredients as both countries share a tropical climate,” he says. “Rather than forcing Colombian and Thai cuisines together, I prefer to find natural connections and let the products guide us.”

Julien Royer, chef-owner of Odette in Singapore, echoes this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding local flavours. “My culinary ideology revolves around the principle that ingredients are a reflection of terroir. My grandmother, Odette, was the one who taught me that respect for seasonality,” he says. For Royer, cooking with Thai ingredients is about respect and balance – finding a natural connection between two cuisines and letting them meet on equal terms.

The costs and benefits of participation

While the festival offers significant exposure and brand building, it also comes with sacrifices. Chefs must balance their responsibilities at home with the demands of such high-profile events. Citrin acknowledges this cost, stating, “Leaving your restaurant means leaving your team, your business, and your family. It has to have a meaningful purpose that extends beyond that one single event.”

Clavijo agrees, explaining that collaboration must go further than mere visibility. “The real value is exchange,” he says. “The lasting benefits of meeting other chefs, discovering new products, and creating ongoing relationships are what make these experiences worthwhile for chefs and attendees alike.”

A celebration of gastronomy

The World Gourmet Festival mirrors the evolving culinary landscape in Bangkok and Asia. As local chefs collaborate with international talents, they bring new perspectives and techniques to the fore. “As Thai chefs, we are proud to be part of the hosting city,” says chef Toi. “Bangkok is no longer simply a destination where international cuisine is presented; it has become an active and influential participant in the global culinary conversation.”

item.title: [SCMP] AI poses new national security threat, outgoing Hong Kong deputy police chief warns
item.description:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.

Kan, 57, who headed the National Security Department, began his pre-retirement leave on Tuesday after 35 years on the force.

Discussing the new threat, the outgoing police official said he had seen overseas examples of AI agents launching attacks on critical infrastructure and other companies’ computer systems, as well as generating misinformation.

Anti-government forces could also use AI to commit crimes related to national security, he said.

“I totally agree … that AI poses a new security threat to national security,” he said. “We have been working to improve our capability in AI in this aspect. I can also tell you one of the tactics to combat AI crime is using AI.”

Kan pointed to AI tools used to help screen social media posts to identify potential “soft resistance” against the government as an example.

“As computers and AI become more powerful, the chances of successfully hiding your criminal intent or criminal acts are actually getting slimmer. So, it’s better not to test the law,” he warned.

The police official also said that anyone who used AI to commit crimes should be held responsible.

Kan said the current legislation was adequate for now to tackle such threats, but he did not rule out the need for new legislation in the future.

“Maybe in the future we need new laws,” he said. “Of course, technology grows very fast. We do not know next year or five years later, what the world will be.”

Discussing the relevant legislation, he cited Section 50 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which governs acts of endangering national security in relation to computers or electronic systems, saying that authorities had anticipated AI-related threats while drafting the law.

He also pointed to the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance, which safeguards critical infrastructure and banking systems from attacks.

In his announcement of Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint last week, Lee touched on plans to enhance the legal system and enforcement mechanisms to safeguard national security.

Kan said the four main national security threats that would require vigilance over the next five years were soft resistance, home-grown terrorism, foreign influence and espionage.

Earlier this year, national security police raided three independent bookstores over allegations that they had displayed or sold titles with seditious intent.

The deputy police chief said his officers had actually read the books and sought legal advice from the Department of Justice before taking enforcement action. “There is no such thing as blind enforcement or making arbitrary arrests,” he said.

Kan also rejected the idea of publishing a banned books list with book titles or ISBNs, arguing booksellers were responsible for ensuring the books they were selling complied with local national security legislation and comparing the situation to how restaurant owners needed to ensure food safety.

“If we issue a banned books list today, and tomorrow you publish another book that turns out to be illegal after our investigation, you’ll say, ‘hey, why are you arresting us if it wasn’t on the list?’ This simply cannot resolve the problem,” he said.

He suggested that sellers read the books before offering them and seek legal advice if in doubt. “If you say it is not easy to get legal advice … then don’t sell it,” he said.

“If you say, ‘you will not publish the book list, and I don’t know where the red line is’ – I feel this is a bit of … soft resistance,” he said, adding that there was a clear definition of sedition under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.

Kan said more people were engaging in soft resistance, which had become even more discreet and underground after the enactment of national security laws.

He added that people used different platforms, including cultural, arts and online media, to spread misinformation, incite hatred and instigate public resentment towards the local and central governments.

On the distinction between soft resistance and freedom of speech, he said that the key determining factors were whether the expression was intended to incite others and whether the criticism was based on concrete facts.

On September 11, three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil were sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail for inciting subversion.

Kan said that whether it was legal to commemorate the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 4 in the future should be judged on a case-by-case basis.

He said that when evaluating applications for protests, police assessed threats to national security, public order and safety, as well as the potential impacts on the freedoms of others.

“Of course, if the rally or protest you join is explicitly taking up the mantle of the alliance’s ideology, or ideas aimed at opposing China and destabilising Hong Kong, then you really need to think twice about whether you’ll end up breaking the law,” he said.

Commenting on the effectiveness of putting bounties on wanted persons who had breached national security laws, Kan said: “Justice may be delayed, but it will not be denied.

“Just because they haven’t returned now does not mean they never will … world politics can change drastically.

“Will those sheltering you today betray you tomorrow? I wouldn’t rule it out. It’s certainly not impossible. When you beg others for protection and shelter, what happens to you once your usefulness runs out? We shall wait and see.”

Kan also noted that national security police had arrested people suspected of handling funds or donations on behalf of absconders, largely cutting off their means of survival.

Asked whether he would join the Committee for Safeguarding National Security after retiring, he said he wanted to take a good rest and spend time with his family first, adding that he did not have any current plans for the future.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore minister Chan Chun Sing’s Mandarin diplomacy strikes China chord
item.description:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.

At the summit on Wednesday, attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and helmed by Chinese defence chief Dong Jun, Chan spoke mostly in English but switched to Mandarin occasionally and cited Mencius, saying: “Power may compel others to comply. But in the end, it is trust that truly wins others over.”

Social media users also drew comparisons between Chan and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, praising the former for displaying wisdom which exceeded that of a counterpart helming the military of a much larger country.

On Chan’s use of Mandarin, a Weixin user commented: “This minister is not an ordinary person; he knows Chinese culture like the back of his hand.”

Many also said Chan’s Mandarin was proof that the language and Chinese culture were gaining traction on the global stage.

The Singapore minister also urged superpowers to shoulder higher expectations from smaller states, stressing that countries should strengthen their own security but not at the expense of others.

“The more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be,” he said in Mandarin.

Singapore welcomed China’s aspiration to be a “responsible major country”, Chan said, adding that Beijing’s “reform and opening up” policy had contributed greatly to regional and global prosperity.

“As the People’s Liberation Army approaches its centenary, there is much potential for it to make a positive contribution to global stability and security,” he said.

Diplomatic move?

Observers hail Chan’s use of Mandarin and historical references as a clever diplomatic move, showcasing an appreciation and understanding of China and its culture.

Stefanie Kam, an assistant professor at S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), described Chan’s switch to Mandarin as deliberate and a “clear effort to show cultural awareness and diplomatic tact”.

“For a defence minister to quote an old Chinese classic like this is quite strategic; it makes it hard for the Chinese audience to disagree because they would be disagreeing with their own classic,” she said.

Adam Liu, a political scientist and assistant professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, pointed out that Chinese leader Xi Jinping often quoted ancient Chinese teachings.

“Speaking in Mandarin and drawing on Mencius is a way of saying: I am addressing you in your own idiom, on your own terms. That tends to land well,” he said.

While Chan’s Mandarin switch-up was largely well received, some netizens were unimpressed, arguing that it should be expected that Chan – who hails from a country where 74 per cent of citizens were of Chinese ethnicity – would be fluent in Mandarin.

As English strengthens its hold as the main language for Singaporeans, the government has reinforced the importance of maintaining a bilingual edge, implementing measures such as public speaking contests and cultural workshops. According to a 2020 census, the use of Mandarin as the language most frequently spoken at home fell from 35.6 per cent in 2010 to 29.9 per cent in 2020.

Dylan Loh, associate professor of foreign policy at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, said the speech showed Singapore’s bilingualism and an ability to code-switch.

“Beyond citing Mencius specifically, the broader context in which it was used is also important,” he said. “The message was respectful and paid compliment to Chinese history and philosophical heritage.”

But Loh said the code-switch was not necessarily a strategic move in itself, noting that leaders had in the past done the same at various forums.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, warned that the Chinese public could view affirmations of culture and ethnic similarities as synonymous with political alignment.

While using a Chinese philosophical expression “may be tactically helpful to smooth ties”, Chong said it could also “create disappointment when a person or the entity they represent take positions that diverge from prior expectations associated with race, culture and politics”.

On Chinese social media, some users interpreted Chan’s speech as veiled criticism of the United States, though observers note the script was vague and aligned with Singapore’s foreign policy.

In his speech, Chan said: “We must work even harder to strengthen our domestic fundamentals, rather than try to externalise our domestic issues.” He also illustrated Singapore’s journey to the global stage since its independence in 1965, through which “leaders avoided exploiting foreign policy for political gain”.

While Chan did not explicitly name a country, some online users who appraised Chan’s speech likely interpreted the reference to winning by force as implying American actions, Kam said.

Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and coordinator at the China Programme at RSIS, said Chan’s speech was broad and in line with the city state’s “pro-Singapore” policy.

“It’s not surprising the Chinese read this as a reference to the US, but the case that China’s domestic issues are not absent in its foreign policy can also be made,” he said. “If you look past the idioms, which are obviously for the Chinese audience, it’s general and mostly speaking on principle.”

Liu said Mencius’ quote was consistent with Singapore’s non-alignment. “The hope is for an international order built on trust, rules and moral principles, which is a position one can hold without pointing at anybody.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
item.description:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.
item.content:encoded:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.

Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation.

South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator.

Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted.

“The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia.

The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.

A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government.

From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.

To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content.

Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.

“Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them.

South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy.

But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide.

Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures.

Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement.

“As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models.

In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown.

Brewing with bots

At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition.

What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business.

“It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers.

Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors.

He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots.

“The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings.

“With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.”

Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools.

“People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said.

That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot.

“That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.”

Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees.

Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important.

“My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.”

No juniors needed?

Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming.

And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade.

This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest.

At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year.

Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum.

“Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension.

The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29.

Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management.

“I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?”

Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University.

“When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said.

“But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.”

New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”.

Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way.

“Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.”

Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology.

“In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said.

“Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.”

AI-fuelled abuse

South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse.

The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024.

Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty.

Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.

In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial.

The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools.

Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.

“Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.”

Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI.

“Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”.

“We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.”

To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution.

“Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school.

Generation chatbot

Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper.

“In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said.

Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks.

“Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province.

While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song.

“It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot.

“I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.”

The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month.

“Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.”

The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic.

“Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.”

Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments.

“Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.”

This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] US families ramp up efforts for loved ones’ release from China ahead of Xi’s visit
item.description:
Chen Youlin, a Chinese-American scientist, travelled back to China in October 2024 for a month-long holiday, including to celebrate his mother’s 80th birthday. As he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing.

For more than 670 days, his wife, Rong Yufang, and other family members have not been able to see or speak with him.

“Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” Rong told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.”
item.content:encoded:
Chen Youlin, a Chinese-American scientist, travelled back to China in October 2024 for a month-long holiday, including to celebrate his mother’s 80th birthday. As he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing.

For more than 670 days, his wife, Rong Yufang, and other family members have not been able to see or speak with him.

“Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” Rong told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.”

Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to Washington next week, cases of several US citizens detained in China are gaining greater attention as their families step up pressure on the Trump administration to press Beijing for their release.

As well as Chen’s family, the relatives of Americans Min Zin, Dawn Michelle Hunt and Nelson Wells Jnr are pressing Washington to intervene with Beijing – but their cases vary. Chen and Zin are being held on national security-related allegations, while Hunt and Wells Jnr have spent over a decade in Chinese prisons over drug convictions.

Families like Chen’s face a dilemma: pursue quiet diplomacy or go public to pressure Washington and Beijing. Many initially favour a low-profile approach, but turn to public advocacy when private efforts fail.

The cases highlight the risks American citizens can face in China’s legal system, even as US President Donald Trump and Xi seek to stabilise ties and Beijing courts foreign investors, academics and tourists.

US government lists individuals as being ‘wrongfully detained’

Chinese authorities have accused Chen of espionage, likely linked to his previous work analysing seismic data, including North Korean nuclear tests.

Another recent well-publicised case involves American scholar Zin, who was detained in China in June. Chinese authorities accused him of espionage and endangering China’s national security.

Both Chen and Zin have been formally designated as “wrongfully detained” by the US government, a status that means officials will prioritise efforts to secure their release.

A lawyer has been hired to represent Chen and US consular officials have been allowed to visit him.

Rong, Chen’s wife, raised concerns about his health and weight loss during his detention. She told the SCMP that senior US officials had assured her that Trump would raise Chen’s case.

“President Trump and his senior team have been 100 per cent on my side,” Rong said.

The State Department’s Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs has also publicly addressed the issue, saying: “Hostage diplomacy has no place in the US-China relationship.”

Chen’s family initially worked behind the scenes, according to its representative, Eric Lebson of Global Reach. It went public after Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi in May but secured no breakthrough.

Trump also raised the cases of Pastor Ezra Jin, who was later freed, and jailed Hong Kong media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying. Lai’s family and supporters want Trump to raise his case again next week.

For Zin’s case, the circumstances are less clear. The Wall Street Journal reported that US officials believe his background as a former student activist in Myanmar and his US-funded academic work may have drawn the attention of Chinese security services.

Edgard Kagan, a China expert at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said the detention of Chen and Zin is likely linked to their academic work, and he expects Trump to press for their release.

Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey is leading a bipartisan resolution condemning China’s wrongful detention of American academics.

The James W. Foley Legacy Foundation says 12 Americans are currently wrongfully detained in China, including some subject to exit bans. It has assessed 42 cases since 1998, though the total number of Americans caught up in China’s legal system may be higher.

In 2024, US diplomacy secured the release of three Americans held for years; Beijing said the US returned four people to China.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Beijing has firmly rejected the “wrongful detention” designations. Asked about Chen’s case, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said there is no “wrongful detention” in China and that judicial agencies handle cases in accordance with the law.

The embassy spokesperson offered more detail on Zin specifically, telling the Wall Street Journal that he is subject to “criminal coercive measures,” meaning he is under investigation, and that his “legitimate rights have been fully guaranteed.”

Two other high-profile cases involving Americans

Two other high-profile cases involve Americans Hunt and Wells Jnr, both of whom have been imprisoned in China for more than 12 years after being convicted on separate drug charges.

Unlike the scholars’ cases, which have been designated as “wrongfully detained”, the families are pursuing the humanitarian release route and say that they are speaking on behalf of ordinary “rank-and-file” Americans.

The families have joined forces, saying both detainees unknowingly carried drugs out of China. Dawn Michelle’s brother, Tim Hunt, said scammers lured her there with a purported competition prize, then gave her purses with drugs sewn into the lining. Wells Jnr was arrested after agreeing to carry someone else’s suitcase containing hidden narcotics, his family said.

Both have worsening health problems, their families say. Wells Jnr’s father said his son has seizures, high blood pressure and diabetes, and was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C.

Peter Humphrey, a former SCMP China correspondent and fraud investigator who was imprisoned in China with his wife from 2013 to 2015, is working with the families. Since his release, he has advised foreign detainees and their families on how to navigate China’s system.

“We have been constantly hearing from our lobbying contacts in Beijing that the Chinese side is very ready to consider a humanitarian release, so long as there is a request from the American president,” Humphrey said.

Joi Chaney, a legal expert working with the families, called the lack of a US-China prisoner transfer treaty a “blockade” the US has placed on itself. Chinese law allows transfers through bilateral negotiations in special cases, but Washington has historically maintained that US law does not, said Humphrey. He said the US State Department asked China in May 2025 to release Wells Jnr and Hunt on humanitarian grounds.

In response to an SCMP inquiry, a US State Department spokesperson said it has repeatedly raised serious concerns about Wells Jnr and Hunt’s health with Chinese officials.

“We have called upon the Chinese to release them unconditionally on humanitarian grounds, at every opportunity, and we will continue to do so,” it said, while adding that decisions on humanitarian release are at the discretion of the host government.

Additionally, in 2025, bipartisan lawmakers introduced the “Nelson Wells Jnr and Dawn Michelle Hunt Unjustly Detained in Communist China Act”, seeking to strengthen the government’s response to Americans detained in China and support their families. The bill has stalled since its introduction.

“We’re not famous people, we’re not sports stars,” Chaney said, arguing that ordinary Americans should be able to count on their government to bring them home. Both families have histories of military and public service. “If you say you respect the people who serve, show us,” Tim Hunt said in a plea to Trump. “Ask for their release.”

When asked about Hunt and Wells, the White House offered a general response rather than addressing the individual cases.

Families put faith in Trump as Xi summit approaches

“President Trump is always concerned about Americans detained abroad. That is why he has brought over 100 individuals – a record number – home from around the world,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said.

Both families said they were disappointed when their loved ones were not released after the last Xi-Trump summit.

Wells Snr described feeling out of it in the weeks after, not wanting to talk. Tim Hunt found it hard to speak to his sister, who felt she had false hope in the lead-up to the meeting.

Addressing the US president directly ahead of next week’s summit, Wells Snr said: “I would tell President Trump that he’s a father. If he had a child that was in the same situation as our child or Tim’s sister, he would do everything in his power to try to bring them home.”

item.title: [SCMP] China, US may unveil measures to boost military ties when Xi visits Washington
item.description:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

In a phone call on Thursday to make final arrangements before the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that both sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchange in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit.
item.content:encoded:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

In a phone call on Thursday to make final arrangements before the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that both sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchange in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit.
