“[We should] strengthen communication, advance cooperation and manage differences, respect each other’s core interests, and send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive and strategically stable relationship and to jointly promoting world peace and development.,” Wang said, according to Xinhua.

The two also discussed the situation in the Middle East, Xinhua reported.

Sources said both sides were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship.

They said officials in the two militaries were interacting at various levels, with the frequency and level of engagement increasing substantially in the past few months.

Despite a still-contentious economic relationship marked by tit-for-tat tariffs, export controls and sanctions, military ties between Washington and Beijing have moved in a more positive direction, with regular dialogue and public commitments to maintaining peace and increasing mutual understanding.

Sources said both sides were rebuilding military channels to speak frequently and prevent any misunderstanding and miscalculation about each other’s intentions.

Ending a two-year hiatus, China and the US held command-level talks late last month in Canada, with a meeting between Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the Pacific Command.

The US Pacific Command said Yang and Paparo discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior American and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and to promote safe and professional conduct between forces.

One source said China and the US were seeking military dialogue at three levels. Those talks would be between the two presidents, who are also commanders-in-chief of their countries’ armed forces; also at the ministerial level, including the US Department of Defence and China’s Central Military Commission; and between frontline commanders, in particular the US Pacific Command chief and the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command chief.

“The presidential-level and frontline commander-level talks are progressing,” the source said, referring to recent meetings between Xi and US President Donald Trump and the talks between Paparo and Yang.

“But actual ministerial-level talks might take a while. One problem has been China’s anti-corruption campaign that [almost] wiped out the CMC, leaving Zhang Shengmin [as the only uniformed official in the body],” he said.

“But we believe they will take place in the near future.”

Another person familiar with the matter said both sides had made clear they wanted new communication channels.

One of the channels could be to revive dedicated arms-control talks between the US State Department and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which gained momentum in 2023 before being suspended in July 2024 over Washington’s continued arms sales to Taiwan.

A source described the talks as a give from the Chinese side that could eventually be broadened to include military personnel – a long-standing US request – “if things go well”.

Washington had planned to send a more senior Pentagon China official to Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum this week, after last year dispatching only the defence attache. But the official withdrew before the forum, with the US delegation instead led by Brigadier General Stacy Kihara of the embassy in Beijing, leaving the official level unchanged from 2025.

A third source said military-to-military contact under Trump’s second term had become more stable but remained “shallow”. The source said deliverables for the Xi-Trump summit were discussed and locked in when Yang and Paparo met face to face in Canada – their first in-person meeting.

The person called that progress “unique” under a Republican president, describing Trump as “a different sort of Republican president”.

A fourth source said the two militaries were working to follow the “strategic stability” guidance agreed by Trump and Xi during their May meeting in Beijing.

After the summit, the two sides referenced the concept of “strategic stability” in their statements, while differing over its phrasing and interpretation.

In July, a senior Pentagon official – for the first time in more than five years – attended and spoke at a reception at the Chinese embassy in Washington marking the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army.

“Under the leadership of Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress,” said Alvaro Smith, deputy assistant defence secretary for China, Taiwan and Mongolia.

He added that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years” and said Washington was not seeking a “conflict with China”.

“This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we made this a reality.”

US undersecretary of defence for policy Elbridge Colby also hosted Chinese Foreign Vice-Minister Ma Zhaoxu at the Pentagon, later saying on social media that the US interacted with its “Chinese counterparts in a spirit of respect, candour, and realism”.

In another sign of closer military engagement, China is cooperating with the US military to recover the remains of American soldiers who went missing in China during World War II.

As part of those efforts, US defence recovery teams travelled to China in early July to resume searches for missing service members.

The renewed engagement marks a significant shift from the Joe Biden administration, when a series of incidents escalated tensions and left military-to-military communication largely stalled.

Beijing suspended several key military dialogue mechanisms with Washington in 2022 after then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi travelled to Taiwan on a high-profile visit.

Taiwan has been the most sensitive issue between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.

Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent nation, but Washington opposes any attempt to seize the self-governing island by force and has pledged to supply it with weapons.

item.title: [SCMP] Escape Manila’s heat for northern Luzon’s pine-scented hills, hanging coffins and other hidden wonders
item.description:
Travellers rolling north through Metro Manila along the Skyway are treated to an elevated perspective of the Philippine capital. The land is pancake flat but the buildings – from bric-a-brac slums to gilded high-rises – reach for the heavens.

My partner and I, too, are headed higher. Our aim is simple – to escape the city heat and exchange the pervasive congestion for nights that aren’t polluted by light, and days by smog. The most obvious solution would be to take a ferry to some exotic isle – after all, the Philippines has 7,000 of them – but we’ve resolved to head in the opposite direction to the Boracay-bound sun-seekers, to the pine-scented hills of Luzon.

The first quarter of the day is spent on a Victory Liner coach, staring at an undulating sea of rice, with only the volcanic profile of Mount Arayat suggesting there may be mountains ahead.
item.content:encoded:
Travellers rolling north through Metro Manila along the Skyway are treated to an elevated perspective of the Philippine capital. The land is pancake flat but the buildings – from bric-a-brac slums to gilded high-rises – reach for the heavens.

My partner and I, too, are headed higher. Our aim is simple – to escape the city heat and exchange the pervasive congestion for nights that aren’t polluted by light, and days by smog. The most obvious solution would be to take a ferry to some exotic isle – after all, the Philippines has 7,000 of them – but we’ve resolved to head in the opposite direction to the Boracay-bound sun-seekers, to the pine-scented hills of Luzon.

The first quarter of the day is spent on a Victory Liner coach, staring at an undulating sea of rice, with only the volcanic profile of Mount Arayat suggesting there may be mountains ahead.

Once we pass the city of Tarlac, lowland farms begin to submit to hill country, as the coach lurches from a cane-straight highway to a winding road that traces the contours of the land. The temperature cools with the altitude and the natural world evolves in tandem. Brilliant wildflowers line the passage north and menacing raptors circle overhead.

Eventually, we encounter the strangest of things in the tropics – forests of conifers, which dominate the slopes on the outskirts of what’s been aptly dubbed the City of Pines. Baguio, where we plan to spend the night, is a little over 200km (124 miles) from Manila. But it’s the altitude, not distance, that distinguishes it most from the capital.

At 1,400 metres (4,600 feet) above sea level, the Americans found a cool spot on a former Spanish ranchería to build a summer capital in the vogue of Shimla, in British India, and duly designed one of the country’s most pleasant cities. Lungfuls of pine-scented air explain why administrators from Boston and Chicago chose to escape here from the muggy oppressiveness of Manila during the worst months of the year.

As we circumvent Burnham Park – a public lake garden designed by architect Daniel Hudson Burnham that remains the city centrepiece – the laid-back atmosphere of Baguio eases our work-frenzied minds. Although many of the finest old houses have been lost to war and the catastrophic earthquake of 1990, a few period buildings – log and stone constructions designed to blend with the mountainous pine forest – still dot the neighbourhood.

Drawn northwest of the park by the imposing City Hall, we stumble upon Café by the Ruins, an American house bombed during World War II only to be reconstructed by local artists using indigenous materials such as bamboo and nipa, the sense of place enhanced by photographs of mountain tribes on the wall and a menu that mixes classic Filipino fare with international dishes. Tortang talong (grilled aubergine omelette with carabao cheese and tomatoes) washed down with tapuey – the local rocket fuel, made with rice, roots and ginger – kindles a satisfied glee at the end of a hard day’s travel.

About 1.5km (one mile) to the north, the Baguio Village Inn is a prim wooden lodge overlooking the city suburbs, which carpet a series of steep hills, resulting in topsy-turvy, chaotic little districts catering to a quickly expanding population.

The following day, morning light is creeping over the hills when we hop a Jeepney to the City Market in search of breakfast. We get more than we bargained for; mountain-grown strawberries are piled outside shop fronts throughout the labyrinthine bazaar, where peanut brittle, sweet wine and honey are offered for sale along with textiles from the ethnically diverse mountains stretching ahead of us for more than 320km (200 miles) and over six provinces.

A brass band appears, and marches through the throng, the trumpets and drums cultivating the feel of a fiesta, recalling the Spanish influence in the Philippine cultural mosaic. However, Iberian colonists didn’t make it far into the cordilleras and mountain peoples were largely spared the corrupting influences of the outside world until the completion of the American-made Halsema Highway, in 1930.

It is along this 96-year-old road that we embark on the next leg of the journey. You can’t pre-book, we just have to wait for a minivan ride at the Sto. Niño Bus Terminal.

Although, not for long; we’re soon travelling through villages in eyeshot of the terraced hills that turn whole mountainsides into a laddered patchwork of rice fields. It’s a stunning vista, but our driver – a 20-something heavy smoker with a novelty skull dangling from the rear-view mirror – handles the minivan as though he’s driving in the Macau Grand Prix. It’s a roller-coaster trip that ends only after six hours of bouncing and clinging on for dear life, when we’re unceremoniously deposited roadside in Sagada.

This remote mountain settlement found its way onto the hippie trail with the arrival of electricity, in the early 1970s, after which intellectuals flocked here to write, paint and make merry on tapuey. Western beatniks followed, “and the artistic influence has left its mark in the form of little boho cafes and inns and a distinctly laid-back atmosphere”, according to my guidebook.

Grandma’s Yellow House is not quite “boho”, but homely and convivial nonetheless. Members of the owning family are cooking and offer us food when we arrive. We have a second-floor room with thick blankets on the beds – it gets cold at night – and our own bathroom, with running hot water some of the time. It’s not the Ritz, but not bad given the remoteness of Sagada.

The town, it turns out, is no longer the getaway for scribes and bohemians it once was. What Sagada can claim to be, though, is blissful, the alpine cool and whispering pines a balm for travellers with stiff limbs and sore buttocks. The town is dotted with weaving houses - selling everything from traditional scarves to guitar straps - and cafes serving local specialities, notably lemon pie.

As the sun sets, the plummeting temperature impels us to return to Grandma’s Yellow House for an early night.

The following day, having risen with the cock crow – literally – we rendezvous with Wihlis Talanay on the terrace of the building that houses Saga Tours a little after sunrise. Inside, our guide for the day offers us a variety of hikes, cave tours and terraced mountain viewings. We opt for a tour to Echo Valley and its famous hanging coffins.

After compulsory registration with the tourist office, he walks us to the church that overlooks Sagada, a not uncommon sight in a Catholic country, except that this one, the Church of Saint Mary the Virgin, “is Anglican, the Spanish never got here”, explains Talanay.

“It’s the Americans who introduced Christianity, this church was built in 1904.”

A Protestant church might be out of the ordinary but the traditional burial sites set on the cliffs of Echo Valley are truly extraordinary.

“The hanging coffins were hung up high as it was believed the higher the dead were placed, the greater chance of their spirits reaching a higher nature in the afterlife,” Talanay explains of a tradition that is fast disappearing.

The coffins are those of distinguished members of the Kankanaey (an ethnic grouping of the Igorot people) and are in various states of repair. They are jammed into crevices, roped to outcroppings and balanced on brackets on sheer cliff faces as if floating. Some have been broken into by foraging animals, the skulls and bones visible as if the dead were preparing to rise.

Our walk across the rooftop of the Philippines proceeds along a mountain track deep in the forest, which is home to cloud rats, forest mice, warty pigs and deer, according to Talanay. Hunting and timber were the economic mainstays in Sagada but recent decades have seen the introduction of cash crops, most notably coffee.

“Welcome to Sagada’s Starbucks,” says Talanay, pointing to the thatch-roofed Baw-eng Coffee Shop, which has a backdrop of vegetation, stands on a coffee farm and serves mountain-grown brews to thirsty hikers. We pair ours with lemon-cream cookies.

Fortified with caffeine, we trek on into the forest. The path climbs then descends to follow a stream, leading through dark caves and patches of upland meadow until it opens onto a clearing drenched in midday sunlight. Butterflies flit everywhere, birdsong chorusing from the tree canopy.

We could walk indefinitely in temperatures this conducive and surroundings this seductive, the pull of nature impelling us towards wherever it is Talanay is leading us, for we have no destination in mind. The act of walking is enough.

Like so many Filipinos, Talanay once travelled overseas to find work, in his case to Britain. No doubt it was hard to make a living in Sagada but, as the last leg of the hike takes us out of the forest to cultivated land marked by a wooden fence, the mud path becoming a narrow stone road, I begin to understand why he returned to this pristine corner of Earth.

We conclude our hike, as all good hikes should end, in a pool beneath a waterfall – feeling a lot farther from Manila than the 400km a crow would fly.

item.title: [SCMP] Pacific island states are trapped in Cold War 2.0
item.description:
In early July, China fired a test missile from a nuclear submarine into the South Pacific for the first time, a weapon capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Washington and Canberra were livid. The Pacific has long been the exclusive testing ground for such long-range missiles from the United States. How dare China!

The reaction from Pacific island states was more measured. While leaders from Tuvalu, Palau and the Solomon Islands strongly criticised the test, the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) failed to draft a united statement. Last month, foreign ministers again failed to agree on criticising Beijing, with Kiribati and Nauru reportedly refusing.

Finally, this month, a PIF statement that “registered concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test” was issued. China was not named, and Nauru disassociated itself.
item.content:encoded:
In early July, China fired a test missile from a nuclear submarine into the South Pacific for the first time, a weapon capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Washington and Canberra were livid. The Pacific has long been the exclusive testing ground for such long-range missiles from the United States. How dare China!

The reaction from Pacific island states was more measured. While leaders from Tuvalu, Palau and the Solomon Islands strongly criticised the test, the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) failed to draft a united statement. Last month, foreign ministers again failed to agree on criticising Beijing, with Kiribati and Nauru reportedly refusing.

Finally, this month, a PIF statement that “registered concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test” was issued. China was not named, and Nauru disassociated itself.

Kiribati previously said singling out China was unfair when the US regularly tested such missiles near the Marshall Islands. In March, the US launched a Minuteman III ICBM from California, landing near the Marshall Islands 6,700km away; it followed a similar test in November last year. The US has test-fired at least 15 ballistic missiles into the Pacific since 2021.

The historical precedent weighs heavily. Between 1946 and 1996, the US, Britain and France conducted over 300 nuclear tests in the Pacific, particularly in French Polynesia and the Marshall Islands, resulting in radioactive contamination, mass displacement, high cancer rates and generational trauma. The double standard is glaring.

Geopolitically, the region resembles a feudal hierarchy: small island nations as vassal states, Australia and New Zealand as local lords, and the US as king.

Since its Aukus alliance with Britain and the US, Australia has increasingly resembled just another vassal. According to a recent Guardian report, US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil – what some analysts describe as a “colonisation”. Data by California’s Nautilus Institute shows the US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more, with defence corporations accessing an additional 18.

Meanwhile, under the Compacts of Free Association, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and Palau operate as US defence outposts, with Washington exercising defence veto power over their foreign conduct.

Australia’s diplomatic recalibration towards China reveals a troubling disconnect. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese initially pursued stabilisation after Beijing lifted punitive sanctions. China ended embargoes on Australian wine, barley and lobster by December 2024 as bilateral trade soared.

Yet stability proved ephemeral. Albanese now speaks openly of China seeking “hegemony” – clearly an exaggeration, paranoia or both. He defended the US missile tests, saying there was no comparison with the Chinese test. He is right – who can compare with America when it comes to weapons tests?

This tougher posture coincides with alarming developments. As US President Donald Trump’s erratic Asia policy erodes Washington’s credibility, Canberra doubles down, gambling its strategic future on a declining Pax Americana. Australia’s flurry of Pacific defence pacts with Fiji, Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu signals renewed great-power competition even as Aukus submarine deliveries remain uncertain.

Beijing has warned of “measures” over any challenge to the Chinese lease for Darwin port even as it distances itself from what it calls “selfish political gains”. Australian public opinion diverges from elite consensus: 61 per cent view China as an economic partner rather than a security threat. Yet Australia’s security establishment reflexively adopts Washington’s hawkish assumptions precisely as their foundation crumbles.

As Laura Tingle, ABC’s global affairs editor, wrote recently: “The world is a particularly confusing place just now. But no one seems more confused about their place in it than Australia.”

Meanwhile, former New Zealand prime minister Helen Clark has issued a pointed warning: Wellington’s rush into Pacific security pacts threatens to erode its cherished tradition of independent foreign policy. Clark – who also led the UN’s development arm for eight years – argued that such moves undermine the Pacific’s future as “a zone of peace”.

For decades, New Zealand balanced independence from superpower blocs with maintaining a nuclear-free Pacific. Both pillars now face strain. “The Australians being in the market for nuclear submarines isn’t helpful,” Clark said, predicting Canberra will host an American base for such vessels.

Her critique targets the premise that Washington can indefinitely guarantee Pacific security while managing global commitments. Invoking Australian strategist Hugh White’s argument that China’s rise makes US primacy unsustainable, Clark cited America’s Iran preoccupation as evidence of overreach. “Apply that to the Asia-Pacific context. It’s not real, is it? So this is all a game of bluff.”

Australian public opinion diverges from elite consensus: 61 per cent view China as an economic partner rather than a security threat.

Clark warned that “New Zealand must never be seen as a proxy”. Her 2003 refusal to send combat troops to Iraq defined her premiership’s principled independence. She accused the current coalition government of having made “unfortunate moves”. On China, Clark counselled pragmatism: “We need to continually work on how we maintain good engagement and dialogue”.

Small nations preserve agency through principle, not alignment. Wellington should remember that. As usual, however, the interests of small island nations are being trampled on amid their larger neighbours’ strategic muddle.

The Pacific islands deserve better than to become pawns in a new cold war. Their residents suffered generations of trauma from nuclear testing conducted by powers that now demand their loyalty in condemning others for far less. They face existential threats from climate change while watching wealthy Western nations prioritise military competition over climate action.

Australia and New Zealand style themselves as Pacific champions, but their actions reveal different priorities. Canberra’s strategic panic drives deeper military integration with Washington, while Wellington’s traditional independence frays. Neither has offered Pacific islanders a vision beyond choosing sides in someone else’s conflict.

Washington, Canberra and Wellington cannot credibly claim to champion Pacific interests while maintaining double standards on missile testing. The US is militarising Australian territory while reducing island states to defence outposts. Australia cannot reconcile economic interdependence with China and security anxieties through military posturing. New Zealand is surrendering the independent foreign policy that gives it moral standing.

The small island states’ months-long hesitation before issuing a mildly worded statement without naming China shows they no longer automatically align with the Anglo-American sphere. They need to assert greater agency if they are to have a fighting chance against climate change and outside dominance.

item.title: [SCMP] Bukhara Biennial spearheads cultural blossoming of the city as well as the wider Uzbekistan
item.description:
It might sound and look like an odd juxtaposition: chef-nun Jeong Kwan, of Netflix documentary series Chef’s Table fame, unearthing kimchi she has been fermenting for 10 weeks next to a new installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley.

Yet, set in Bukhara’s 16th century Khoja Kalon Mosque, the two made perfect sense as collaborative highlights of the closing ceremony of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, which ran from September 5 to November 23 last year.

A contemporary art festival, the Bukhara Biennial was conceived by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) and forms part of a broader plan to revitalise Uzbekistan’s living heritage as well as establish a permanent cultural district in the historic city. Its first theme, “Recipes for Broken Hearts”, was inspired by Uzbekistan’s national dish, plov. A hearty meal of rice layered with meat, spices and vegetables, the ideas of healing and restoration imbued in plov were the conceptual crux of the gastronomy, art, craft, architecture, music and performance on display.
item.content:encoded:
It might sound and look like an odd juxtaposition: chef-nun Jeong Kwan, of Netflix documentary series Chef’s Table fame, unearthing kimchi she has been fermenting for 10 weeks next to a new installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley.

Yet, set in Bukhara’s 16th century Khoja Kalon Mosque, the two made perfect sense as collaborative highlights of the closing ceremony of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, which ran from September 5 to November 23 last year.

A contemporary art festival, the Bukhara Biennial was conceived by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) and forms part of a broader plan to revitalise Uzbekistan’s living heritage as well as establish a permanent cultural district in the historic city. Its first theme, “Recipes for Broken Hearts”, was inspired by Uzbekistan’s national dish, plov. A hearty meal of rice layered with meat, spices and vegetables, the ideas of healing and restoration imbued in plov were the conceptual crux of the gastronomy, art, craft, architecture, music and performance on display.

Gormley’s Close (2025) – created from mud bricks with Uzbek artist Temur Jumaev – channelled the theme by exploring vulnerability, communal recovery and a reconnection to ancestral roots. Jeong Kwan’s kimchi was woven into a collaborative culinary performance with Indian artist Subodh Gupta. Blending Korean temple food with Bihari fare, the hybrid meal was served inside Gupta’s pavilion-like installation, Salt Carried With the Wind (2024-25), situated outside the Ayozjon Caravanserai, one of four in an interconnected complex, on a site once occupied by Bukhara’s spice market.

All through the event, the locations were significant, as the Bukhara Biennial was designed to house site-specific installations, soundscapes and performances not in purpose-built, white-cube galleries, but in restored or adapted caravanserais (merchant inns), madrasas (educational institutions), trading domes and mosques. While fellow Silk Road stopover Samarkand and the national capital, Tashkent, are undergoing their own cultural transformations, this preservation-first approach is what sets Bukhara apart.

Since its establishment in the 6th century BC as one of the main centres of the Persian Empire, Bukhara’s status grew as a spiritual nexus for Sufism and as an intellectual hub and home to scholars, poets and artisans. That Bukhara has lived many lives is evident from both its monumental buildings, spanning the 5th to 20th centuries, and the most intricately embroidered gold zardosi motifs and ikat prints on silks and various textiles found in the shops of the Old Town.

In the city’s Registan square, the curved, mounded walls of the Ark of Bukhara, a sizeable citadel, stand tall. Built in the 5th century, the compound housed rulers and their courts until 1920, when it was attacked by the Soviet Red Army, which deposed the emir of Bukhara and established Bolshevik rule. Next to the fortress stands the most prominent reminder of that later era: the steely, industrial Shukhov Tower, a water supply, forming a visual paradox that differentiates Bukhara from the more uniform Tashkent, where the Soviet influence is starkly evident in the brutalist buildings that dominate that city.

Across the street from the Ark of Bukhara, the early-18th century Bolo Hauz Mosque dazzles with its intricate, three-dimensional muqarnas decoration and vibrant mosaic tilework. Its linear lines present a striking contrast to the more rounded, ancient structures elsewhere in the Old Town, both charting the evolution of Islamic architecture. Just a short walk away stands the 10th century Ismail Samani Mausoleum, the soft, circular geometry and woven pattern capturing an aesthetic from when the region’s prominent Zoroastrian community was in the early stages of converting to Islam.

Revitalising these venerated sites, and others, was a crucial aspect of the agenda, as “the plan to reanimate restored and previously closed landmarks and open them up as living sites of making and dialogue was […] appreciated not only by the inhabitants of Bukhara, but also the tourists”, claims Gayane Umerova, chairwoman of the ACDF and the commissioner behind the inaugural Bukhara Biennial.

She enlisted Dubai- and Tokyo-based Lebanese architect Wael Al Awar and his studio, Waiwai, to execute this vision, to revive and make accessible to its inhabitants as much of Bukhara’s history as possible. In addition to repairing mosques, caravanserais and other structures, the most dramatic intervention the architect made was to pedestrianise large parts of the Old Town. “We created outdoor spaces, seating and platforms where the local community could gather recreationally, and use beyond the biennial,” says Al Awar.

Aligned with Umerova’s desire to present Uzbek artists and artisans on a global stage, the curatorial theme of the first Bukhara Biennial was born from curator Diana Campbell’s interest in rice cultures. “Most cultures use rice in some way, and there’s some version of plov in every culture,” says Campbell, citing the likes of biryani, paella, Korean bap with kimchi and West African jollof rice, all of which were served to the public at the Rice Cultures Feast, another part of the closing programme.

A key aim of the event was to stimulate local communities, the ACDF having spent seven years researching and mapping out the forms of craft across the country. “Supporting artisans is part of a strategy to develop the creative industry in Uzbekistan,” says Umerova. “We are looking at ways to nurture what we have already, by protecting our heritage and developing a framework that is sustainable and inclusive for artisans.”

All 70 artworks – each a collaboration between a recognised artist and a local craftsperson or -people – were made on site, in Bukhara.

“By placing artisans and craft masters at the heart of the programme and pairing them with international artists, we invited visitors to experience craft not as a souvenir product, but as a living, sophisticated cultural practice,” Umerova says. “It frames craftsmanship as something to observe, learn from and respect.”

Some of the most transformational and noteworthy works were housed in the 16th century Gavkushon Madrasa, and highlighted the specific artisanal crafts Bukhara is celebrated for. Local ceramicist Abdulvahid Bukhoriy’s Blue Room (2024-25), made with coppersmith Jurabek Siddikov, was lined entirely with blue-glazed tiles produced by hand, the immersive installation featuring a central metal sculpture and delicate ceramic panels, the elements depicting aquatic motifs often found in Uzbek textiles – a nod to age-old beliefs that fish possess the power to absorb human illness.

Miniature master Davlat Toshev transformed two adjoining rooms with his signature hand-painted “wallpaper”. Featuring traditional visual themes such as pomegranate trees, Toshev employed ebru, a marbled-paper painting technique widely believed to have originated in Bukhara. Toshev has a large studio in Bukhara’s Old Town, where he conducts workshops for deaf and mute children, using art as a method of expression and communication, as well as a way to keep traditional mediums alive.

Less than 200 metres (656 feet) from the Gavkushon Madrasa, Brazilian artist Marina Perez Simão and Bukharan mosaic master Bakhtiyar Babamuradov mirrored the heavens. Across the courtyard floor of the Fathullajon Caravanserai – a 19th century Silk Road resting stop – they laid out Untitled (2024-25), a fantastical celestial map. Quickly becoming one of the event’s most photographed works, the vibrant installation paid homage to Uzbekistan’s legacy in astronomy and the creation of early space-mapping instruments.

Kwan’s involvement in the Bukhara Biennial was more significant than it might have seemed at first glance, with members of the Koryo-saram, the Korean diaspora in Bukhara, assisting in the preparation of the kimchi and the resulting meal. In 1937, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, concerned about the military threat from Japan, exiled 172,000 Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia. Now, Uzbekistan is home to the world’s fifth-largest overseas Korean population.

Increased global attention on Uzbekistan as a result of the Bukhara Biennial has established a gateway into a historically under-visited destination, and the massive funding poured into the exhibition marks an effort by the Shavkat Mirziyoyev administration to build cultural infrastructure, revitalise the nation’s creative landscape and attract foreign investment after nearly three decades of post-Soviet stagnation.

“We want to inspire younger generations to take the creative path and to equip those already in the creative industries, including artisans, with the same opportunities and infrastructure they’d experience internationally,” says Umerova, noting that 40 per cent of the country’s population is under 35 years of age.

Projects in the works for the city’s new cultural district include the Jadids’ Legacy Museum, scheduled to open in 2027. Set in the restored 19th century home of Usmon Khodjaev, a leader of the Jadid reform movement and the first president of the short-lived Bukhara People’s Soviet Republic (1920-24), the destination will be dedicated to the initiative that modernised education across Central Asia. Farther afield, in Tashkent, the Centre for Contemporary Arts (CCA Tashkent), housed in a former tram depot, opened earlier this month, and the National Museum of Uzbekistan is scheduled to launch in March 2028.

“Since we launched the 2025 Bukhara Biennial, Uzbekistan has become globally recognised for its role in fostering arts and culture across Central Asia,” says Umerova, who notes that the opening of the CCA Tashkent marks “an exciting next step – and a historic moment, not just for the people of Tashkent, but for the citizens of Uzbekistan more widely. As the country’s first contemporary art centre, I believe it will inspire the next generation of artists, curators, poets and thinkers”.

Bukhara’s inaugural biennial surpassed all expectations, clocking up a total of 1.8 million visitors. Umerova credits it with encouraging “a more thoughtful kind of tourism. People came not just to see monuments, but to understand the stories embedded in them”.

Dates for the next edition of the Bukhara Biennial have been set for September 3 to November 21, 2027. Thai architect Kulapat Yantrasast will direct it, leaning on themes of urban space, ecology and sustainable development. In line with the ACDF’s mission to foster community involvement, admission to venues and public spaces will remain free.

“When you bring art tourists, who actually look, care and value the work and sites, that’s a genius strategy,” says Campbell, who specialises in curating large-scale exhibitions centred on community engagement in regions with sparse cultural infrastructure, most notably as the artistic director of the Dhaka Art Summit, in Bangladesh.

In an era defined by content overkill, the ability to evoke genuine awe and wonder sometimes feels like a lost art. In Bukhara, it is simply an ancient art form being powerfully revived.

item.title: [SCMP] Wing Shya: photographer to Wong Kar-wai on working with the great and good of Hong Kong cinema
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.

I DID A double major: graphic design and fine art. In the summer, I’d drive to San Francisco, or fly to New York on the cheapest ticket I could find. I could earn a few dollars drawing people in Washington Square Park, in Greenwich Village. I had so much energy then.

AFTER GRADUATING IN 1991, six classmates and I opened a graphic-design company in Vancouver. Eight months in, we were doing well. One afternoon at a restaurant in Chinatown, I picked up a Hong Kong gossip magazine and looked at the layout. I said to my friends, “I have to go back – this design is terrible. I want to do something in the city.” They tried to talk me out of it. But within a week, I’d sold my car and bought a ticket home, without telling my mother. I flew back and rang the doorbell. She opened it and said, “Why are you here? You’re not welcome. We have no space.” I slept on the sofa.

WORK WAS HARD to find, but in 1992, I won a biennial photography prize and gave the money to my mother – it’s the right order of things. In 1993, I got a job at J. Walter Thompson (JWT), the advertising agency, but only lasted about a year; I had too much ego and was always fighting clients. I ran into an old school friend, Jan Lamb Hoi-fung – a singer who DJ’d at Commercial Radio Hong Kong – on the street by chance and he got me hired as the creative director there. It was a tiny department, just two of us, responsible for everything – stage design, ads, CD covers, concerts. I worked hard and I loved it. I got to know the biggest Cantopop stars: Jacky Cheung Hok-yau, Andy Lau Tak-wah and Faye Wong – she was there all the time.

THROUGH A FRIEND, Eric Kot Man-fai, my portfolio landed in front of Wong Kar-wai, in 1996. He said I could shoot some promotional pictures. On a Japanese commercial he directed, I hid behind a sofa so the crew wouldn’t throw me out of the tiny set – and when the official photographer could not get enough pictures, my photos were the only ones that worked. Because of that, Wong Kar-wai sent me to Argentina a year later, for Happy Together, starring Tony Leung Chiu-wai and Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing.

I HAD NEVER done film stills professionally. I didn’t even own a sound blimp – the soundproof box for your camera so you can’t hear the shutter going off. Because of this, I mostly shot between takes. I captured the actors sitting, waiting, hanging out: Tony and Leslie just breathing, not performing. One afternoon, on a rooftop, the street noise was so loud that my shutter was no longer an issue and I could finally shoot freely. Most of my images that you know from that film came from that one afternoon.

THEN, THE COLOUR. I was shooting slide film. Wong Kar-wai demanded to see the images immediately, but there were no labs where we were in Argentina that could process slide film. We found a shop that only did negative film. Because slide film is positive film, they ran mine through the wrong chemicals, and that turned everything green. Argentina’s grey walls became luminous. In the end, Wong Kar-wai loved it. It became the visual language of the whole film. I can call it a mistake, or I can call it, “I had no choice. It ended up like this.” After that, I left the radio station and started my company, Shya-la-la Workshop.

ONE DAY, WE were shooting in a train station – it was too noisy for sound recording – so I could shoot freely. Leslie was annoyed at me for distracting him. My shutter was too loud, but I kept going. I explained to him, “I’m only scared of Wong Kar-wai, not you. Because he hired me, only he can fire me.” He looked at me for a long moment, then said, “I like your attitude. When we get back to Hong Kong, you’ll work for me.”

HE MEANT IT. From that day until he died, I shot almost every photograph of Leslie for his work, his concerts, behind the scenes, albums and tours. He was the most considerate person I’ve known in this industry. He remembered everyone’s habits, every name, if you took milk in your coffee. He looked after the whole crew, from driver to delivery boy. We travelled together for concerts, shot in countries I’d never been to. I still think about him.

FOR In the Mood for Love (2000), Wong Kar-wai gave me one instruction: the film is about red. He gave me some music to listen to, and that was it, initially. So, in 1999, I went to Tokyo, bought 40 or 50 different rolls of film, shot test after test and laid every print in front of him. He picked one: an old, obscure film – barely still in production, its colour deeply reddish. I called the manufacturer; they were closing the following month because nobody was buying their film any more. “How many rolls remained,” I asked. “Two hundred,” they said. I bought every single one.

THAT PHOTO FILM was made in the 1960s or 70s, and its dyes were slowly failing – that’s why my shots for In the Mood for Love look the way they do. After we finished the film, there was none left anywhere in the world.

THERE ARE PEOPLE who I learned almost everything from. One, of course, is Wong Kar-wai, who gave me access to everyone, all these famous faces. I learned how to crop a photograph by watching him on the monitor. But another one of my real teachers is William Chang Suk-ping – the famous production designer and art director. Even now, we work together regularly. Just the other day, I was on a shoot, with William beside me. I learned what makes a picture by watching what Wong Kar-wai and William chose to keep and what they threw away. I don’t think of my work as mine alone. It is a long conversation with two people I deeply respect.

IN 2010, FOX came to Hong Kong to make a Chinese film – my feature-film directorial debut, Hot Summer Days. Stars such as Jacky Cheung, Maggie Cheung Man-yuk, Nicholas Tse Ting-fung and Daniel Wu Yin-cho all appeared in it, for very little money, as a favour to me because we had 20 years of trust.

DIRECTING FELT LIKE another universe. You have to think about logistics, 80-people crews, egos, dangerous rigs, scenes and even the crew lunches! I’ve made more films since. I still shoot fashion campaigns, recently for Chanel and Bottega Veneta, and – fingers crossed – I am now writing a television drama.

MY FIRST BOOKS came about because cultural curator Shelly Verthime told me at a dinner many years ago that she wanted to make a book. One day, in 2015, she called from Hong Kong International Airport, so I put a hard drive with every photo I owned into a taxi and sent it to her, at the terminal. She spent a year and a half editing alone. An investor funded the printing and an exhibition in Shanghai, in 2017. My shows in Japan (in Tokyo and Kyoto), the books (Chaos [2020], Solace [2024], Is [2026] and more) – they happened all because someone pushed. I never start these things myself.

MY WORK HAS been in the Mori Art Museum, in Tokyo, and in the V&A, in London. I don’t think about it much. I’ve done it already, and the future is more exciting to me than the past. What I still love is being on set – the mess, the crew eating together, the gossip, the waiting. I think the universe already has a script written. My job is only to follow my heart and see what page it turns to next.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Ode to the horse: 5,000 years of human-equine connection on display in new Kazakh museum
item.description:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.

Located around 70km from Almaty, the Ush Qiyan Open-Air Museum sits near the village of Akshiy, in the Enbekshikazakh district – the kind of place most travellers pass without noticing.

Opened this summer, it rises from the flat landscape as three circular log dwellings with sloping roofs – constructed from more than 1,000 logs, the exhibition brochure proudly proclaims – and is designed to evoke what some researchers believe are among the oldest known permanent settlements of the steppes.

Ush Qiyan receives no government funds, has launched no grand marketing campaign – it is just a father, his son and their semi-domesticated horse named Ayan grazing outside.

“Kazakh culture is, first and foremost, the culture of the horse,” says Nurbol. “In gratitude to these beautiful animals, we built this museum as a temple of knowledge to enlighten people.”

Before there were empires and criss-crossing trade routes, before valiant steeds carried armies across continents and monks towards enlightenment, there was a culture that first looked at a wild horse and saw something more than prey.

It is believed that the Botai people lived in what is now northern Kazakhstan, in the 4th and 3rd millennia BC. Mighty they were not.

As far as archaeologists could detect, the Botai built no cities, wrote no epics and erected no monuments that would survive the centuries and catch the eye. Instead, what they left behind were traces of dwellings, scattered pottery and the bones of horses – thousands upon thousands of them, now housed at the North Kazakhstan Regional Museum of History and Local Lore, in Petropavl.

Archaeologists around the world now widely believe that the Botai were the first to domesticate the horse, though the claim is debated each time new evidence comes to light. Experts argue that the proof is in the bones, which show signs of bit wear on the teeth, from the bridle gear used to control them, and in the residue of mare’s milk found in their pottery, leading them to theorise that the Botai were not just hunting horses, but riding them, milking them and living alongside them. If true, it would be one of the most consequential partnerships in human history. Migration, trade, warfare, the spread of ideas and empires – all of it would eventually travel on horseback.

And yet, there is a twist. Genetic research suggests that the animal the Botai domesticated is actually the ancestor of the Przewalski’s horse – the stocky, pot-bellied wild horse that still roams parts of Central Asia. In other words, the first horse believed to be part of human culture eventually returned to the wild, rather than develop into the modern steeds we see today.

Ush Qiyan attempts to capture this paradox – the last wild-horse species being descended from domesticated ancestors, raising questions around whether the breed is truly wild or simply feral – telling a complicated story about a partnership that was formed, dissolved and formed again, as the modern horse, tamed later in the Early Bronze Age, became the engine of human history.

It all started with Ayan, a stallion who seems to straddle both worlds. In the spring of 2021, Nurbol went looking for a light-hued horse in the Altai mountain range, in eastern Kazakhstan. He had no particular reason for doing so; he says he simply, suddenly, felt like having one.

A friend had told him about a remote village with no internet and a horse bearing a rare isabelline colour. Having negotiated a price, it took Nurbol three nights by truck to take Ayan back to Almaty.

“He was born wild, near Lake Zaysan,” says Nurbol.

Ayan is, according to Nurbol, a Zhabe – one of Kazakhstan’s oldest horse breeds, distinguished by its stout frame, thick neck, muscular croup and substantial body weight. But with a pale, almost metallic coat that glows golden in sunlight, Ayan is no ordinary Zhabe.

Whether the isabelline colouring is genetically possible for this breed is another matter, but Nurbol is not a man to let science get in the way of a good story.

“It was a sign from above,” he says, referencing the heavens. “Our horse bears all the hallmarks of an ancient celestial horse. It has a powerful mind and transmits information telepathically.”

Separating fact from fiction is a secondary concern for Nurbol.

He is a researcher whose published works focus on history, archaeology and ancestry. At the same time, he is a believer who sees little boundary between myth and reality. In his telling, Ayan the horse is both a living animal and the latest chapter in a legend that began with the Botai people and culture five millennia ago.

“In the Chinese epic Journey to the West, the White Dragon Horse came from the West,” says Nurbol, noting that, in the text, “the tale of the monk [Tang Sanzang] who met a White Dragon Horse happened somewhere in our area. [Kazakhstan] is a land of legends where myth and reality intertwine”.

Ayan eventually inspired the construction of Ush Qiyan, which began in the summer of 2024. It took about two years to finish, building only in the warmer months, with a small crew, and involved no architects or contractors in the conventional sense – just workers stripping bark from logs under a punishing sun.

“Construction was not easy,” Nurbol recalls. “It was very hot. People were breaking down like matchsticks.”

All the logs had to be processed and cut by hand, following what Nurbol dubs “experimental archaeology” – a scientific approach to understanding how ancient nomads built their dwellings, and the physical labour involved. It was, in his words, an attempt to recreate not just the look of the Botai world, but the toll it took.

Money for the project came entirely from the Baimukhanovs, and though that choice was deliberate, it had consequences. Nurbol remembers days when, due to a lack of funds, “we were idle and wondering how to raise money to continue construction. [But] this was our conscious choice, and we are pleased with the result”.

Ilyas was born in Almaty and grew up tagging along on his father’s scientific expeditions across Kazakhstan. Ush Qiyan, in some ways, is the culmination of a childhood spent among artefacts and open landscapes. Now in his early adulthood, Ilyas speaks with the composure of someone a decade older.

“My father and I are like-minded people,” he says. “I represent the younger generation, a new perspective.” While Nurbol supplies the vision, the younger Baimukhanov thinks about sustainability, management systems and visitor services.

His own “eureka!” moment came years earlier, in the Botai region of northern Kazakhstan, where he met the influential archaeologist Viktor Fedorovich Zaibert, who discovered, excavated and opened the Botai settlement site in 1980, in the Aiyrtau district. In doing so, Zaibert gave the world some of the earliest evidence for horse husbandry and domestication. “He [was] an amazing person,” Ilyas recalls. “He told fascinating stories about history.”

What struck him were the traces of ancient circles still visible in the earth – the outlines of dwellings long gone – and the bones and pottery scattered across the ground, some more than 5,000 years old.

“I am happy to have interacted with such a great archaeologist and seen the artefacts in person. It’s unforgettable,” says Ilyas. Zaibert died in 2022, but his influence, legacy and memory live on in the log walls of the museum.

A visitor to Ush Qiyan moves through the three log structures, each roof shaped like an inverted basket, echoing the ancient yurts of the early nomads. Inside, scientific replicas of nomadic dress from various periods, made from materials such as hide, bone and leather, created for the 2018 documentary Equus: Story of the Horse, which Nurbol co-produced, hang alongside other props. Installations showing reconstructions of historical dwellings and horse sculptures fill the spaces between, and films are screened for guests who want to linger.

In another room, Daniyar Sarbassov, a 36-year-old artist from the Bayanaul district, showcases his work: castings of horses, mostly.

“Daniyar is our friend,” says Nurbol. “He’s a talented sculptor with great potential.” But the connection to the museum runs deeper than friendship. Sarbassov’s horses are not decorative – they carry, as Nurbol puts it, “the code of the Great Steppe”.

One of his pieces, an aluminium-and-bronze statue titled Zhuyrik (2022), was sculpted earlier, in his studio, when Sarbassov had no knowledge of Ayan, or the world Nurbol was building. But when he spotted the ivory-coloured horse, something shifted. “After seeing Ayan, I decided that this work would be better placed at the entrance of the museum,” he says.

In Sarbassov’s description, Zhuyrik is not simply a horse running.

It is “a creature that merges with the wind and moves together with the air”. Its smooth surface catches the natural light from the structure’s oculus as it shifts throughout the day, seemingly dissolving the boundary between the horse’s body and the surrounding space.

“A truly swift horse is difficult to perceive in its entirety,” he says. “Its speed is often experienced through the impression, trace and sensation of movement left in our memory.”

As its metallic shine echoes Ayan’s coat, Sarbassov calls it “a spiritual symbol of the museum”. He hopes it will remain there permanently, and that visitors will find their own meaning in the work: “One viewer may see freedom in the image of a horse, another may be reminded of their ancestors, while a third may discover an entirely different meaning. My hope is that they will pause for a moment to reflect on their own history, their homeland and their place as human beings within this vast expanse of time.”

Outside, Ayan grazes, unaware of the symbolism attached to him. Nurbol considers him the living echo of the story Ush Qiyan exists to tell: the wild horse that came to humans, changed their world and still carries that independence in its blood. Whether that story belongs to history or to myth is, by now, beside the point.

Between them, a father and son have built a temple to the horse, raised by hand, off the beaten track. “We live in a complex era of digital technology; it’s difficult to be surprised by anything,” says Nurbol. “But at the same time, we look to the future without forgetting the past. Our museum is like a time machine.”

But a time machine moves forwards, too. More visitors will be drawn by the same road that connected cultures. Ush Qiyan sits beside it, ready to welcome those who pause on their way to somewhere else. “The Great Steppe has always been a place of meeting,” says Nurbol. “We are open to dialogue with the world.”

item.title: [SCMP] Paul French lifts veil on final months of China’s last emperor in the Forbidden City
item.description:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.

In 2018, his City of Devils: A Shanghai Noir was a Kirkus Reviews’ “Best Book of the Year”. In 2024, Her Lotus Year: China, The Roaring Twenties and the Making of Wallis Simpson received much coverage and quotably upbeat reviews (“Her Lotus Year stays in the mind as a bright, shining, lively snapshot,” says The Spectator. “Delightful to read.”).

Now, it’s the turn of Puyi in The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City, which falls into a royalty subgenre that French calls “doomed monarchy”.

Although he’s writing – primarily – for a Western audience, as a category, it has promising global reach. Earlier this year, French was told by his Chinese publisher that only one other foreigner has shifted (and signed) more books in China: British author and historian Simon Sebag Montefiore, whose 2016 work on those quintessential doomed monarchs, The Romanovs: 1613-1918, was a massive hit.

Puyi, of course, didn’t meet his doom with an execution in a cellar. He was six years old in 1912, when the Manchu empire ended and the new Republican government decided to leave him behind the walls of the Forbidden City – an oddity, roaming around the “Great Within”, attended by eunuchs (“teapots without spouts” was the local term). With his peculiar upbringing and background, that child would grow into the adult who, during the second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945), would become his country’s “Great Traitor”.

French, who was a language student in 1980s Beijing and lived in Shanghai for many years before returning to Britain in 2014, had been marinating this story for a while. He sensed that – “a bit like Wallis Simpson”, the American socialite whose relationship with Britain’s King Edward VIII led to his abdication – people sort of knew about Puyi but not really. He’d been struck by the blank stares he met when he mentioned him to Chinese-language students at a couple of British universities.

French realised that it’s been almost four decades since he, along with many others, had been “blown away” by the Bernardo Bertolucci epic, The Last Emperor (1987), which was – an amazing achievement – filmed inside the Forbidden City.

While he was wondering how to tackle the topic, he wrote an article about Puyi’s wife, Wanrong, in 2024, for this magazine. “Wanrong is so beautiful and there are so many pictures of her and I thought it would be fun,” he says. “I did mention, in a couple of lines, that she’d had a tutor and this was one of the things the film had missed.”

In fact, Joan Chen – who played Wanrong in the film – makes a single reference to her tutor as a “Miss Windsor”. Bertolucci, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother-in-law, Mark Peploe, knew Wanrong was educated but not by whom, so they made up a name with British royal resonance. Wanrong’s tutor, however, was not British. Isabel Ingram was an American “mishkid” – a child of missionaries – born in Peking (Beijing) in 1902 and educated at Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, in the US.

After the PostMag piece came out, French was contacted by a man called Kenneth Mayer, who told him he was Ingram’s grandson. “He said, ‘Thank you so much for noticing Isabel; no one else does,’” French recalls. “And then he said, ‘By the way, you really should read her diary and she has some letters from this Johnston guy …’”

French was staggered. He hadn’t known about the diary, and the “Johnston guy” was Reginald Johnston, Puyi’s Scottish tutor, played in the film by Peter O’Toole.

Johnston had written a memoir which, in its 486 pages, makes a single reference to “the Empress’s American friend who had been her teacher of English both before and after the Empress entered the Forbidden City as a bride”; and his letters and journals had been destroyed after his death in Edinburgh, in 1938.

Diary! Letters! Such finds are history’s gold dust. Even better, Ingram, who died in Virginia in 1988, had typed up all of it. (French, who revels in his North London unacademic blokeishness, makes some cheerfully unrepeatable comments about the trials of handwritten research materials.) Once he’d read the Ingram documents, he knew he had his book. Ingram was 20 when she became Wanrong’s tutor, in October 1922. A few months later, on December 1, Wanrong, aged 16, married Puyi, also 16.

French decided to focus The Last Emperor of China on the 23 months between that five-day wedding – “the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see”, he writes – and the couple’s expulsion into the “Great Without” on November 5, 1924, which brought an end to more than 500 years of (occasionally interrupted) dynastic occupation of the Forbidden City.

Apart from sporadic chunks of necessary context, the book is like a wonderfully evocative play with four principal performers – a middle-aged Scottish man, a young American woman and two teenage Manchu royals – on a spectacular stage.

French says he’s only too aware that he joins a long line of Puyi biographers, but what Ingram brings to his version is the voice of modernity. Formal lessons with Wanrong, who had a golden fountain-pen and silver inkwell, rarely took up more than an hour or two. Afterwards, there would be hair-braiding, hat-selecting, wardrobe-rummaging, dancing to gramophone records, chocolates and cigarettes.

Ingram’s language – “I love her for life”; “cute little thing”; “the Empress is still darling”; “he nearly died on the spot” – could be that of a Californian blogger, and the film these scenes evoke isn’t the Bertolucci drama; it’s Clueless, in every sense. Her diary also testifies to Puyi and Wanrong’s genuine friendship as they go cycling and kite-flying and dog-walking around their vast, mouldering compound. Many happy photographs are taken.

For French, Ingram is an important witness to the growing intimacy between the newlyweds. As he says, a great debate among biographers concerns Puyi’s sexuality and whether he was asexual or homosexual. Famously, on his wedding night, the last emperor had sloped off to the Hall of Mental Cultivation for a think.

“He’s 16!” says French, and goes on to note that “the single most surprising thing [in the diary] is when Isabel writes about ‘the curtain being drawn’ and there are no lessons today … Obviously, like all young people, they work out what goes where”.

But Puyi and Wanrong’s isn’t the only unexpected romance in the book. It becomes clear through his letters that Johnston, 28 years older than Ingram, is attracted to her. French believes he was “heartbroken” when she refused him, which is why her name was never mentioned in his memoir. Perhaps. (On the other hand, this reader thinks it was more about Johnston’s considerable, publicity-hogging ego.)

At any rate, Johnston’s letters to Ingram veer in tone from housekeeper (“I am sorry to hear chewing gum has been introduced into the palace”) to stalker (“Who is the young man you kept looking at so earnestly all the time?”). Eventually, he becomes self-deludingly creepy. “Did you explain to the Lockharts how and why you refused to let me kiss you when we were on the Emperor’s swing together?” he writes. “And yet it would only have been a remote, innocuous fatherly salutation!”

By then, the quartet had broken up. On November 5, 1924, several hours after the early-morning palace coup, Ingram was taken by rickshaw to the Forbidden City as usual, but was barred from entering. At the Gate of Divine Prowess, the commandant told her that Wanrong had gone into the “Great Without” “hatless, coatless, baggage-less”. Ingram, who would leave China in 1927, never saw her dressing-up companion again.

In the Bertolucci film, when soldiers arrive to evict Puyi and Wanrong, they are playing tennis. In real life, he was peeling her an apple, that ancient symbol of expulsion, in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Soldiers took a – distinctly unhappy – photo, which is in the book, of his abandoned bedroom: an adolescent muddle of kung fu novels and toys.

“Once they go outside the gilded cage, they’re lost,” says French. “You could write another book about Puyi in Manchuria and try and get into the psychology of what happened to that relationship when he’s manipulated, with no advisers, and she knows that they’ve made a horrendous mistake and slips into opium abuse.”

In this immensely readable book, however, French steps only briefly beyond the palace gates and into that future when Puyi was crowned the emperor of Japan’s puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1934 – another doomed monarchy.

Another sombre note is the contrast between Ingram’s spirited diary and the fate suffered by Wanrong in the final summary, which is heart-wrenching.

Puyi survived and, in the 60s, made several return visits to the Forbidden City. Premier Zhou Enlai liked to keep an eye on him.

Asked what he thinks of Puyi now, French replies, “I do take the Zhou Enlai line. He’s supposed to have invited Puyi to a lunch and told him, ‘You weren’t to blame for becoming emperor and what happened then. But you can be blamed for what happened after.’”

item.title: [SCMP] Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze
item.description:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.
item.content:encoded:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.

Repeated, prolonged exposure to haze wreaks havoc in the human body, triggering inflammation, asthma attacks and other respiratory problems.

“That is already a signal that their body is not simply being irritated,” Asma said. “It is having a clinically significant response to the exposure.”

Left unchecked, that exposure can scar lungs, cause cardiovascular illness and lead to cancer, as PM2.5 particles small enough to cross into the bloodstream spread the damage far and wide.

In Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index (API) Malaysia uses climbed as high as 519 this week, surpassing a level so hazardous it triggered a state of emergency in the Bornean state’s Serian district that was lifted only once the air was clear enough to breathe.

Singapore, which had gone three years without air quality breaching unhealthy levels, restarted daily haze alerts and in the Philippine capital, more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) from the wildfires, schools were forced to shut their doors.

Climate experts warn of a meteorological double-whammy conspiring to make this the hottest year on record for Southeast Asia. “Super El Nino” – a massive warming of the Pacific Ocean that chokes off regional rainfall – is being stacked on top of a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which cools regional waters, further cutting off moisture.

Together, they act as a force multiplier, fuelling droughts, heatwaves and wildfires from Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra to the Mekong nations of Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

Extreme weather is only part of the story, however. The fuel for the fires is the land cleared, year after year, for palm oil, pulpwood, corn and sugar cane, on plantations that drain water from the region’s peatlands until they become as dry as tinder.

It’s agribusiness vs the atmosphere, observers say – and for now, agribusiness is winning, despite decades of Asean pledges, a real-time satellite-powered fire-detection system and US$1.5 billion in funding to tackle the crisis that has yet to be raised.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, facing an electorate once again struggling to breathe, called on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to take action. “Asean ministers must seriously look at it”, he told reporters, “because it is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies”.

The crisis is also decimating some of the world’s greatest stores of biodiversity. Pitiful photographs from Kalimantan of rescued pangolins curled into defensive balls and orangutans with their fur singed orange-black have refocused the world’s attention on the issue.

But climate advisers warn against a convenient narrative taking hold: that this is simply the fault of this year’s “super El Nino”, rather than the businesses making billions from the burning.

“El Nino and dry conditions are risk multipliers, not the root cause,” said Renard Siew, a climate change specialist at the Centre for Governance and Political Studies in Kuala Lumpur.

“We cannot govern El Nino away,” he added. “But we can manage land better, prevent fires, enforce regulations and reduce the underlying vulnerability. Climate change is effectively making the consequences of weak governance more severe.”

History repeats

By far Southeast Asia’s worst haze offender is its most populous nation and largest economy.

Indonesia’s peatland fires began alarmingly early this year, with hotspots detected way back in January – months before the typical dry season burn.

More than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) have burned so far and police have named 138 arson suspects, including eight companies implicated in forest and land clearance.

But arrests are of little comfort to the families forced to live under a cloud of toxic haze.

Lina Rose, a mother of four in Sarawak, has had to keep her children indoors for most of the recent school holidays.

“I’m worried about my child who has asthma,’’ she said. “The sky looks so gloomy that you think it’s going to rain, but then it doesn’t.”

Residents hark back to 2015, when Indonesia’s worst haze crisis in decades – fuelled by the same slash-and-burn clearance for palm oil and pulpwood – released thousands upon thousands of tonnes of carbon into the atmosphere and blanketed tens of millions of people, from Sumatra to Singapore, in choking smog for months on end.

Jakarta, faced with international fury, labelled that year’s crisis a “crime against humanity of extraordinary proportions” and belatedly signed on to an Asean road map promising haze-fire skies by 2020.

But that deadline came and went – and still the haze continued. A second road map followed in 2023, with a new target year of 2030. Yet few believe this new framework will be any more effective than the first.

The reason comes down to Asean’s modus operandi: consensus and non-interference are not conducive to policing environmental crime across borders, analysts say.

Meanwhile, the palm oil, pulp and paper conglomerates whose business models depend on cheap land clearance have every incentive to keep enforcement weak.

“The fundamental shift has to be from ‘managing haze’ to preventing the conditions that create it,” Siew said. “That means stronger land-use governance, better fire prevention and peatland management, clearer accountability across supply chains and much greater investment in local capacity.”

To its credit, the newer haze-control road map does “contain something its predecessor lacked”, according to Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a legal expert and researcher at Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies – namely, measurable indicators, “including zero days at the highest alert level for two consecutive years”, as well as pledges to reduce burned area by 10 per cent and hotspots by 5 per cent, with a midterm review due in 2028.

But the mechanisms for holding anyone accountable remain weak.

“The consensus principle and the related ‘Asean Way’ approach have led to the creation of mechanisms that are ambitious but have been described as toothless,” said Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of political ecology at the University of Malaya. “This is because the mechanisms often lack strong operationalisation or punitive measures.”

Sanctions would not work, Fahrizal said, as Asean members would never agree to impose them on one another, adding that the latest road map “is not a binding instrument” with reporting done by member states themselves.

Asean’s consensus-based approach has allowed Jakarta to commit to haze-free targets with no penalty attached to missing them. After 2015, it did impose a moratorium on peatland clearance and created an agency to restore affected areas, eventually rehabilitating some 1.6 million hectares (6,177 square miles).

But Indonesia also produces more than half the world’s palm oil and its industry has found ways to adapt, securing permits for “sustainable” farming on the one hand while surreptitiously clearing protected areas on the other.
