The peatland restoration agency, for all the good it did, was dissolved last year.

Fahriza said the most “realistic” option for enforcing anti-haze measures was to employ independent, third-party verification of data that could be reviewed collectively to impose “consequences for reputation and access to financing”.

Absent that, Asean’s credibility – and relevance – would “ultimately be judged by the citizens breathing the smoke, not by the number of documents signed”, he said.

Patchwork fixes

Advocacy groups are done waiting for another of the bloc’s road maps to fail.

On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights called for the region’s latest haze crisis to be treated as a “human rights emergency”, urging Asean member states to use an October summit in Vietnam to close enforcement gaps and hold corporate offenders to account by forcing companies to publish fire and land-use information for independent scrutiny.

Some smaller-scale bilateral cooperation has also emerged. Thailand and Laos signed a data- and resource-sharing agreement on Wednesday aimed at pre-empting wildfires before they spread, echoing a similar arrangement Bangkok struck with Myanmar last month.

External pressure is building too, with mixed results. The European Union’s threatened ban on palm oil linked to deforestation has been delayed to 2027, after Indonesian objections and Brussel’s own need to lock in a new trade deal amid rising US tariffs.

Then there are the built-in weaknesses in Asean’s own crisis-response tools: under the bloc’s latest haze agreement, accepting emergency firefighting help from abroad remains entirely voluntary.

“At the moment, the arrangement exists, but ultimately it cannot function without the explicit invitation of the host country,” Varkkey said.

“This should be a scientific decision, when the haze is bad enough to warrant external help, not a political one.”

Singapore perhaps best captures the tension between profit and public safety: its companies are heavy investors in Kalimantan’s palm oil sector, yet its people – the region’s wealthiest – no longer tolerate haze imported from beyond their borders.

The city state’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 lets it prosecute companies for haze pollution regardless of where the fire was lit, a legal reach that was tested after the 2015 pollution crisis when six companies, including Indonesia’s Asia Pulp & Paper Group, were investigated – a move Jakarta called an affront to its sovereignty.

As of 2021, four of the cases remained open, Singapore’s environment minister told parliament. There has been no public confirmation of their closure in the years since.

Meanwhile, Singapore still wheezes whenever Borneo burns.

Wildlife photographer Eddie Vanderloot, 47, has learned to recognise a tight chest and itchy eyes as unmistakable signs that the air has turned.

“Constantly planning activities around the air quality gets tiring and it’s hard not to feel worn down by it,” he said.

“Even with all the windows closed, a mask on, an air purifier and air conditioners switched on, the haze still affects me for hours.”

item.title: [SCMP] Golden years: in Southeast Asia, growing old is big business
item.description:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.
item.content:encoded:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.

Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.”

The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65.

These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home.

Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline.

Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market.

For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead.

“I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.”

For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said.

Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up.

“I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.”

A middle ground

Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed?

Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer.

It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old.

In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children.

“Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required.

In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far.

The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability.

Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments.

“The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said.

Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month.

Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023.

Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge.

A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000.

The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market.

Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living.

Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two.

More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers.

Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030.

“This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said.

Ageing in luxury

With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly.

The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services.

More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia.

Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”.

“Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said.

At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce.

A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500.

“Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.”

Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden.

Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said.

Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list.

Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said.

Crossing borders

For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost.

The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand.

“Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes.

Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand.

“You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI.

Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added.

“Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.”

Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost.

Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement.

Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts.

“The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.

“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.

Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.

Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.

These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.

Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.

“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.

Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.

“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

item.title: [SCMP] A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
item.description:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.

As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets.

Earlier this month, Chinese renewable energy company Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online in Ulanqab. The AI computing facility has, at its heart, a 120,000-square-metre AI data centre, roughly the area of 20 standard football pitches, according to a company statement.

Designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators, the campus has a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts, a scale that would make it one of the world’s largest AI computing facilities.

For comparison, Colossus 2, the massive US-based AI data centre run by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to a ranking by consultancy Epoch AI.

Envision selected the Ulanqab location because it could pair computing infrastructure directly with renewable power, with the Galaxy Campus partly powered by Envision wind farms, according to the firm.

Ulanqab accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s, according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

“Much of that wind once simply blew past, wasted,” said Yang Wenlong, a project director at Envision Group. “Now it can be turned into electricity for computing, and then into tokens.”

About 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s energy was powered by green electricity, including solar power, Yang noted.

A decade-long pivot

Ulanqab’s shift from raising cattle and potato harvesting to the AI frontier has followed a decade-long path.

In 2013, Huawei Technologies began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab.

Short video giant Kuaishou initiated construction of a data centre in 2020, and completed the first phase of a centre designed for 300,000 servers several years later.

Traditional data centre operators VNET, Centrin Data and Chindata have since added green, AI-focused computing projects in Ulanqab, and Hangzhou-based AI model start-up DeepSeek was reportedly set to add one gigawatt of computing capacity in the city earlier this year.

As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, according to local government figures.

The city has a combined 12.5 gigawatts of capacity under development or planned, three times the 4.2 gigawatts projected for Johor, the southern state of Malaysia that has emerged as one of the largest data centre sites in the Asia-Pacific region, according to recent research by investment bank Goldman Sachs.

“We are no longer selling computing power; we are selling tokens,” said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data management bureau, referring to the industry’s preferred measure for the units of text processed by AI models.

China’s appetite for those tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025, before exceeding 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data.

This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them. For Ulanqab, the wind blowing across the grasslands is no longer merely an energy resource – it helps to power an AI query.

And every AI token comes with a cost.

The power economy

“Every one million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data.

In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power.

Rates vary by supply arrangement, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (US$0.05) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can account for 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant.

At full utilisation, a one-gigawatt AI computing centre might consume as much as 8.76 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. Cutting the electricity cost by just 0.1 yuan per kilowatt-hour might reduce a centre’s annual power bill by about 876 million yuan.

For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is no marginal advantage – it is a central part of the business model.

But it is only half the equation. The electricity consumed by computing equipment ultimately becomes heat that has to be removed.

That is how Ulanqab’s cold, dry climate provides another advantage. With an annual average temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius, the city can use outside air as a natural cooling resource for much of the year, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and leaving more electricity available for computing.

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes directly to computing, while a higher figure indicates more power is consumed by supporting systems such as cooling and power conversion.

Leading data-centre clusters in the region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of close to 1.5, meaning that more of each watt reaches its chips.

A difference of only a few cents can translate into hundreds of millions of yuan in savings at gigawatt scale. Those efficiencies matter because the amount of electricity consumed by computing has been rapidly rising.

China’s data centres consumed about 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.6 per cent of national power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA).

By 2030, annual consumption by the sector was expected to reach about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times 2025 levels, and account for roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use, according to Wang Hongzhi, director of the NEA.

A coordinated system

The race to secure electricity for AI infrastructure is not unique to China. In the US, the rapid expansion of AI data centres has raised concerns about whether existing power grids can keep pace with demand, with some projects facing delays because of a bottleneck in securing enough electricity.

This is in contrast to Ulanqab, where AI giants and tech behemoths are betting that its wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a cheaper and more sustainable foundation for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

For China, the challenge is not only generating enough electricity, but also ensuring that electricity supply and computing capacity grow in tandem.

In 2026, China’s Government Work Report called for the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply for the first time, reflecting Beijing’s push to better align its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure with the country’s power system.

The concept, known as “computing-power and electricity coordination”, aimed to bring together electricity generation, grid capacity, energy storage and computing resources so that renewable power could be used more efficiently to support growing AI demand.

Jiang Yi, spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, described the new power grid as providing stable, clean electricity, the computing network as the “brain” directing intelligent power-grid scheduling and renewable energy consumption, and the communications network as the “highway” supporting cross-regional computing.

That vision goes beyond simply building more data centres. It requires linking electricity, computing and communications infrastructure into a more coordinated, national system.

For Ulanqab, that could make its advantages more valuable. Its wind farms provide renewable electricity, data centres then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia.

But China’s computing boom has created another challenge: not all that capacity is being used.

While demand for AI computing is surging in some of the country’s biggest technology centres, large amounts of capacity elsewhere remain underused, leaving servers, power infrastructure and expensive data centre facilities running below their potential.

Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) puts the gap in stark terms. In 2025, China’s intelligent-computing centres had about 3.8 billion card-hours of intelligent-computing capacity available, but only about 1.4 billion card-hours were actually used, putting utilisation at just 36.8 per cent.

CAICT has called for closer coordination between computing supply and demand, including better scheduling of computing resources and more precise matching between users and available capacity.

The mismatch reflects the geography of China’s computing buildout. Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates, while much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based.

Moving up the value chain

For Ulanqab, the next challenge is therefore not simply building more servers, but making sure those servers are connected to real demand.

The city is now seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan for 2026-28, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens.

The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, focusing on green computing for large AI model training and inference, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent.

The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models.

For a user sitting thousands of kilometres away, an AI query may take only seconds to answer.

Behind that response, however, is a chain of infrastructure stretching back to places such as Ulanqab: servers drawing electricity, cooling systems removing heat and wind turbines turning the movement of air across the grasslands into power.

The next time someone asks a chatbot a question, part of the answer may begin with the wind passing through the grasslands of Inner Mongolia – transformed first into electricity, then computing power and finally into the words that appear on a screen.

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.

Rather than operating via a single entity, this public capital flows through a layered matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately managed funds. It is a system that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets, with an alternative perspective on what can be considered a return on investment.

Last year, state-affiliated investors supplied more than 90 per cent of the committed capital tracked in China’s private-equity market, a surge from just under 79 per cent in 2021, according to domestic data provider Zerone.

This mandate comes directly from the top. At a high-level national science and technology gathering in Beijing on July 8, President Xi Jinping urged financial capital firms to “invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology”.

How this capital is deployed could determine whether China will succeed in its ambitions to become a self-reliant tech superpower – or suffocate its economy under the weight of state-engineered overcapacity.

How the money moves

“2018 was roughly the turning point for us,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital, a Hangzhou-based investment firm with about 40 billion yuan (US$5.91 billion) under management. Puhua aimed to raise between 7 billion and 8 billion yuan in 2026, with state-affiliated investors expected to account for about 90 per cent of the total, he said.

According to Shen, it was around eight years ago that traditional private-business owners in eastern Zhejiang province started to pull back their investments in Puhua, as they realised that venture funds’ long holding periods had failed to match their liquidity expectations.

China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage

– Zhou Kaibing, Hangzhou Venture Capital Association

Around the same time, dollar funds began retreating amid escalating US-China tensions. More recently, restrictions on investment in sensitive technologies from both sides have deepened the financial divide, while Beijing’s aggressive push into strategic technologies has drawn a diverse array of state investors.

This state support arrives in vastly different forms and at distinct stages of a company’s life cycle.

For CXMT, which is headed for a blockbuster public market debut in Shanghai next week, a combination of national, provincial and municipal investors supplied the massive capital, credit support and project construction resources required to build a capital-intensive memory chipmaker from scratch. Industrial and private investors came later.

It is one of the clearest examples of the “Hefei model”, under which the provincial capital of central China’s Anhui uses state investment vehicles to back strategic industries, absorb early risk and anchor companies locally before bringing in market capital.

By contrast, state funds entered Unitree Robotics much later in the game. That financing came after the robot maker had already proven its technological and commercial viability, timing that aligned with Beijing’s elevation of robotics to a strategic priority.

Unicorn artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek, initially funded entirely by private wealth, only recently drew backing from the national AI fund after emerging as a powerful symbol of China’s challenge to US tech supremacy.

Hong Kong-listed Zhipu, whose market cap at the market close on Friday was HK$585.95 billion (US$74.72 billion), attracted a cluster of local government funds when it neared its initial public offering in January, as cities vied for a stake to secure a share in the booming AI sector – or remain economically relevant.

One main delivery mechanism for state capital is the fund-of-funds model.

Puhua Capital, for instance, has twice been selected to manage sub-funds backed by the National SME Development Fund, which is financed by central and local fiscal capital alongside smaller state and institutional investors.

In this set-up, the national fund typically provides a 30 per cent anchor commitment. Puhua would raise another 30 per cent to 40 per cent from provincial, municipal or district-level state vehicles, before securing the remaining balance and deciding where to base the fund.

Puhua would retain its day-to-day investment autonomy, but operate under strict oversight. An appointed observer, separate from the investment committee, could join deal discussions from an early stage and veto proposed investments.

Furthermore, at least 70 per cent of the capital must be deployed into “522” companies – businesses with no more than 200 million yuan in annual sales, 200 million yuan in assets and 500 employees. Performance metrics and related-party transactions would be regularly audited.

“The requirements are higher,” Shen said, “but so is the support for policy direction and industrial coordination.”

In this way, a fund-of-funds brings in broader outside capital while steering it to policy priorities. Meanwhile, the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund, launched late last year, operates further upstream, channelling central fiscal money through regional funds into hundreds of professionally managed sub-funds focused strictly on early-stage technologies.

Some point towards specific industries. For example, the “Big Fund” – China’s flagship semiconductor investor – concentrates capital into this fiercely competitive arena, taking equity stakes directly and backing specialist funds across the chip supply chain.

Others can be deployed through local platforms that take stakes or finance construction, as in Hefei, as well as via investments and acquisitions by state-owned companies.

Who bears the risk?

Capital is pouring into strategic industries through funds with longer lifespans as exit routes expand. Platforms like Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market and the Hong Kong stock exchange now allow these companies to go public sooner, enabling broader retail investors to share in the potential gains.

“A loop is gradually taking shape, directing more capital towards hard tech companies,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture-capital firm spun out of an institute under the state-run Chinese Academy of Sciences. The firm’s early bets on China’s photonics sector have begun to see tangible returns amid the AI boom.

However, state investors and private funds do not always share the same scorecard. While a market fund is judged mostly on financial returns, local governments must also account for the number of factories built, jobs created and taxes generated – competing goals that can weaken financial discipline and fuel intercity rivalries.

This local tournament has made China’s industrial policy unusually entrepreneurial – and competitive. Beijing signals the strategic direction, while cities fiercely contest fund structures, industrial estates, credit support and real-world applications.

In the nascent stages of an industry, this rivalry can foster healthy development, or what Shen described as “a hundred flowers blooming”. But it can also lead to severe overcrowding, driven by local governments’ fear of missing out on the next big macroeconomic wave.

The solar panel and electric vehicle (EV) sectors offer stark cautionary tales for today’s policy darlings, such as AI, semiconductors and embodied intelligence.

Expanding production capacity can benefit a single city seeking to boost its local economy, but when dozens of cities replicate the strategy simultaneously, the result is crippling overcapacity and collapsing profit margins on a nationwide basis.

“China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage,” said Zhou Kaibing, chairman of the Hangzhou Venture Capital Association. He noted that some companies with little initial appetite for scaling up began to aggressively add capacity after winning government support.

The structural risks of this approach were highlighted by state broadcaster CCTV in April through the downfall of Neta, a once-prominent EV brand owned by Hozon Auto.

Local governments in Tongxiang in Zhejiang province, Yichun in central Jiangxi province, and Nanning in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region all took equity stakes in Hozon, providing factories, land, subsidies and financing to secure production bases within their regions – even as the carmaker remained deeply unprofitable.

As its products lost ground in a brutally competitive domestic market, the company fell into court-supervised restructuring in 2025. The failure has put billions of yuan in state-backed equity, subsidies and fixed industrial assets at risk.

This raises an uncomfortable question for policy architects: are these losses an acceptable cost of doing business in a nascent industry, or do they represent a fundamental failure of discipline in public investment?

Zhou argued that to mitigate these risks, governments should avoid trying to act as talent scouts themselves. Instead, they should delegate capital management to professional fund managers, who are better equipped to pick market winners and diversify risk.

The state investment system excels at moving money, but it is still learning how – and where – to take risks, he said.

Course correction

Beijing, however, is very much aware of these structural vulnerabilities.

At the same science and technology gathering in Beijing, Xi issued a pointed warning, saying that regions must adapt policy to local conditions rather than blindly chase hot sectors or engage in wasteful, copycat development and “involution-style” competition.

The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure. You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return

– Mi Lei, CAS Star

Policymakers are now attempting a delicate balancing act: mobilising unprecedented capital for technology while imposing rigorous discipline on how it is deployed.

In recent years, this policy response has been rolled out in stages. The State Council’s 2024 policy document, which introduced 17 guidelines on promoting high-quality venture capital, served as the sector’s broadest overhaul since 2016.

It encouraged “patient capital” with a more long-term outlook, shifting the evaluation metrics from a deal-by-deal basis to that of a fund’s full life cycle, while protecting managers from liability for honest failures and broadening exit strategies beyond initial public offerings.

By 2025, new rules shifted the focus directly onto government fund management. This guidance curbed overlapping funds and duplicate local investments, demanded more professional management and called for a greater tolerance for legitimate, due-diligence-backed investment losses.

This year, the State Council’s guidance for investment approval extended the course correction to the factories, industrial estates and public liabilities that often accompany state-backed investments. It also tightened its oversight of fixed-asset projects, enabling it to halt disorderly capacity expansion while introducing lifetime responsibility for officials whose unlawful investment decisions cause serious economic consequences.

“The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure,” said CAS Star’s Mi. “You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return.”

The ultimate test for the equity investment model with Chinese characteristics is whether its bureaucracy can not only learn to accept the inevitable losers that are inherent to venture capital, but also retain the discipline required to cut their losses after failed bets.

item.title: [SCMP] Apple’s biggest-ever leak happened in India. Will firms rethink their China relocations?
item.description:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.
item.content:encoded:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.

India began to deliver. In 2022, the country produced around 6 per cent of all iPhones, but by 2026, that figure was expected to surpass 25 per cent, according to data from Counterpoint Research.

However, this year Cook’s vision faced a sobering reality check. In June, a massive cyberattack by hacking group World Leaks hit Tata Electronics, Apple’s Bengaluru-based partner for iPhone parts and assembly, leaking more than 200,000 files on the dark web. Analysts called the leak the biggest in the company’s history.

“India has proven it can scale production; now it must prove it can scale trust,” said Christopher Tang, a professor specialising in global supply chain management at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

While India managed to ramp up labour-intensive assembly, attract major suppliers such as Foxconn and Tata, and leveraged government incentives, the incident revealed that the ecosystem still needed to catch up in three vital areas: information governance, supplier discipline, and cyber-operational integration, Tang noted.

“India can become a major global manufacturing hub,” Tang said. “But overtaking China as the world’s premier factory is a much higher bar.”

The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data

Christopher Tang, UCLA

Made in India?

The files from the Tata leak included Apple’s component and supplier lists, as well as photos of the firm’s unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, exposing sensitive details of the chips on its main circuit board as well as hundreds of parts, according to Reuters.

Apple, Tata and the Indian authorities were reportedly investigating the incident. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.

“This leak is significant because Apple’s secret sauce that creates its competitive advantage depends not only on Apple’s own systems but also on every node in its manufacturing network,” Tang said.

“The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data or highest-complexity product ramps too quickly to newer hubs,” he added.

This year’s leak was only the most recent test of India’s fast-expanding manufacturing capabilities. In 2024, Tata suffered a fire that led to a production halt at its facilities in Tamil Nadu, a state in the country’s south.

Despite the fallout, analysts said they did not expect the breach to diminish the importance of India in Apple’s ongoing efforts to diversify its global manufacturing.

“The current situation will be very much of a remediation-and-move-on situation, rather than an existential threat to Tata’s partnership with Apple,” said Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research.

“Ultimately, we believe this doesn’t halt India’s momentum, but it will surely lead to an industry-wide re-evaluation” of the information technology infrastructure of electronic manufacturers, Pathak said.

Still, the breach cast a shadow over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “Make in India” initiative to transform India into a global manufacturing and innovation hub, challenging China’s dominance as the “world’s factory”.

The expansion of Apple’s manufacturing network in India helped drive the country’s broader industrial upgrade. In recent years, the US tech giant’s major suppliers, including Foxconn and Tata, have scaled up operations heavily across the country from Tamil Nadu to neighbouring state Karnataka.

Foxconn, also known as Hon Hai Precision Industry, injected another US$1.5 billion into its India unit last year.

However, Apple’s aggressive expansion plans in India also faced pressure from its home country. US President Donald Trump said publicly last May that he had asked Cook to stop building plants in India and step up production in America.

Beyond Apple, India has also attracted South Korea’s Samsung and Chinese handset makers including Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo to build production bases there.

India has surged to become the world’s second-largest mobile phone maker by volume, with 99.2 per cent of its locally sold handsets produced inside the country, according to official data.

Just last week, New Delhi unveiled a new US$6.5 billion initiative, the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme, to incentivise smartphone brands that produce their devices locally and source domestic components. The initiative targets US$460 billion in domestic mobile phone production over the next five years, with a significant increase in exports.

Hedging or diversifying?

India has been gaining an increasingly significant role in Apple’s supply chain. Last year, Cook revealed that most of the iPhones sold in the US were produced in India. In the meantime, almost all iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and AirPods products sold in the US market were made in Vietnam.

China, on the other hand, would continue to manufacture the vast majority of products sold in the rest of the world, according to Cook.

Apple’s geographic diversification efforts, known as the “China plus one” strategy, sought to shift away from total reliance on the Chinese manufacturing powerhouse amid geopolitical tensions and a supply bottleneck.

The diversification efforts accelerated during the Covid-19 pandemic, when virus control protocols in China dragged some of Apple’s product shipments to a halt at one point.

“For Apple, ‘China plus one’ is primarily a hedge against geopolitical risk, rather than a decision driven purely by commercial efficiency,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.

“This incident will not reverse its strategy, but it reminds Apple that diversification is not a simple copy-and-paste of the China playbook,” Sun said.

When talking about China’s manufacturing advantages, observers have usually focused on China’s low cost, efficiency and sheer scale, while underestimating its suppliers’ ‘soft power’ in commercial confidentiality, rapid response and systemic risk control, he added.

“Supply chain security is, in itself, a core manufacturing capability,” Sun said.

While Apple has previously faced product leaks in the form of unauthorised photos and smuggled parts from factory floors – including facilities in China – the scale of the recent cyber breach was unprecedented, according to analysts.

Every added node is an added point of vulnerability

Sun Chenghao, Tsinghua University

Sun noted that a leak of this magnitude was highly unlikely to hit long-established Chinese Apple suppliers, although the possibility could not be wholly dismissed.

“The key is not just firewalls; it’s the organisational discipline, tiered authorisation, physical isolation, supplier compliance auditing and a culture of secrecy forged over decades of collaboration,” Sun said.

A global supply chain alert

Analysts noted that the strategy, adopted to mitigate geopolitical risks, inadvertently exposed the supply chain to other risks.

“The more fragmented a supply chain becomes, the more a company must share blueprints, test data, supplier lists, quality standards and internal workflows across more touch points,” Sun said.

“Every added node is an added point of vulnerability.”

A source within Apple’s supply chain noted that cyberattacks are a universal threat, which is increasingly prevalent after the explosion of artificial intelligence technology.

“It’s not just Tata; all suppliers have been under attack in some way,” said the person, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the matter. “What happened to Tata sounded an alert across the supply chain globally.”

While India faces immediate scrutiny, experts stressed that cybersecurity required an ongoing arms race extending beyond any single company or region.

“No country or supplier ecosystem is immune,” UCLA’s Tang said.

item.title: [SCMP] Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
item.description:
Wu Shicun is the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies and chairman of the Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance. In this interview, the first in a series about the South China Sea dispute, he discusses ways Beijing can respond to rival claimants.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

With Manila intensifying its “transparency” campaign, how does China view the current situation and what challenges does it face?
item.content:encoded:
Wu Shicun is the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies and chairman of the Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance. In this interview, the first in a series about the South China Sea dispute, he discusses ways Beijing can respond to rival claimants.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

With Manila intensifying its “transparency” campaign, how does China view the current situation and what challenges does it face?

Manila’s so-called “assertive transparency” initiative operates on its own distinct logic and playbook. [The initiative includes documenting and publicising what Manila calls Chinese grey-zone tactics, such as blockades and the use of water cannons.]

Since 2023, the Philippines has deliberately intruded into the waters around Renai Jiao [the Chinese name for the disputed Second Thomas Shoal], deliberately provoking China into intercepting its vessels or deploying water cannons.

On-board media outlets then package these confrontation scenes into short, viral videos and disseminate them globally. These clips manufacture an international perception that “China is the bully in the South China Sea and the Philippines is the victim”. This is the core mechanism behind their public relations strategy.

Behind this are Philippine domestic political considerations, aimed at securing more budget and equipment support from the Philippine Congress for its coastguard.

In contrast, Beijing’s energy has been primarily concentrated on rule-making. For instance, in promoting consultations for a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea (COC), negotiations have been grinding steadily forward for over a decade since 2013.

Concurrently, working group meetings on the implementation of the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea [DOC] recently convened for their 56th session in Vietnam. These institutional frameworks are where China invests the bulk of its diplomatic capital.

Regarding narrative construction, there was a period when China was in a passive position, especially during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and later when the Philippines intruded on Sabina Shoal and spread false information such as “China intends to occupy the feature”.

But as we gradually recognised the Philippines’ tactics and the Western media backing behind the scenes, we began to adjust our counter-strategy, sometimes proactively clarifying to the international community Manila’s false narratives and exposing their deliberate methods of smearing China.

This is exactly why Beijing is now proposing to proactively construct a new South China Sea narrative. This shift is a direct lesson learned from countering the Philippines’ playbook.

Our strategy has undergone a profound paradigm shift; it is expected to become even more proactive in the future. Because as a responsible major power, China must always tell the truth.

Meanwhile, extra-regional countries such as the United States and Japan use the Philippines’ narrative as an excuse to intervene in South China Sea affairs, thereby binding their military apparatus to the Philippines.

The United States wants to use its military bases and supply them with weapons. Japan, through signing the reciprocal access agreement with the Philippines, has lowered the threshold for Japan’s Ground, Maritime, and Air Self-Defence Forces to enter Philippine bases; Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and other countries have also signed visiting forces agreements similar to the reciprocal access agreement with the Philippines.

Recently, Japan also participated in the US-Philippine Balikatan military exercises. In this year’s exercise involving seven countries, Japan sent more than 1,400 personnel, three warships and helicopters for the first time, and conducted live-fire drills with a surface-to-ship missile system during the exercise. This was also the first time Japan used a show of force overseas after World War II.

Even many middle powers are seeking to cash in on the friction and seek geopolitical benefits, relying on the Philippines to stir up trouble. The combination of various factors has enabled the assertive transparency initiative to achieve its expected PR goals for a period of time.

However, today the international community – other Southeast Asian countries – has gradually seen through these tactics, and the initiative’s influence is gradually weakening. The global public is no longer so easily buying into its fact-distorting hype.

With deepening defence ties between Japan and the Philippines, and strengthened Vietnam-Philippine maritime cooperation, what challenges does Beijing’s bilateral strategy of engaging in direct talks with claimant countries face and how should China respond?

This is indeed a new development. Other rival claimants are attempting to join forces to counter China on certain issues. At the same time, they have been lukewarm towards China’s initiatives that are designed to foster regional peace, stability and environmental protection while delivering tangible benefits to littoral states.

Some coastal nations are quietly conducting exclusive economic zone delimitations, which effectively encroach upon China’s rights and claims in the South China Sea, with some even crossing over into waters under Chinese jurisdiction.

Our policy remains consistent: resolving disputes through peaceful means, bilateral consultations and negotiations. Yet, we’re seeing increasingly frequent contact between Vietnam and the Philippines recently.

Beyond state visits, they have privately hammered out internal agreements to tighten maritime cooperation, explore the possibility of bilateral maritime delimitation, conduct joint law enforcement and share intelligence. Manila has even gone so far as to encourage Vietnamese fishermen to operate in the waters surrounding Huangyan Island [Scarborough Shoal], an attempt to pile pressure onto China’s maritime law enforcement.

Data shows that a considerable number of Vietnamese fishing vessels have appeared in waters around Huangyan Island. Video footage captured during our annual Sansha and South China Sea patrols reveals a substantial presence of boats flying the Vietnamese flag.

Considering the straight-line distance from Vietnam to these waters is nearly 1,000km (600 miles), such long-range cross-sea fishing operations are economically unsustainable for ordinary fishermen.

Without government subsidies and escort protection provided by the Vietnamese and Philippine coastguard authorities, these fishermen are likely to return empty-handed. Therefore, there is undeniably state backing and financial aid behind this.

There is clear growing coordination between rival claimants and with extra-regional countries, and Beijing is fully aware of it. However, I do not believe this poses a substantial threat to China’s rights and claims.

If they ever choose to make these delimitation agreements public – agreements that bypass China and violate our sovereign rights – Beijing simply will not recognise them, and it has a comprehensive suite of countermeasures at its disposal.

These countries are well aware of this reality, which explains why they prefer to quietly put delimitation on hold. Take the delimitation between Vietnam and Indonesia as an example. Although both sides signed a delimitation agreement, the boundary maps and geographical coordinates that should customarily be submitted to the UN Secretary General have yet to be provided.

Could you elaborate on what specific measures Beijing might take?

No matter how other countries attempt to draw these maritime lines, if an action infringes upon China’s interests, we will not only refuse to recognise it but will simply carry on with business as usual.

Take the attempts by Japan and the Philippines to delimit boundaries in the waters east of Taiwan – even if they draw their lines, China will absolutely never recognise them. Such behaviour will ultimately prove counterproductive for them, instead prompting China to further strengthen maritime law enforcement operations and enhance its actual presence in relevant waters.

I don’t believe these countries have thought this through properly. The era when China had its hands tied is gone. If they are trying to play petty games, they have completely miscalculated.

Why does Beijing treat Vietnam and the Philippines differently in the South China Sea dispute and how should it balance maritime tensions with Hanoi against the commitment to building a community with a shared future?

A US scholar previously asked me whether China was applying a “double standard” to Hanoi and Manila.

I told him plainly that when it comes to infringements in the South China Sea, China has no double standards. China has red lines whenever its rights and claims are violated – it’s simply the handling methods that differ.

The Philippines relies heavily on hyping things up through “megaphone diplomacy”, playing the victim card to court international sympathy. Manila deliberately provokes China’s rights and claims, anticipating that China will step in to carry out law enforcement and use water cannons. In its pursuit of so-called transparency, Manila behaves rather like a child who screams the moment you barely touch them.

As for Vietnam’s island-building, China’s opposition has been consistent and clear. We have repeatedly lodged diplomatic representations through both state-to-state and party-to-party channels, demanding that Hanoi halt such constructions.

These activities violate the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea, disrupting regional peace and stability while complicating the situation and escalating tensions. Its actions also do nothing to help the ongoing negotiations for the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea.

Data published by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI) confirms Vietnam’s actions. For example, Vietnam has been carrying out reclamation work across 18 islands and reefs [in the Paracel Islands].

Hanoi’s dredging across the archipelago has pushed its total artificial land mass past 11 sq km (4 square miles), putting its reclamation scale on a trajectory to rival or even exceed what China built between 2013 and 2015.

It is the tactics deployed by Beijing that differ, purely because Hanoi and Manila employ entirely different methods. Vietnam operates quietly.

Moreover, China does not wish for these island-building activities to derail the broader Sino-Vietnamese relationship, as the disputes do not represent the entirety of our bilateral ties. We are keen to avoid a situation where poor management or mishandling of maritime friction damages our bilateral relations or harms China’s ties with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Crucially, there is a deep-seated consensus between our two ruling parties, encapsulated in the “16-character guideline” [friendly neighbourliness, comprehensive cooperation, durable stability and looking towards the future] and the “Four Goods” spirit [being good neighbours, good comrades, good partners and good friends]. This is the big picture of Sino-Vietnamese relations.

How effective has China’s island-building been in protecting its maritime interests over the past decade and does Beijing still hold its “Big Triangle” strategic advantage – the highly fortified outposts at Fiery Cross, Mischief, and Subi Reefs – in the Spratly Islands, given Vietnam’s accelerated reclamation activities?

Whether China’s strategic edge remains intact largely depends on Vietnam’s subsequent moves once its island-building projects are wrapped up. Although Hanoi has pledged to deploy only civilian facilities, it remains to be seen whether they will actually walk the talk.

Vietnam occupies a considerable number of features, most notably Barque Canada Reef, which boasts the largest reclaimed footprint and is highly capable of supporting an airstrip.

According to data published by the AMTI, some experts estimate that Vietnam could eventually possess six to seven runways and 15 harbours across the Nansha [Spratly] Islands.

If these facilities are geared towards military purposes, might they be opened up for shared use with the US or Japan down the line? After all, Vietnam’s military and security cooperation with Washington and Tokyo has deepened significantly and intelligence-sharing is already under way.

Should they begin to pose a security threat to our civilian facilities, fishermen and garrisoned troops on those reefs, Beijing will certainly roll out appropriate countermeasures.

However, taking a broader view, this will not, in the short term, exert a disruptive or game-changing impact on China’s current capacity to safeguard its rights, law enforcement or project its maritime power.

You’ve said island-building could continue if necessary. Where would be the most critical location for reclamation, Scarborough Shoal or Antelope Reef? Why has China chosen this moment to dredge Antelope Reef after refraining from large-scale reclamation for the past decade?

Whether to build on Huangyan Island depends on several factors. Firstly, will intrusions into the territorial sea baseline around Huangyan Island that China announced in 2024 become the norm, as well as challenges from the Philippines and other external forces in future?

If parties enter territorial waters or fly through airspace without declaration and permission, China will certainly take countermeasures. Therefore, this potential security threat is an important precondition.
