“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond the Rose Garden and the military review, Trump and Xi get down to business
item.description:
After weeks of frustration, delays and posturing, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met on Thursday, holding talks on several bilateral irritants and announcing an ill-defined “new joint arrangement” as they kicked off the most consequential day of their high-stakes summit.

The arrangement was “good news for businesses, ordinary people and the global economy”, Xi said, according to state news agency Xinhua, without elaborating. “We must turn this vision into action,” he added.

Earlier in the day, Trump suggested that the two sides made progress on a Board of Trade mechanism aimed at reducing tariffs on non-strategic products in equal measure.
item.content:encoded:
After weeks of frustration, delays and posturing, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met on Thursday, holding talks on several bilateral irritants and announcing an ill-defined “new joint arrangement” as they kicked off the most consequential day of their high-stakes summit.

The arrangement was “good news for businesses, ordinary people and the global economy”, Xi said, according to state news agency Xinhua, without elaborating. “We must turn this vision into action,” he added.

Earlier in the day, Trump suggested that the two sides made progress on a Board of Trade mechanism aimed at reducing tariffs on non-strategic products in equal measure.

At Thursday’s state dinner, Trump gave Xi a large sculpture of a bald eagle, the US national symbol, adding that he and Xi represent different political systems but “the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better”.

“Together we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations,” he said.

Xi, in his second speech of the day, followed in offering a toast to the US president, adding that this was the second state visit between the two leaders in a year “making history”.

“This has added new substance to the constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability and provided new strategic guidance for China-US relations.”

Both leaders also reaffirmed support for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 groupings, which have summits in November in Shenzhen and in December in Miami respectively, teasing two more possible meetings this year.

The leaders started the morning with a formal arrival ceremony on the White House South Lawn and Rose Garden that included nearly 500 military personnel, the Chinese and American national anthems and opening remarks from the presidents.

Both leaders adopted a notably rosy tone throughout the day, highlighting areas of common ground, cultural touchstones and partnership efforts during World War II.

There was much the two nations could achieve, Trump said, citing people-to-people connections that “even made us allies in World War II”.

Trump added that security, technology and “superintelligence”, a term he has offered up to replace artificial intelligence, were key topics of discussion between the two sides.

“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” he said.

Xi followed in a similar vein, inviting 100,000 young Americans to visit China, offering a pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta and calling for greater cooperation.

“I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future,” Xi said in front of US and Chinese flags.

“China and the United States are different in national conditions,” added Xi during his first summit on US soil since 2015. “But through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better.”

Xi gave a nod to Trump’s “America first” catchphrase twice during the day even as he emphasised the importance of recognising China as an equal, underscoring the messaging by both leaders to their respective domestic audiences.

“Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” he said.

“Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world.”

Their comments were followed by a military review in the Rose Garden, part of which Trump has cemented over, capped by a flyover of military aircraft before the pair retired for bilateral meetings behind closed doors.

Their time without their respective retinues lasted less than an hour. Xi stressed Beijing’s position on Taiwan, urging Trump to “carefully” consider the US’ stance and oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

China’s first lady, Peng Liyuan, and US first lady Melania Trump also attended the welcome ceremony, attracting much attention during the event before they broke off to tour the National Museum of Asian Art.

Beneath the day’s florid language and repeated statements of friendship are a host of critical issues.

Analysts expect few breakthroughs or substantive deliverables during the summit, which ends on Friday, involving such difficult issues as artificial intelligence safeguards, rare earth minerals, trade tariffs, Taiwan arms sales, the Iran war, Ukraine and bilateral military relations.

“This is going to be a summit that’s relatively underwhelming with a small number of deliverables, but I think that works mainly to China’s advantage,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, given the lack of movement on overcapacity or other structural issues.

Relative to last year’s escalating tariffs and harsh rhetoric, however, many welcomed signs of a floor, however wobbly, under the fraught relationship.

One deliverable of sorts emerged hours before Xi’s aircraft even touched down when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two sides would extend a trade truce reached nearly a year ago in South Korea, but only for two months.

In far loftier and substantive comments than his US counterpart, Xi touched on military communication, fentanyl, AI, investment and the need for more communication.

The nations’ militaries could “maintain regular dialogue” as part of an overall relationship that involved “healthy” competition that was “kept within bounds”, he said.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control,” the Chinese leader added. “We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States.”

Xi’s visit drew local supporters outside the White House, many singing the Chinese song “Bless the Motherland”, as well as pro-democracy protesters, including a parade of Tibetan protesters that marched from the Chinese embassy.

Thursday’s talks are the heart of the three-day trip and followed Trump’s unusual move of greeting Xi in person at the foot of the jetway on Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews after a 15-hour flight, an expression of Trump’s respect for, and desire for respect from, the Chinese leader.

But the world has come to expect the unexpected from Trump, a proud disrupter who relishes slamming through norms and flexing his power and US military might.

Planners organised the summit to mirror Trump’s summit in Beijing four months ago. The time on the ground will be limited, with no side visits outside the capital and Thursday’s state dinner. The reciprocity was meant to underscore respect and the equality of the two wary competitors, an issue of particular importance to Beijing.

While the White House has been juggling its Iran war of choice, a Canadian trade showdown, Trump’s record-low popularity and pending November elections, summit preparations have been frustrated by the small number of US decision-makers and an impetuous president inclined to rip up plans on short notice, according to sources.

With low expectations for deliverables this week, some movement on artificial intelligence is high on the agenda. The issue has been a source of rising tensions in recent months as the two nations tout competing visions, promote rival national champions and oversee different regulatory environments.

Another entrenched problem, one of particular concern to the US side, is Iran. Trump badly wants Beijing’s help in forcing Tehran to the bargaining table to end a war he started over six months ago.

But China, which had been buying more than 80 per cent of Iran’s exported crude before the conflict, has baulked at increasing the pressure on its Middle Eastern partner, although it has stopped short of supporting Tehran in obvious military ways.

Another key issue involves the 90 per cent of global rare earth mineral processing that China controls. In recent months, Beijing has dispensed these critical resources sparingly to US companies.

China unsheathed its highly effective cudgel after “Liberation Day”, when Trump threatened tariffs of over 80 per cent on the Asian export giant, affording China enormous leverage that it is in no hurry to give up.

“China-US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world,” Xi said on Thursday. “But without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems.”

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese CEOs fly to US on own, await invites to Trump’s state dinner for Xi Jinping
item.description:
A small group of Chinese CEOs holding US visas has arrived in Washington after travelling separately from President Xi Jinping’s official entourage, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

But with the clock ticking and the business optics of the Chinese leader’s White House visit hanging on the final twists of diplomatic negotiations, the executives are still waiting to find out whether they will secure a seat at Thursday’s state dinner for Xi.

“Beijing’s security protocol is very different,” one of the sources said, noting that the executives did not fly with Xi’s official party or aboard his aircraft, unlike the American CEOs who arrived in Beijing alongside President Donald Trump in May.
item.content:encoded:
A small group of Chinese CEOs holding US visas has arrived in Washington after travelling separately from President Xi Jinping’s official entourage, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

But with the clock ticking and the business optics of the Chinese leader’s White House visit hanging on the final twists of diplomatic negotiations, the executives are still waiting to find out whether they will secure a seat at Thursday’s state dinner for Xi.

“Beijing’s security protocol is very different,” one of the sources said, noting that the executives did not fly with Xi’s official party or aboard his aircraft, unlike the American CEOs who arrived in Beijing alongside President Donald Trump in May.

Two sources said it was unlikely any Chinese business leader applied for a new visa for the summit. They also said the final decision on whether the Chinese corporate chiefs would join state visit events was tied in part to talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, and the matter came up during their meeting on Wednesday.

Bessent and He met that day at the World Bank in Washington, their second encounter in four days after talks on Sunday in New York to tackle what Bessent called “unfinished business” ahead of the leadership summit.

After Wednesday’s meeting, Bessent announced that the two sides had agreed to extend the “Busan arrangement” on trade – reached after Xi-Trump talks in the South Korean city – by two months, until January 10.

While US officials had played down the prospect of an extension being announced this week, the South China Morning Post had reported in August that an extension was “almost certain”.

Two sources said the extension had left the door open for the executives to appear at the state dinner and at possible side events.

However, their presence might ultimately yield more optics than substance, according to one source. They said the small delegation was unlikely to deliver the soft-power punch Beijing had hoped for, and some executives could even use the occasion to voice their dissatisfaction with US investment restrictions directly to officials. Indeed, the CEOs’ attendance was largely a formality, the source said.

Another source familiar with the matter said Trump’s priority remained negotiating the new Board of Investment, rendering efforts to seat Chinese CEOs at the state dinner a “lower policy priority”.

For Beijing, however, the optics matter.

Having Chinese CEOs at the state dinner would help to balance the presence of US technology bosses and put China’s own corporate and technological muscle on display. The Chinese side viewed business leaders taking part in the banquet and other events as a message that the world’s two largest economies were intertwined, one of the sources noted.

“I think given the current circumstances, some Chinese business representation at the state banquet is possible. Even if that didn’t take place, the American business leaders will arrange some gathering with them,” the source said.

The same source said some of the names under discussion included executives from Alibaba, Xiaomi, CATL and BYD. Alibaba owns the SCMP.

Another source said the backup group was likely to draw from Chinese electric-vehicle companies, which were the keenest to explore investment opportunities in the United States.

According to one source, some American business leaders with substantial commercial interests in China were likely to entertain their Chinese counterparts privately if they did not make it to the banquet. Several top executives from Chinese artificial intelligence companies were foregoing the summit over security concerns, the source said.

Another insider said the White House banquet venue could seat up to 100 guests, while the Chinese side had been allotted about 30 seats. In the event that the Chinese business leaders could not attend, the administration would invite a few more US guests, tapping into strong demand for the limited seats.

On the US side, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook are among the business leaders confirmed to be attending Thursday’s dinner, after accompanying Trump to Beijing four months ago. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman – who was not part of Trump’s delegation in May – is also on the state dinner guest list.

The May trip has become a heavily debated template for US-China diplomacy. Trump brought about 18 major chief executives with him, with Huang famously joining Air Force One at the last minute during a refuelling stop in Alaska.

While their visit yielded no headline corporate deals, an informal gathering took place between Chinese and American counterparts in Beijing, and some US executives stayed on for a few days after Trump’s departure. Trump also had several CEOs come to the bilaterals simply to be introduced.

Something similar was discussed for Xi’s reciprocal visit to Washington but was no longer on the table, sources said.

The SCMP reported on Tuesday that differences over possible investment announcements had created roadblocks for a Chinese business delegation potentially accompanying Xi.

A source familiar with the discussions said both sides had yet to reach common ground over the Board of Investment, particularly regarding potential Chinese ventures.

Another source said a lack of communication and differing interpretations of the reciprocity principle had derailed the original plan.

Beijing viewed the presence of Musk, Huang and Cook in Trump’s May delegation as a standard that should be mirrored in Washington. The US side, the source said, treated reciprocity as applying only to senior leadership. Poor logistics and a lack of formal engagement or arranged meetings for Chinese businesses coming to Washington added to the uncertainty.

The last-minute uncertainty over the state dinner follows the same pattern the SCMP described in August. Sources said then that Chinese officials were rattled by disorganisation and poor coordination inside the Trump White House in the weeks before Xi’s trip, and that they had already watched the same chaos play out ahead of the US leader’s May state visit to China.

item.title: [SCMP] What Xi Jinping’s letter to old friends in Iowa means in an altered America
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Khushboo Razdan looks at how a presidential appeal to America’s heartland is playing out.

Of the countless preparations being made for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s highly anticipated American trip, arguably the first came in the form of a personal letter.

On February 16, seven months before his White House visit, Xi wrote to friends in the midwestern US state of Iowa, sending a Chinese New Year card across the Pacific.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Khushboo Razdan looks at how a presidential appeal to America’s heartland is playing out.

Of the countless preparations being made for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s highly anticipated American trip, arguably the first came in the form of a personal letter.

On February 16, seven months before his White House visit, Xi wrote to friends in the midwestern US state of Iowa, sending a Chinese New Year card across the Pacific.

In it, the Chinese leader repeated a line Beijing uses when official relations are strained, saying the hope of the relationship “lies in the people”, its foundation “is grass-roots connections” and its future “depends on the youth”.

Xi wrote to Luca Berrone and the circle that welcomed him in 1985 on his first-ever US visit – Sarah Lande, Gary Dvorchak, Rick Kimberley and Terry Branstad, a former Iowa governor and former US ambassador – as well as students from the youth exchange initiative the Chinese leader announced in 2023.

No matter what direction politics took, Xi told them in the letter, the will of the two peoples “will not change”.

China’s leader appears to have invoked his long-standing personal ties with Iowa to soften the atmosphere ahead of his White House visit, as American farmers remain deeply sceptical amid severe trade war losses battering the heartland.

The personal thread may be intact, but the agricultural partnership that once gave it weight is not. And while those familiar faces still anchor the friendship narrative, they are also in the blast zone.

Grant Kimberley lives in both realities.

In February 2012, during Xi’s second visit to Iowa, his family hosted the then Chinese vice-president at the Maxwell farm. Kimberley, then 36, said ni hao in the yard. He is now senior director of market development at the Iowa Soybean Association.

“The significance of the letter was as much about the relationship as the message itself,” said Kimberley, son of Rick Kimberley, calling it “a reminder that personal relationships built on mutual respect over decades still matter”.

Yet, the letter did not change trade policy or market conditions.

Farmers appreciate goodwill and friendship, Kimberley said, but ultimately look for “stable trade relationships and practical results”.

He said he believed Xi “has a genuine appreciation for Iowa and its people”. And he still saw farm trade as “the ballast of the overall relationship”.

Diplomacy mattered “because communication is always better than misunderstanding”, Kimberley continued, saying the real test was whether “markets remain open, customers remain engaged and trade relationships remain reliable”.

The market that once seemed reliable now switches on for summits.

US agricultural exports to China plummeted from US$24.5 billion in 2024 to US$8.4 billion in 2025, a two-thirds contraction that pushed China from a top-five farm customer to sixth.

Soybeans took the biggest hit, tumbling from US$12.6 billion to about US$3 billion. From late May through late November 2025, official data showed no US soy shipments to China. Beijing instead bought from Brazil.

North Dakota State University later estimated that Chinese retaliation cost US agriculture US$14.9 billion from March 2025 to February 2026. Iowa, California and Illinois each lost about US$1.2 billion.

Soybeans alone accounted for US$6.8 billion – nearly half the total. Even after federal aid, the American Soybean Association put 2025 soybean losses at nearly US$75 an acre.

This is the second major escalation in the US-China trade war since the original conflict began in 2018. The first taught Beijing it could live without Iowa beans. The second taught Iowa something else: China can walk away, while Washington’s relief arrives later and smaller.

America’s new soybean marketing year began on September 1. The US Department of Agriculture said Chinese buyers took 136,000 tonnes that day, followed by flash sales of 202,000 tonnes and 192,000 tonnes in the next two sessions.

After Xi and US President Donald Trump met in South Korea in October last year, China pledged 12 million tonnes in the short term, then 25 million tonnes a year through 2028, alongside about US$17 billion a year in wider US farm purchases.

New crop sales to China resumed as the Washington date neared. The USDA said state buyers were buying against the Busan pledge. Commercial crushers continued to prefer Brazilian beans because of the 10 per cent tariff.

American soy still pays that tariff. Brazilian soy does not. Brazil kept selling through 2025 without waiting for a presidential summit.

Whether the new US cargoes keep coming after Xi leaves Washington is the test Kimberley’s members will watch for.

According to Tao Wang, who teaches the history of US-China relations at Iowa State University, the February letter was more than a new year’s greeting.

Xi sought “to reach not only his old friends but also, through them, a bigger American public”, Wang said.

Iowa is useful because the tie is more than 40 years old and “looks personal, not only diplomatic”.

“There is a farm calculation in that,” added Wang, who said keeping faith with a state that still wants to sell soybeans could “help strengthen the American groups who want stable, cooperative economic ties with China”.

Wang refrained from suggesting that Xi asked anyone to lobby Washington. But he noted the letter’s timing came after a difficult period that included a surprise leaders’ call touching on Taiwan and “alongside signs that China will buy soybeans again”.

A friendly letter, he said, was “a low-cost way to warm the atmosphere” before the White House visit.

One would be hard pressed to call the 2026 and 2012 trips identical.

In 2012, Xi was vice-president and looked the part of a future leader, Wang said. And the Iowa city of Muscatine had a job: to put a face on the rising statesman.

In 2026, Xi was “the supreme leader with a full agenda of high-stakes negotiation”, the professor added.

A stop on the Mississippi River “does not fit this kind of visit any more”, Wang said, adding that Xi’s letter offered a way to keep “that Iowa channel warm” without diverting precious time during the trip to Washington.

Until now, the personal and student channels have proved fruitful.

The “50,000 in 5 Years” programme Xi announced during his 2023 US visit still sends Iowa pupils to China, with the sister-state link through the non-profit Iowa Sister States and Hebei province moving delegations and farm exchanges.

“More than a thousand young Iowans have already gone through this youth exchange initiative,” Wang estimated.

What has fallen by the wayside is “open, unscrutinised institutional cooperation”, especially at universities, he said.

Wang pointed to a letter in March from Iowa state congressman Taylor Collins, the Republican chairman of the Iowa House Higher Education Committee, to Drake University in Des Moines, the state capital, demanding files on its China partnerships.

There was also an Iowa House-passed bill introduced in January that would stop Iowa universities hiring H-1B visa holders from China, he said, noting there were fewer Chinese scholars, researchers and students than a decade ago.

The break with farmers is colder. After Iowa became a target of retaliation, growers “now see Beijing less as a stable partner and more as a transactional, unpredictable customer”, Wang added.

Jonathan Hassid, who teaches China politics at Iowa State, is unsentimental about Xi’s letter.

Hassid described it as a means “to bypass normal diplomacy and speak directly to ordinary citizens”, adding that it had received “little attention in the US or Iowa presses and is probably unfamiliar to most Iowans”.

Nor could the circumstances be said to resemble 1985.

“Candidates for political office regularly attack China” now, Hassid said, recalling that at this year’s Iowa State Fair, a low-flying aircraft towed a banner accusing a politician of having “sold out Iowa to China”.

Beijing hoped that direct appeals might “slowly shift attitudes over time”, he added. “Whether the approach works is an open question.”

Tourism both ways thinned after the coronavirus pandemic, Hassid said, and Chinese language enrolments “declined dramatically”.

“The golden age of US-China people-to-people ties has passed.”

And while Muscatine cherishes its Xi story, “most Iowans are simply unaware”.

As Hassid sees it, “these visits matter more to the Chinese Communist Party than they do to most local Iowans”.

Earlier this month, that disconnect was evident in the political chatter coursing through a riverfront hotel in Minnesota’s capital.

Jeff Winton, a New York dairy farmer, spoke at the Midwestern Legislative Conference in St Paul attended by several hundred state senators, representatives and officials.

The talk in the halls spanned beef imports, the fight with Canada, diesel and fertiliser after the war in Iran, drought, the November midterms and people feeling worn out.

“Not once did China or President Xi come up during any of the conversations I had,” Winton said. “I truly believe that there are many more important things on farmers’ minds right now than China and President Xi.”

At best, the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington was “political theatre” as the midterms approach, he added, “and nothing more than that”.

The symbolism of the visit could be said to be mutually beneficial. Xi can invoke an Iowa relationship that predates the trade war. Trump can point to Chinese purchases returning.

For farmers, neither means much if the market disappears again when the politics turn.

John Bartman, an Illinois farmer, had not seen Xi’s letter until this week. He interpreted it as “another head of state that doesn’t want to deal with Donald Trump”.

Bartman portrayed farmers as “stuck in the middle”, arguing that “food shouldn’t ever be used as a point of leverage”.

China’s relationship with the American heartland changed under Trump, he said, with Beijing willing to “use any type of leverage” to get a better price.

Of Xi’s Washington visit, Bartman said China “still hasn’t even bought half of what they promised”.

As for Trump, the farmer said the US president “needs to have a good showing in rural America” ahead of the midterm elections.

“If China buys one bushel … Donald Trump will make a big deal out of it … when he clearly doesn’t” support farmers.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines impeachment: is path now clear to convict Sara Duterte?
item.description:
The Philippine Senate has made it mathematically easier to convict Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, but observers say the ruling could intensify a battle over an impeachment trial already viewed by the public as deeply divisive.

The Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, ruled on Wednesday that only senator-judges who are able to take part in the trial should be counted in determining the threshold for conviction.

Under the Philippine constitution, a two-thirds vote of the Senate is required to convict an impeached official.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine Senate has made it mathematically easier to convict Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, but observers say the ruling could intensify a battle over an impeachment trial already viewed by the public as deeply divisive.

The Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, ruled on Wednesday that only senator-judges who are able to take part in the trial should be counted in determining the threshold for conviction.

Under the Philippine constitution, a two-thirds vote of the Senate is required to convict an impeached official.

Four senator-judges have been unable to regularly take part in the trial: Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are detained over plunder cases; Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is at large, wanted on an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; and Loren Legarda is abroad on extended medical leave.

The court has ruled that their absence should not count towards the denominator for the two-thirds requirement, reducing the number of votes needed for conviction from 16 to 14.

Thirteen senators voted in favour of Wednesday’s ruling and one voted against, while six senators widely seen as allied with the Duterte clan did not take part in the proceedings.

The ruling followed testimonies from four retired Supreme Court justices who appeared before the court, three of whom advised that the two-thirds rule must exclude senators unable to participate.

Duterte-Carpio’s impeachment trial before the Senate addresses allegations that she made grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and his family, as well as charges she misappropriated more than US$10 million in confidential funds during her time as education secretary between 2022 and 2024.

If convicted, she will be barred from running for public office, thwarting her intention to seek the presidency in the 2028 election.

Not set in stone

The lower threshold resulting from Wednesday’s ruling effectively increased the chances of conviction, said Paolo Tamase, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines College of Law.

Tamase, who teaches constitutional law, said the decision to lower the threshold was sound, with the retired justices providing a “clear, learned justification” for interpreting the constitution in line with the realities of the Senate’s composition.

“The constitution intends a conviction in impeachment to be difficult but not impossible. These are unusual times for the Senate, with many of its members facing corruption complaints and the more functional reading of the threshold allows impeachment to continue as a mechanism for accountability,” he said.

However, Tamase said the ruling also “leaves the possibility for absent senators to appear before the verdict and affect the maths, which means nothing is set in stone”.

Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and the founder of independent polling firm Momentum Research, said the ruling meant the prosecution now had to change focus from overcoming a narrow numerical threshold to winning over persuadable senators.

“The prosecution is no longer confronting what initially appeared to be a very narrow path to conviction,” he said. “The battle now moves towards persuadable senators and, ultimately, whether the prosecution can consolidate a broad coalition around at least one article of impeachment.”

Arguelles said securing 14 votes for a guilty verdict was “considerably more feasible” now, given that 13 senators had already voted in favour of the new threshold.

“Of course … we should not treat yesterday’s 13 votes as 13 automatic votes for conviction. But the arithmetic tells us that conviction is no longer a remote scenario,” he added.

Questioning legitimacy

Senator-judges aligned with Duterte-Carpio could still move to undermine the credibility of the proceedings in the court of public opinion, political observers told This Week in Asia.

“The minority may become even more emboldened to question the legitimacy of the proceedings at every opportunity,” said Jean Encinas-Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

“Clearly, it means that it has now become easier to convict Sara,” she said, adding: “Politics has always been full of surprises in the Philippines.”

Franco said the Duterte camp might ultimately challenge the decision before the Supreme Court “just to show that they still have options”.

Tamase, however, said the testimony of the retired justices would make it harder for the vice-president’s camp to argue that the Senate had committed a “grave abuse of discretion”, reducing the likelihood of a Supreme Court reversal.

Arguelles said the Duterte bloc had to make strategic use of its numbers.

“If they believe they cannot prevail inside the impeachment court, one option is to contest the legitimacy of the process itself and take that argument outside the chamber,” he said. “Their non-participation has both an institutional and a public dimension.”

Arjan Aguirre, an assistant professor of political science at Ateneo de Manila University, called the ruling a “risky yet inevitable move” that could undermine public faith in the outcome.

“Public opinion adds another layer here. Several senators seen as acquittal-leaning are themselves facing separate corruption allegations tied to the flood-control scandal, which could make an acquittal vote look self-protective rather than a principled outcome,” he said.

“Even if Duterte-Carpio manages to get convicted, the public will view the outcome with a low sense of legitimacy because people will know that it was adjusted.”

According to Aguirre, unexcused absences function as de facto acquittal votes because senators cannot abstain during a final verdict. “They can just choose not to attend to further undermine the process,” he said.

Defending her vote to lower the threshold, Senator Risa Hontiveros said the absence of certain senators during a trial should not paralyse the entire institution.

“Beyond discussions about denominators, fractions and rounding, what we need to determine is: who among us is currently present in court and has the capability to fulfil our sworn duties?” she said.

How the trial unfolded would have implications for the 2028 presidential election, Arguelles said.

“All eyes will be on who, if anyone, crosses over. A defection would matter not only for the impeachment verdict, but for the broader configuration of political alliances going into 2028,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why younger Filipinos are warming to China despite maritime tensions
item.description:
Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay.

Formento, 29, has worked as a cashier for about a year. She follows developments in the South China Sea through news reports shared on her social media feeds, including frequent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese forces in the disputed waters.

While she found such incidents “disappointing”, she ultimately thought better of Beijing than Washington, which she blamed for the high energy prices affecting the Philippines and the rest of the world.
item.content:encoded:
Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay.

Formento, 29, has worked as a cashier for about a year. She follows developments in the South China Sea through news reports shared on her social media feeds, including frequent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese forces in the disputed waters.

While she found such incidents “disappointing”, she ultimately thought better of Beijing than Washington, which she blamed for the high energy prices affecting the Philippines and the rest of the world.

“That’s why I prefer China to the United States. Just look at what is happening … because of the US-Iran war – fuel prices are skyrocketing,” she said.

Formento’s views point to a broader contradiction in how Filipinos see China: even as Beijing remains distrusted over its actions in the disputed waters, younger Filipinos are more likely than older generations to view the country favourably.

A new survey released on July 15 by the US-based Pew Research Centre found that 47 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 viewed China favourably, compared with 44 per cent of those aged 35 to 49 and 27 per cent of those 50 and older.

The survey also found that 61 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 had confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 32 per cent among those 50 and older.

The findings stand out against a long-running pattern of distrust towards Beijing, according to Social Weather Stations (SWS), a Philippine polling organisation.

SWS has measured Filipinos’ trust in China annually since 1994 and quarterly since 2012. Beijing recorded a positive net trust rating in only nine of 74 surveys, with its rating falling to a record low of minus 54 in 2024 on a scale ranging from plus 100 to minus 100.

China’s net trust rating remained negative in 2025 and 2026, while the US, Japan and Australia recorded higher levels of trust among Filipinos.

Pew’s findings do not establish why younger Filipinos have more favourable views of China, but experts point to how they encounter the country in everyday life, as well as a generational shift in perceptions of its economic and political rise.

“As I see it, younger Filipinos encounter China in many different ways. They see Chinese technology and consumer products, entertainment, travel content, and social media posts about life in China,” said Jan Robert R Go, associate professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

“This is where I find the idea of ‘everyday China’ useful. By this, I mean the China that people encounter in their daily lives, often outside formal politics and diplomacy. These experiences may give younger Filipinos a wider range of impressions of China.”

But Go cautioned against interpreting more favourable views of China as evidence that younger Filipinos are turning away from the US.

“I find the 61 per cent figure particularly interesting because it suggests we should be careful about assuming that attitudes towards China all move together,” he said.

“Someone can have confidence in Chinese leadership on the world stage, appreciate Chinese popular culture, and still distrust China on territorial issues.”

Indeed, the Pew survey found that 76 per cent of Filipino respondents overall named China as the country’s top threat, while 86 per cent said they were very or somewhat concerned about territorial disputes involving China and neighbouring countries. Pew did not provide age-group breakdowns for those questions.

Arnaud Leveau, a geopolitics professor at Paris Dauphine University, said the coexistence of these views was among the most notable findings.

“Strategically, this tells us something about the emerging generation in Asia. The political landscape may become less binary. Younger citizens may be willing to recognise China’s power and even aspects of its leadership while refusing to accept Chinese pressure on their sovereignty,” Leveau said.

Generational memory could also help explain the gap, he said.

Older Filipinos grew up in an environment in which the US occupied a particularly central strategic and cultural position, while China was more distant, poorer and associated with communist rivalry.

Younger Filipinos have instead grown up with an economically powerful and technologically sophisticated China that is deeply integrated into Asian trade and supply chains.

“Their China is the China of smartphones, digital platforms, high-speed rail, electric vehicles, large cities and a major Asian consumer market,” Leveau said.

“For younger Asians, China’s rise is already part of the normal international landscape. They did not experience the transition from a US-dominated regional system in the same way as older generations. Multipolarity is not a disruption for them; it is increasingly the world they have always known.”

Edmund Tayao, a law professor at the San Beda University Graduate School of Law in Manila, urged caution in interpreting the Pew findings without comparable polling from Philippine research organisations, saying he would prefer surveys from two or three of the country’s most respected polling groups.

He also pointed to social media as a potentially important influence on respondents’ views, saying the dominance of online content and what he described as China’s “vigorous campaign” could shape perceptions, particularly when users might struggle to distinguish reliable information from misinformation.

Tayao said some Filipinos might also view China favourably because they were impressed by the speed of its development and hope the Philippines could achieve similar progress.

Such exposure, Go said, did not necessarily mean younger Filipinos were becoming more sympathetic to Beijing on political questions.

“I also wouldn’t assume this makes younger Filipinos apolitical,” he said. “They may simply be responding to China through a wider range of experiences.”

Go noted that it was too early to say whether the age gap represented a lasting generational shift.

“What we do not know yet is whether that difference will remain as younger Filipinos grow older,” he said, adding that developments in the South China Sea, economic conditions, domestic politics and media coverage could all change how Filipinos viewed China.

“So, for now, I would treat the age difference as an important pattern to watch. We need to see whether it appears consistently over several years before calling it a permanent generational change.”

item.title: [SCMP] US turns to South Korea to ease ammunition bottlenecks amid global conflicts
item.description:
Washington is increasingly turning to South Korea to ease ammunition supply bottlenecks triggered by wars in the Middle East and Europe, potentially accelerating Seoul’s integration into the US defence industrial base.

Analysts say the United States may struggle to replenish stockpiles quickly enough if conflicts in Iran and Ukraine drag on, creating opportunities for South Korea’s defence industry to expand its presence in the US market.

Jang Won-joon, a defence science professor at Jeonbuk National University, said the war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had made Washington acutely aware of shortfalls in its domestic defence production capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Washington is increasingly turning to South Korea to ease ammunition supply bottlenecks triggered by wars in the Middle East and Europe, potentially accelerating Seoul’s integration into the US defence industrial base.

Analysts say the United States may struggle to replenish stockpiles quickly enough if conflicts in Iran and Ukraine drag on, creating opportunities for South Korea’s defence industry to expand its presence in the US market.

Jang Won-joon, a defence science professor at Jeonbuk National University, said the war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had made Washington acutely aware of shortfalls in its domestic defence production capacity.

The US burned through US$22.3 billion worth of ammunition in just four months of the Iran war, according to the Pentagon, putting its defence industry under scrutiny and exposing what critics call a structural problem.

Washington is now expected to build defence production networks with allies across the Indo-Pacific, including South Korea, Japan and Australia to help close the supply gap.

“The US can’t do everything on its own and it is turning to allies in selected sectors such as munitions, missiles and battleships,” Jang said. “South Korea has emerged as a key partner for the US in such efforts.”

Defence industry cooperation with South Korea could serve as a model for other US allies, Jang said, citing the US$150 billion “Make American Shipbuilding Great Again” initiative proposed by South Korea to revitalise the US maritime and shipbuilding sectors as part of a broader investment package aimed at securing lower tariffs.

The initiative is anchored by South Korea’s largest shipbuilders – HD Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean – working alongside government ministries.

“The US is likely to present defence industry cooperation with South Korea as a successful model to encourage other allies to follow suit,” Jang said.

South Korea’s leading defence company, Hanwha Aerospace, has moved quickly to take advantage of the US ammunition bottleneck by expanding its integration with the American defence industry.

On Tuesday, it announced a US$2.2 billion investment over seven years to build a production hub for 155mm (6.1-inch) artillery shells at a US Army site in Arkansas – potentially giving it an advantage in securing other American military contracts.

Hanwha’s vertically integrated facility, covering the entire ammunition production process from raw materials to finished products, is set to manufacture components and propellant charges for 155mm shells.

The US has been falling well short of its production targets for the shells because of manufacturing bottlenecks and contractor issues. Global supply is tight largely because the Ukraine war has consumed shells far faster than Western factories can replace them.

Last month, Hanwha Defence USA, the company’s American subsidiary, signed a contract with the US Army to deliver six K9 Mobile Howitzer wheeled prototypes, in an initial deal worth roughly US$100 million that could reach US$263 million if an option for an additional 12 units is exercised.

Hanwha is also building a facility in Opelika, Alabama for prototype assembly, integration and testing.

“We will help take the capabilities of the US ammunition industry to the next level while actively contributing to the expansion of defence cooperation between the two countries,” said Michael Coulter, head of Hanwha Defence USA.

Other South Korean manufacturers are also attracting global attention. LIG Defence & Aerospace, formerly LIG Nex1, is seeking to expand its market share in interceptor missiles, despite constraints on domestic manufacturing capacity.

But industry officials warn that US shortages will not automatically translate into orders for South Korean firms. Foreign companies still face high barriers to entry, including “Buy American” procurement rules, strict tech-security regulations and demanding US military certification requirements.

Kim Mi-jung, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade specialising in the defence industry, said deeper integration into the US industrial base was necessary for South Korea to clear these legal hurdles.

“To advance into the US defence market, South Korea and others have little option but to set up and invest through US subsidiaries,” she said.

Kim and other analysts say South Korea is well positioned to help replenish depleted US stockpiles, including 155mm shells, because the threat from North Korea has forced Seoul to maintain production capacity and substantial reserves even as other countries scaled back.

“South Korea is almost the only option for the US to renovate its ageing ammunition production facilities on a short timeline,” Kim said, adding that the cooperation would strengthen Seoul’s leverage in trade and investment negotiations with Washington.

Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said the Hanwha deal could pave the way for cooperation on other platforms, including maritime and aerial systems, missiles, drones and AI-based weapons.

“South Korea is in effect the only arms supplier which the US could rely on to replenish its depleted arms depot quickly,” Doo said, adding that the two allies maintained interoperability across many weapons systems, including 155mm artillery.

Washington could also turn to Hyundai Rotem’s K2 main battle tanks to address shortfalls, Doo said, and to LIG Defence & Aerospace’s Cheongung interceptor missiles to supplement Patriot systems that were also in short supply.

“Defence cooperation with the US would benefit both countries, strengthen the bilateral alliance and give South Korea significant opportunities to expand its presence in the global market,” he said.

Many countries no longer wanted to buy “finished weapons”, Jang added, but rather the “ability to sustain war” through local production, technology cooperation, maintenance, repair and overhaul, training and the capacity to rapidly scale up in a crisis.

With this in mind, South Korea “must move beyond exports of finished weapons to ‘package exports’”, he said. “And ultimately to ‘ecosystem exports’ that support a country’s ability to sustain war.”

Zack Cooper, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the South Korean defence industry’s ability to produce cheaply, quickly and at scale “makes cooperation attractive for the US”.

“Allied co-production is one potentially attractive avenue to increase defence output, so is definitely attracting attention in Washington,” Cooper told This Week in Asia. “There are still many political hurdles that companies and countries will need to overcome, but I think there’s a lot of potential in deepening this type of cooperation.”

item.title: [SCMP] The US-China tech war has evolved since the last Xi-Trump summit. Who has the edge now?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fourth part of this series, Sylvia Ma looks at the economic and technological levers available to both in their protracted rivalry.

For years, Huawei Technologies has served as a central battleground in the contest between the world’s two largest economies. As Washington tightens restrictions, the Chinese tech giant continues to find new ways forward – to the point that “becoming Nvidia” is now an internal goal.

Days before President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States for a high-stakes meeting with his American counterpart Donald Trump, Huawei announced a major technological breakthrough: a system that it said was capable of enabling up to 1 million processors to operate as a single, unified computer.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fourth part of this series, Sylvia Ma looks at the economic and technological levers available to both in their protracted rivalry.

For years, Huawei Technologies has served as a central battleground in the contest between the world’s two largest economies. As Washington tightens restrictions, the Chinese tech giant continues to find new ways forward – to the point that “becoming Nvidia” is now an internal goal.

Days before President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States for a high-stakes meeting with his American counterpart Donald Trump, Huawei announced a major technological breakthrough: a system that it said was capable of enabling up to 1 million processors to operate as a single, unified computer.

The announcement followed earlier semiconductor advances, namely the Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture, which aim to deliver high-performance chips without relying on the most advanced lithography tools, whose sale to China remains restricted.

Ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, Huawei rotating chair Xu Zhijun last week voiced a widely shared hope among entrepreneurs that the world’s two superpowers could “coexist and get along in a peaceful way” and that government actions would avoid interfering with normal, innovation-driven market competition.

“With increasing geopolitical tension, those days [of globalisation and full competition] are leaving us,” Xu said, asserting that enterprises were now trapped in a reality where “you cannot buy what you want to, you cannot sell what you want”.

As geoeconomic competition continues to reshape US-China relations, the sources of leverage available to Washington and Beijing are also coming under scrutiny.

Four months after Trump visited the Chinese capital in May, when both sides agreed to work towards “constructive strategic stability”, traditional economic levers, such as pledges to order Boeing aircraft, have almost flatlined. At the same time, the technological contest has accelerated, spanning China’s push to catch up in artificial intelligence and semiconductors and Washington’s drive for self-reliance in rare earths – one of Beijing’s main trump cards.

“The more interesting change is that both sides appear increasingly conscious that their leverage is reciprocal,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “Neither side has a decisive advantage without imposing significant costs on itself.”

While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis

Chasing the AI frontier

Since May, Chinese AI developers have increasingly sought to combine powerful open-weight models, whose parameters are made available for developers to download, modify and run, with a broader domestic hardware base to reduce reliance on Nvidia chips.

When Moonshot AI launched its 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 in July, it made the weights available to developers. The model was soon adapted to run on Alibaba Group Holding’s Zhenwu M890 and Huawei Technologies’ Ascend 910C chips, while new models from Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and Alibaba – owner of the South China Morning Post – have followed.

Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said the release of such “capable models” had “arguably” narrowed the gap at the frontier.

Although the US still leads in proprietary frontier models, Washington has increasingly shifted its focus to how Chinese developers gain access to those capabilities. A report released by three US government agencies earlier this month accused six Chinese AI firms of using “distillation” – a technique in which a smaller system is trained on responses generated by a more powerful one – to extract capabilities from American-developed models.

China’s Ministry of Commerce rejected the allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation as groundless, warning that Beijing would retaliate if Washington weaponised the claim to stifle the country’s tech sector.

Elly Rostoum, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), disagreed that China’s progress could be explained solely by distillation, calling such claims “short-sighted”.

“Even if they distil it, they are smart enough to take the technology, distil it and build on it within six weeks – in such a short time – as we’ve seen with Moonshot AI,” she told a media briefing last week.

Meanwhile, Joe Khawam, managing director of legal and AI policy at the Law Reform Institute in Washington, said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had weighed sanctions over distillation, some policymakers could favour a diplomatic solution given the risk of Chinese retaliation.

“One of the big questions is how truly important distillation is for specific Chinese AI companies to maintain their position as fast followers in frontier AI models,” he said.

Yao Xu, secretary general of the Centre for Global AI Innovative Governance at Fudan University, said the two countries held leverage in different parts of the AI technology ecosystem. “The United States has the chips, but lacks effective planning and public persuasion,” he said.

“China can do better at planning and securing public trust in policy, but we lack the chips.”

The battle over advanced semiconductors

Although the US retains a major advantage in cutting-edge chips, Chinese players have spent the past four months bolstering the domestic hardware ecosystem underpinning the country’s AI models.

“The US has a lot of leverage around ... [the] ecosystem for advanced chips,” Kevin Allison, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at CEPA, told the same media briefing. “China has yet to catch up, although it’s been making progress kind of under pressure from US export controls.”

Unable to access the machines capable of extreme ultraviolet lithography – the cutting-edge chipmaking technology dominated by Dutch giant ASML – Chinese companies such as Huawei and Alibaba’s T-Head division are pursuing alternative ways to improve performance.

Huawei, for instance, anticipates a major domestic shift towards its AI infrastructure for model training next year, as its Ascend processors gain ground on Nvidia in China despite supply bottlenecks.

Washington continues to bar Chinese firms from accessing the most advanced Nvidia chips, even after approving sales of the H200 model, and has yet to close loopholes that allow remote access to processing power hosted in overseas data centres.

In early August, Bloomberg reported that US regulators were reviewing how Chinese AI companies accessed Nvidia chips through computing power rented overseas.

“While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

Alex Capri, a senior lecturer at the National University of Singapore’s business school, said he expected the coming Xi-Trump talks to renew interest in Beijing’s push to secure relief from export controls on high-end chips and lithography equipment. That could include Washington extending its suspension of the “50 per cent affiliates rule”, which would otherwise expand tech export restrictions to overseas subsidiaries that are at least 50 per cent Chinese-owned. The suspension is set to expire in November.

As foreign memory-chip giants increasingly devote production capacity to high-bandwidth memory, which supports AI computing, Chinese manufacturers such as Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) have continued expanding their presence in conventional memory, strengthening China’s domestic memory supply chain.

Data released by Counterpoint Research last month showed that YMTC had entered the world’s top three NAND suppliers by shipment volume for the first time, accounting for 14 per cent of global bit shipments.

Leverage beyond rare earths

Beyond AI models and chips, both the US and China have increased their use of restrictions and export controls across technology and other supply chains, creating additional sources of potential leverage.

On the American side, the regulatory dragnet is expanding rapidly into downstream hardware.

The Federal Communications Commission expanded its Covered List in July to include foreign-made advanced robotic devices and connected power inverters. It is also reportedly drafting a ban on new Chinese-made optical transceivers used in data centres, with officials aiming to publish and implement the measure later this year.

Analysts at Bernstein described the recent US ban on new foreign-made mobile robots as “the formal beginning of US-China decoupling in robotics,” in a note published last month.

Although China’s robotics industry remained reliant on US AI chips and simulation platforms, it had moved faster in scaling training datasets and acquiring high-value data, the analysts said. Data would consequently be Beijing’s “base case” response, with rare earth magnets potentially serving as an escalation lever, they added.

China accounts for about 60 per cent of global rare earth mining and nearly 90 per cent of processing, according to the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies. As the world’s leading producer of rare earth elements, it has long used critical minerals as a strategic lever in its protracted trade conflict with the US.

Washington has accelerated efforts to reduce its rare earth dependence, with Elon Musk earlier this month touting the Cybercab’s rare-earth-free motor, although analysts regarded the development as only a slight step towards meaningfully weakening China’s leverage across industries.

At the federal level, USA Rare Earth secured access to up to US$1.6 billion in US government funding in June to build out a domestic mine-to-magnet supply chain – though Rostoum of CEPA said China had “a 20-year head start in going around the world” on a “shopping spree” to secure critical minerals.

“The Chinese definitely have the upper hand when it comes to rare earths,” she told the media briefing last week.

Beyond rare earths, analysts also pointed to China’s ability to leverage its position in global manufacturing and supply chains.

“As the US seeks to de-risk from China, Beijing retains considerable leverage through the depth and scale of its industrial ecosystem, something that is much harder to replicate quickly than individual supply chains,” said Giovannini, also a fellow at the University of Hong Kong’s Asia Global Institute.

“The key question ahead of the meeting is therefore less about which side has more leverage and more about which side is willing to bear greater economic costs in exercising it.”

Additional reporting by Coco Feng, Iris Deng, Howard Liu, Vincent Chow and Wency Chen

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Thailand’s bid to wire the world’s AI revolution
item.description:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.

“They are essential to our daily life. They are in all electronics you are using,” said WellTek founder Jennifer Deng, who established the Thai subsidiary of her China-based Jiangxi Welgao Electronics in Ayutthaya two years ago.

Thailand is now Southeast Asia’s No 1 producer of PCBs – often described as the nervous system of modern electronics, channelling essential signals through increasingly complex arrays of semiconductors, resistors and capacitors – and the fifth largest in the world.

Deng’s US$75 million WellTek plant, built in under a year, is the first of two planned for Ayutthaya, a major Thai industrial zone once dominated by Japanese carmakers and global electronics giants, now being rewired for the artificial intelligence age.

Circuitous success

Malaysia may lead the field in lucrative semiconductors and Vietnam in electronics assembly, but PCBs give Thailand its competitive advantage in Southeast Asia’s race for tech relevance.

Its rise in this niche owes as much to the trade wars triggered by Washington as it does to the smart timing of Thai authorities in welcoming global companies seeking new bases away from the tariff line of fire.

“The market demanded movement to Thailand,” Deng told This Week in Asia from WellTek’s Ayutthaya headquarters, where workers in crisp company polo shirts hustled down corridors beneath posters bearing the mantra “Conscience and Altruism”.

Over the next few years, Deng not only wants to build a second factory but treble output to more than 3.6 million square metres (38.8 million sq ft) of PCBs per year.

Thailand’s existing PCB industry gave it a head start over rivals, she said, explaining that “Europeans and Americans all requested we are outside of China, and our main partners are here in Thailand.”

Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary general of Thailand’s government-run Board of Investment, told an investor forum on Wednesday that the country was at a “turning point”.

Investment in the PCB and electronics component sector topped US$10 billion over the past three years, he revealed, calling this proof of how Thailand should pivot its economy.

“We need to restructure our economy … and the electronic industry, especially PCBs, is a very good example [of how to do it],” he said. “The key question is where do we go from here?”

For Narit, the country’s future growth depends on climbing the value chain, backed by a higher-skilled workforce trained for the AI age.

Printed fortunes

PCBs are a rare success story in a decade of patchy industrial policy that has left Thailand a regional growth laggard.

Many of the ideas floated to accelerate growth through new manufacturing chains and a splurge of foreign investment have been delayed, watered down or scrapped entirely on contact with the reality of delivering big infrastructure projects in a politically febrile kingdom.

Trade dispute and fuel-price spikes from distant wars have further hurt an economy that expanded just 2.4 per cent last year – a relative crawl compared with Vietnam’s 8 per cent.

Yet around 60 per cent of all new investment into Southeast Asia’s PCB industry has flowed into Thailand since 2023, according to the Thailand Printed Circuit Association.

Phutana Daoruang, the association’s general manager, said Thailand already had the PCB infrastructure, built up by a dozen or so Taiwanese firms, when Donald Trump’s first presidency fired the starting gun on companies fleeing US tariffs.

Thailand’s location and logistics networks, tax breaks, industrial estates and skilled workforce allowed the new factories to plug straight into electronics clusters like Ayutthaya, with the upgraded deep-sea port at Laem Chabang – a two-hour drive away – providing a maritime gateway to China.

“We pitched to compete with Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam as the fundamental infrastructure was already here,” Phutana told This Week in Asia.

“Thailand is quite suitable, we are quite strong in logistics and electricity supply is stable – especially compared with Vietnam and Malaysia.”

There are now around 50 PCB companies in the country, forming a sector that meets a modest 5 per cent of world demand but is eager to capture more of a global market forecast to reach US$100 billion in the coming years.

The ambition is to export eight to 10 times more PCBs than Thailand currently does – reaching roughly US$18 billion to US$25 billion in trade volume and a 20 per cent global market share.

Lofty as that sounds, it may not be impossible given the trillions of dollars flowing into data centres that need increasingly complex layers of PCBs.

“It’s quite complicated and uses very specialised material,” Phutana said of PCB manufacturing. “Thailand has the fundamentals to do it.”

Running hot

AI has changed the stakes for PCB manufacturers. A PCB destined for use with an AI accelerator card – roughly the size of a sheet of A4 paper – is a very different beast from the boards that are found inside car key fobs.

Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres.

Thailand has attracted billions of US dollars of data-centre investment in recent years on the promise of booming AI demand – so much, so fast that the capital is arriving well ahead of the physical buildout of centres themselves.

But data centres are voracious consumers of water and electricity while creating comparatively few jobs, and domestic critics argue that beyond a handful of landlords, Thailand risks getting the environmental costs without the economic rewards.

Delta Electronics Thailand, the local arm of the Taipei-headquartered “grid to chip” manufacturer that became the first company on the Thai stock exchange to be valued above US$100 billion in February, is now eyeing a bigger prize – the power and cooling systems that keep those centres humming.

In the Thai electronics world, Delta is the gatekeeper to the big data-centre contracts – and as it grows, Thailand and its PCB makers are desperate to keep it on side.

“Thailand is moving beyond cost competitiveness towards higher-value industries,” Delta said in a statement, pointing to “advanced engineering talent, energy infrastructure readiness and supply chain depth” as the areas that, with “continued progress” and “pro-business policies”, could give the country a lasting regional edge.

Not everyone shares that confidence. Analysts the world over have grown increasingly nervous about an AI investment bubble and what its bursting might do to countries that have calibrated their industrial strategy on the boom continuing.

Even Delta admits to being “mindful” of “tariff uncertainty, engineering talent gaps, supply chain constraints, intensifying competition in AI infrastructure” and the difficulty of scaling manufacturing “while maintaining quality and profitability”.

Down on the factory floor, the constraints are more immediate. PCB manufacturing demands “a crazy amount of water each day”, according to Thailand Printed Circuit Association chief Phutana – and it needs to be “high purity”, competing directly with the needs of households and other industries.

“The next wave of investment is there. Everyone in AI servers and data centres is looking for new land to expand their facility.” he said. “The customers cannot wait.”

Layered on top of water constraints is a supply squeeze on laminates – the non-conductive, rigid base material that forms the physical foundation of circuit boards – and essential chemicals, a knock-on effect of the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting imports.

Thailand’s Board of Investment says it is exploring ways to free up more water and power, but critics argue the country is sprinting ahead of its own capacity to sustainably keep pace.

Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director at environmental monitor and advocacy group EEC Watch, said automation had killed the jobs case for hosting PCB plants at all.

Relocation incentives meant most equipment was imported, he said, with little technology transfer or upskilling of local workers – turning Thailand into an “assembly line” for foreign capital rather than a genuine beneficiary.

“The factories that come here don’t use as much labour as they used to,” he said. “If they come from Chinese capital, they barely hire Thai workers at all. Blue collar [workers] are Myanmar, white collar are Chinese.”

Despite the scepticism, there is a more hopeful reading – one rooted less in job numbers than in opportunity.

Thailand’s education system produces precious few science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates each year and PCBs may be one of its rare growth industries suited to hiring them.

“Thailand faces a severe shortfall in meeting the surging demand for PCB and electronics workers,” said Panisa Harnpathananun of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council in Thailand.

She estimated the sector would need roughly 225,000 high-skilled workers over the next five years, against the around 1,100 electronics engineers Thai universities produced in 2024.

“This deficit is driven by an ageing population and a structural educational mismatch,” Panisa said.

Plans are afoot to close that gap, including a “sandbox” scheme to fast track engineering degrees and proposals to retrain redundant car industry workers for PCBs and semiconductors.

In a country short on other engines of growth, Panisa said PCBs might offer “the most critical opportunity and the strategic careers” its graduates were likely to find.

item.title: [SCMP] Summits for all diplomatic seasons: how the US has set the stage for Xi Jinping
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US is his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump. From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations.

Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit

In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US is his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump. From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations.

Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit

In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America.

According to then US president Barack Obama, “Our decision to meet so early [in Xi’s term] signifies the importance of the US-China relationship.”

Instead of heading to the diplomatic protocol-heavy capital of Washington, Xi’s historic first meeting with Obama took place at the Annenberg Retreat at Sunnylands, a 200-acre (81-hectare) estate in Rancho Mirage, California.

Originally built as a winter haven by publishers and philanthropists Walter and Leonore Annenberg – close friends of former US president Dwight Eisenhower – the estate holds a unique place in American history as a secluded sanctuary that has often hosted political heavyweights.

Its rare blend of luxury and isolation made Sunnylands an ideal setting for the summit. Without the rigid and pre-scripted constraints of traditional diplomacy, its selection was considered unusual.

But some suspicions remained. Xi and his delegation opted to stay at the nearby Hyatt Regency in Indian Wells rather than at Sunnylands, a move many in the American media attributed to concerns about possible US eavesdropping.

Over June 7 and 8, Xi and Obama engaged in more than eight hours of dialogue spanning two formal sessions, a private dinner and a morning walk, during which they took a break in the shade on a custom California redwood bench that Obama presented to Xi.

During the dinner, Xi reportedly toasted Obama with Moutai, China’s famed high-end liquor.

China said the summit established the groundwork for a “new model of major-country relations”.

White House officials later said the meetings built a stronger relationship between the two leaders, while yielding progress on important global challenges like cybersecurity, North Korea and greenhouse gas emissions.

Xi’s first US state visit: a packed ‘unforgettable journey’

In September 2015, Xi embarked on his first formal state visit to the US. His cross-country itinerary began in Seattle, where he met with senior American officials and business leaders, continued to Washington for formal diplomatic engagements with Obama, and concluded in New York to attend the 70th anniversary summit of the United Nations.
