While the mainland had integrated its coastguard into a military command structure, Taiwan retained a civilian coastguard in peacetime and was preparing it for wartime operations, she said.

“The institutional models and the political purposes are quite different,” she said.

Taipei’s preparations date back at least to 2005, when the Wei Hsing patrol vessel fired an HF-2 during the annual Han Kuang military exercises.

Within the Anping class, the Anping fired an HF-2 in 2022 and the Bali fired an HF-3 in 2024, while an unidentified vessel of the class fired two HF-2s in 2025, according to a navy report to lawmakers.

The approach became more visible during this year’s Han Kuang iteration in August, when the Bali was fitted with Hsiung Feng missiles and operated alongside navy Kuang Hua VI missile boats in a coastal-strike drill involving the navy’s newly established Littoral Operations Command.

There is no indication the exercise changed the coastguard’s wartime command arrangements, but it showed a coastguard patrol vessel operating alongside navy missile boats in a strike role.

Those operational preparations have been accompanied by moves to strengthen links between the navy and coastguard leadership.

Hours after Friday’s drill, Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling said a navy flag officer would fill the coastguard’s restored third deputy director general post, describing the move as part of closer cooperation between the two services.

The position was restored under legislation passed in June, with the government citing peacetime-to-wartime conversion and the coastguard’s expanding military-related duties among the reasons for adding another deputy.

A Taiwan coastguard expert, speaking anonymously because he was not authorised to comment publicly, said that arming coastguard vessels with anti-ship missiles could help close the gap between law enforcement and military responses if a confrontation involving mainland Chinese warships escalated into armed conflict.

However, the expert said the approach also risked blurring the line between law enforcement and military action, complicating crisis responses.

For the PLA, this would mean treating some Taiwanese coastguard “white hulls” – not just naval “grey hulls” – as potential anti-ship missile threats, the expert added.

Despite that added complexity, Bradford said the missile-armed coastguard vessels would not fundamentally change the military balance.

“Given the size of the PLA Navy and [PLA] Air Force, these are not going to be a game-changer,” he said. “Yet in naval warfare, every opposing vessel adds risk to your plan and forces you to make increasingly difficult choices.”

Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but most are opposed to changing the status quo by force.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Xi and Trump use their leverage to actually make progress?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fifth part of a series, Fan Chen and Orange Wang look at the negotiating chips and areas where progress might be made.

There will be some powerful bargaining chips on the table when Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet in Washington this week.

Both sides have economic and geopolitical leverage, and according to one analyst the negotiations will be as much about what they have chosen not to do to avoid retaliation.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fifth part of a series, Fan Chen and Orange Wang look at the negotiating chips and areas where progress might be made.

There will be some powerful bargaining chips on the table when Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet in Washington this week.

Both sides have economic and geopolitical leverage, and according to one analyst the negotiations will be as much about what they have chosen not to do to avoid retaliation.

Others pointed to critical areas where the two powers are locked in fierce competition but could instead be working together – from artificial intelligence and military dialogue to trade and biosafety.

But analysts agreed that keeping bilateral ties on a stable track would be a priority at the summit, and that was likely to be helped by a “tacit understanding” between Beijing and Washington on sensitive issues such as Iran and Taiwan. North Korea is also expected to be on the agenda.

Since Trump visited China in May, both countries have seen that the leverage they hold actually “works”, according to Taiyi Sun, an associate professor of political science at Christopher Newport University (CNU) in Virginia.

He said rare earths and critical minerals remained a key bargaining chip for China, while America still had leverage from its advanced semiconductors and related technologies.

Sun noted that Washington still had options, including another tariff increase based on its Section 301 trade investigation and its delayed US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan.

Likewise, he noted that Beijing had room to adjust its commitments to buying American oil, planes and agricultural products.

“What looks like goodwill today can become leverage tomorrow,” Sun said.

But he said that while both capitals had powerful tools at their disposal, “neither can use them without expecting significant retaliation”.

Expectations have been low for the presidential talks – the second face-to-face encounter between Xi and Trump this year.

Still, Sun said artificial intelligence “could produce one of the summit’s least expected outcomes”, suggesting the US and China might share the strongest interest in preventing “catastrophic misuse or loss of control” of the emerging technology.

AI governance has become a prominent part of the strategic rivalry between the world’s two largest economies.

The issue has been in the spotlight in recent days, with warnings that the technology could create an extinction-level event for humanity and heated debate over slowing down development of advanced models.

In marathon talks in New York on Sunday, US Trade Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng agreed to set up a dialogue on artificial intelligence with a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. The US said a bilateral Board of Trade was also operationalised during the talks.

Strengthening communication on AI will be a key goal of the Xi-Trump talks, according to Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University.

He said the two sides were likely to discuss domestic regulatory approaches and notification mechanisms for shared threats such as terrorism and transnational criminal groups using AI for malicious purposes.

“They may also explore communication protocols for major AI risk events, including a US-China emergency hotline for critical AI incidents,” Zhao said, adding that these proposals were already under discussion through unofficial channels.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration accused Chinese firms of stealing and copying American models through “industrial-scale distillation campaigns”. In response, Beijing said Washington was seeking a “monopoly” on the technology and warned of countermeasures.

Huang Ping, assistant dean of the Chinese University of Hong Kong- Shenzhen’s School of Public Policy, said that given the timing, the US accusations would boost its leverage in the discussions on AI.

He said a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI was of “very high” urgency, noting that they had clear differences over the definition of security and the purpose of regulation.

But he remained “cautiously optimistic” about outcomes of the AI talks, saying he expected a statement on principles, a follow-up working mechanism and preliminary arrangements in some areas.

According to Huang, Beijing and Washington were likely to discuss the rules, pace and boundaries of their AI rivalry. But he noted that their technological advantages, market interests and industrial growth remained the biggest issues – highlighting the clash between China’s low-cost, open-source ecosystem and an American commercial model that relies on closed-source, high-priced services.

Ahead of the summit, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi on Thursday urged Washington to stick with its commitment to “constructive strategic stability” in the relationship during a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Zhao from Fudan said reinforcing and acting on that commitment would be Beijing’s “primary goal” for Xi’s US trip – his first state visit to the country since 2015.

Both sides agreed to the concept in May, though the White House in its statement included US demands for “fairness and reciprocity”.

Political scientist Zhu Zhiqun, from Bucknell University in Pennsylvania, said both the US and China “genuinely desire a stable and constructive relationship”.

He also noted that Trump valued his personal relationship with Xi, seeing their rapport as key to stabilising bilateral ties.

“When facing serious internal and external challenges such as rising gas prices and a prolonged war in Iran before the November midterm election, the last thing Trump wants is a rocky relationship with China,” he said.

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, expected Trump to “express further support” for constructive strategic stability when he met Xi.

“With the Russia-Ukraine war grinding on and the Middle East morass expanding, Trump aims to preserve a tactical thaw between the two countries,” he said, adding that Xi was also likely to avoid a personal rupture with Trump.

According to Sun from CNU, China has gained leverage since the Iran war began in February by avoiding using its “enormous purchasing power in the global energy market” and not adding more pressure on international oil prices.

“I see that restraint partly as a favour to Trump – reciprocity for Trump’s restraint on issues that Beijing cares about,” he said, pointing to the US president putting the latest Taiwan arms sale on hold.

“There is a tacit understanding between Trump and Xi on this front,” Sun added. “Neither side needs to publicly announce a quid pro quo for such an understanding to function.”

Taiwan has long been “the first red line” for Beijing in managing its ties with Washington.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that the US was considering postponing major arms sales to the island until after November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, citing Beijing’s strong opposition to the deal and US defence industry constraints.

The SCMP also reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing possible announcements to strengthen military ties during Xi’s visit to the US.

A potential trip by Trump to China to attend the Apec gathering could provide an opportunity for another face-to-face meeting with Xi, as well as a chance to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

The SCMP reported earlier this month that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue.

Zhao from Fudan said it was possible that Trump and Xi had already discussed this in May, and that there had been further talks between Beijing and Pyongyang during Xi’s subsequent visit to North Korea in June.

“As a result, I think Trump himself remains very interested in pushing for a new summit with North Korea’s top leader – and Shenzhen is a very likely location,” he said, adding that Pyongyang would be looking to improve its international standing with such a meeting.

But he noted that China’s influence on its neighbour was limited and that friction between Washington and Seoul – following the recent cancellation of joint military drills – could stall diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.

Wyne from the International Crisis Group noted that some of Trump’s advisers would likely be “wary of making China a diplomatic intermediary”.

“Trump himself, though, would likely have little – if any – objection given his affinity for strongmen, his frustration that South Korea did not assist US efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and his hope that another tete-a-tete with Kim could burnish his peacemaking credentials by helping de-escalate tensions across the Korean peninsula,” Wyne said.

According to Sun, North Korea is not a Chinese bargaining chip. “China can help open the door, but it cannot simply deliver Kim,” he said.

There have been efforts to build positivity ahead of Xi’s trip to Washington, with the two governments signalling progress in discussions on reciprocal tariff cuts covering some US$30 billion in trade on each side and on counternarcotics cooperation.

Zhao said extending the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea in October was likely to be the “most realistic deliverable” from this week’s talks.

“This summit is vital for how China and the US coordinate their economic and trade relations and operationalise mechanisms such as the trade and investment councils,” he said.

Meanwhile, growing warnings over AI-enabled biosecurity threats have fuelled calls for the two powers to work together in the health sector.

Yanzhong Huang, a senior fellow for global health at the Council on Foreign Relations, said health issues were “unlikely” to be a summit focus, with fentanyl a possible exception.

“That does not mean there are no urgent issues between the two sides. Pharmaceutical supply-chain resilience, China’s rise in biotech, dual-use research, and AI’s application to health are increasingly treated as health-security challenges,” Huang said.

“US-China health cooperation is possible, but it will remain narrow and ad hoc,” he said, adding that given the lack of trust, formal cooperation in sensitive areas was unlikely and “joint R&D even more so”.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s UN Security Council bid tests non-aligned diplomacy
item.description:
Indonesia’s bid for another term on the United Nations’ premier security body stands a good chance of success given Jakarta’s growing global engagement, analysts say, but its balancing act between competing powers could complicate efforts to speak for the Global South.

Jakarta’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that it would launch its campaign this week for a fifth term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2029–2030.

The ministry said it was seeking the seat to represent the priorities of developing countries at the UN’s most powerful body and that its campaign would focus on peacekeeping, preventive diplomacy, conflict prevention and civilian protection.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s bid for another term on the United Nations’ premier security body stands a good chance of success given Jakarta’s growing global engagement, analysts say, but its balancing act between competing powers could complicate efforts to speak for the Global South.

Jakarta’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that it would launch its campaign this week for a fifth term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2029–2030.

The ministry said it was seeking the seat to represent the priorities of developing countries at the UN’s most powerful body and that its campaign would focus on peacekeeping, preventive diplomacy, conflict prevention and civilian protection.

“Indonesia aims to act as a bridge builder, establishing common ground, maintaining dialogue within the council and seeking practical solutions. We will also bring the voice and priorities of the Global South,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Yvonne Mewengkang told reporters on Thursday.

“Indonesia [also] wants a Security Council that delivers results. It might sound overly ambitious, but why not? That is precisely what Indonesia aims to bring: an effective and responsive Security Council,” she added.

The council has 15 members: five permanent members with veto powers – China, France, Russia, Britain and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

Indonesia has previously served four terms on the council: 1973–1974, 1995–1996, 2007–2008 and 2019–2021.

Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in Padang, West Sumatra, said the country’s bid stood a good chance considering its active global engagement under President Prabowo Subianto.

“Popularity does matter,” he said, adding that securing the seat could help strengthen Prabowo’s goal of making Indonesia an active contributor to the international community.

Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has visited nearly 30 countries and attended a number of high-profile summits to position Jakarta as an active mediator and independent middle power.

Apart from joining Brics as its first Southeast Asian member, Prabowo has actively advocated for the Global South at international forums such as the G20, emphasising fairness and strategic autonomy for developing countries.

Radityo Dharmaputra, a foreign-policy analyst and lecturer at Surabaya’s Airlangga University, said the odds of a fifth term on the council “are in Indonesia’s favour”, adding that Jakarta was one of the most consistent contributors to UN peacekeeping troops.

He said Indonesia was expected to push hard for Palestinian statehood, humanitarian access and for any stabilisation mission to remain anchored in a UN mandate rather than in a US-led framework.

“On Ukraine, I would expect Indonesia to present itself as a bridge builder calling for a ceasefire and dialogue,” Radityo added.

However, Indonesia will still need to mount a strong diplomatic campaign, taking lessons from the Philippines’ defeat by Kyrgyzstan last June. Manila lost to Bishkek for a non-permanent seat by a wide margin of 142 to 49 votes – a loss partly resulting from Manila’s treaty alliance with the US, which worked against it among non-aligned nations.

Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate international relations professor at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said that while Indonesia stood a good chance of getting a seat, the UN might look to consider other countries. He pointed out that former Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi was appointed UN special envoy on water in November 2024.

The Security Council bid also reflected the “personal ambition” of Prabowo, who had often sought high-profile arenas to “showcase his leadership”, Yohanes added.

A voice for the Global South?

Rifki said a seat on the council might not automatically make Indonesia the voice of the Global South due to Jakarta’s mixed positions on several international issues.

“Jakarta’s external approaches under Prabowo have been confusing for many Indonesians. Many have criticised his unclear direction in exercising foreign policies,” he said.

“How can Indonesia support the freedom of Palestine while sitting side-by-side with Israel on the ‘Board of Peace’, a problematic organisation led by [US President Donald] Trump?”

Indonesia strongly supports Palestinian independence and a two-state solution, maintaining that it will only formally recognise Israel as a sovereign state once Palestinian statehood is established.

In January, Indonesia joined Trump’s “Board of Peace” to oversee post-war governance, reconstruction and demilitarisation of the Gaza Strip, but Prabowo later suspended his country’s participation.

Rifki said that Indonesia’s ability to exert influence on behalf of the Global South would also be constrained by the “privileges of veto power” held by the five permanent members of the council.

“To make the council more effective, reform is a must,” Rifki said.

Critics have long called for reform of the council as its permanent members, in place since 1945, each wield a veto power that often paralyses its ability to resolve international conflicts and crises.

Apart from sharp disagreements among nations on how to expand the council, amending the UN Charter governing its make-up would require a two-thirds majority in the UN General Assembly as well as ratification by two-thirds of member states – including all five permanent members of the council.

Radityo said that other countries might see Indonesia as a “fence-sitter” or a “hypocrite” for championing Palestine’s statehood while remaining neutral on Ukraine. Indonesia had consistently framed the Ukraine war “as a tragedy to be ended through dialogue rather than as an act of aggression”, he said.

Abstaining from votes would be harder to hide on a 15-member council than in the General Assembly, Radityo said.

“So ambiguity becomes much harder to maintain,” he said, adding that Indonesia could contribute credibly as a non-Western, non-aligned voice in humanitarian areas – such as helping with prisoner exchanges, returning deported Ukrainian children and ensuring nuclear safety in war zones like Zaporizhzhia.

“By 2029, the council may be dealing with monitoring a ceasefire rather than the war itself,” Radityo said, adding that Indonesia’s peacekeeping experience would serve it well should this outcome come to pass.

For Prabowo, winning the council seat would indicate “to the world and to the domestic audience that Indonesia is respected”, he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Home at last? Why house arrest for Malaysia’s Najib is no done deal
item.description:
Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak appears to have entered the home stretch of his years-long bid to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest.

The 73-year-old has spent nearly two years fighting to serve his sentence at home, after claiming a royal order issued alongside his 2024 sentence commutation granted him that privilege.

The 2024 decision had already halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine – to 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) – for misappropriating funds from SRC International, a former unit of state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak appears to have entered the home stretch of his years-long bid to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest.

The 73-year-old has spent nearly two years fighting to serve his sentence at home, after claiming a royal order issued alongside his 2024 sentence commutation granted him that privilege.

The 2024 decision had already halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine – to 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) – for misappropriating funds from SRC International, a former unit of state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

Najib must first settle that fine before he can be released from prison, but even if he manages to raise the funds, his future is far from certain.

Malaysia has no law governing house arrest and the rules for Najib’s detention are still being worked out.

Here’s what we know so far about how it will work, what Najib needs to do to go home – and why he could yet find himself back behind bars.

Crowdfunding freedom

Najib was granted his request for house arrest on Friday, when the Federal Territories Pardons Board, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim, agreed to let him serve the remainder of his six-year SRC sentence – until August 23, 2028 – at home.

He must first pay the fine, however, and comply with the pardon’s other conditions. Any breach would void the arrangement and see him returned to prison, according to the official statement announcing the decision.

His supporters in Umno – the Malay nationalist party he led for nine years until his government was ousted in the 2018 election – have already started passing the hat around. A solidarity fund launched by the party raked in 1 million ringgit within a single day, with many supporters reportedly chipping in 10 ringgit or 50 ringgit apiece.

Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said on Monday that Najib’s family had yet to pay the fine, which must be settled with the Kuala Lumpur High Court registrar before any transfer from prison can go ahead.

Yet even once the money was paid, the process “may take some time”, Dusuki said.

Najib’s lawyers have said raising the money is complicated because a “significant part” of his assets, bank accounts and properties remain frozen or subject to government enforcement proceedings.

Decree deja vu

The pardon Najib was granted in 2024 by then king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah not only cut his jail sentence and slashed his initial 210 million ringgit fine, it was also accompanied by a separate decree Najib’s lawyers insisted allowed him to serve the balance of his prison term at home.

The document did exist, but the High Court ruled in December that it was unenforceable since house arrest had not been deliberated at the Pardons Board meeting and Malaysian law contained no provision for carrying it out. Najib then withdrew his appeal in April.

Article 42 of Malaysia’s Federal Constitution gives the king broad powers to grant pardons, reprieves and respites.

But the text does not spell out precisely how far that clemency can go, according to Malaysian constitutional lawyer Andrew Khoo.

“The actual ambit of the Pardons Board, in terms of the scope of the clemency that may be granted, is not specified in the constitution or in regulations connected therewith,” Khoo said.

“Given that this provision relies on the historical royal prerogative that has been received by convention, it could be argued that there are no limits to the scope of the clemency.”

Home as a prison

Malaysia still has no law specifically governing house arrest, leaving authorities to look to existing prison rules for a way to make Najib’s new arrangement work while the government develops separate legislation on home detention.

Police and prison officials have assessed Najib’s residence in the upmarket Langgak Duta neighbourhood of Kuala Lumpur, local media reported on Monday, with a mobile police station deployed nearby.

Authorities said the bungalow had not yet been formally confirmed as his detention site.

“One possible technical way the prison authorities can enforce a house arrest is to designate Najib’s house as a prison,” Malaysia-based constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said.

Such an arrangement could also subject Najib to prison-style restrictions, Lim said, including limits on electronic devices, food and who he can meet.

“There are restrictions … I’m not sure whether that is in line with the idea of a house arrest,” he said.

Back behind bars?

Even a successful move home would only cover Najib’s SRC sentence, relating to some 42 million ringgit that was transferred into his personal accounts.

In December, the High Court convicted him in a separate 1MDB case involving 2.3 billion ringgit (US$564 million) and sentenced him to a further 15 years in prison.

Justice Collin Lawrence Sequerah rejected Najib’s claim that the case was a politically motivated witch hunt, pointing instead to “cold, hard and incontrovertible evidence” against him and ordering the new prison term to begin only after his SRC sentence ends.

Najib is currently appealing that conviction, but as things stand, he would be legally bound to return to prison in 2028.

“If he remains convicted in the 1MDB matter and his house arrest period has finished, he has to go back to the normal prison,” Lim said. “Unless, of course, there is a further clemency bid by him which is successful.”

Pardon the politics

Friday’s pardon decision followed a strong year at the ballot box for the United Malays National Organisation. Its Barisan Nasional coalition swept 48 of 56 seats in Johor in July, then took 18 of 36 in Negeri Sembilan the following month – more than any other bloc.

Umno continues to press for its former president’s release, ensuring the issue remains one of the most sensitive in the party’s uneasy governing partnership with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition.

That has never sat well with the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key coalition partner for Anwar and one of Najib’s fiercest critics over 1MDB. Tensions flared again following the house-arrest decision, with DAP secretary general Anthony Loke offering his resignation as transport minister in protest.

Political scientist Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid called Najib’s house arrest “a double-edged sword” for Umno.

“Malay voters are now divided,” he said. “Some who have supported Umno all along will continue to do so, but floating voters [such as] those without any party loyalty will likely distance themselves from Umno [even] further.”

While house arrest for Najib could “marginally improve Umno’s prospects” in some of its traditional strongholds, it also risked alienating middle-class Malay and anti-corruption voters, Ahmad Fauzi said.

item.title: [SCMP] Analysts tip a stronger hand for China ahead of Xi-Trump summit in Washington
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the second part of a series, Fan Chen looks at Beijing’s stronger position going into the high-stakes visit.

Beijing is poised to begin this week’s summit with Washington from a position of strength, bolstered by a flurry of recent diplomatic outreach.

Chinese confidence could be further reinforced by the United States’ latest push to make headway on conflicts in Ukraine and Iran – wars that observers say Washington may need Beijing’s cooperation to help resolve – even if a near-term truce remains unlikely.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the second part of a series, Fan Chen looks at Beijing’s stronger position going into the high-stakes visit.

Beijing is poised to begin this week’s summit with Washington from a position of strength, bolstered by a flurry of recent diplomatic outreach.

Chinese confidence could be further reinforced by the United States’ latest push to make headway on conflicts in Ukraine and Iran – wars that observers say Washington may need Beijing’s cooperation to help resolve – even if a near-term truce remains unlikely.

Just weeks before his Washington trip, Chinese President Xi Jinping embarked on one of his most intense overseas itineraries, paying a state visit to Egypt after wrapping up the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Xi also attended the Brics summit in New Delhi last weekend, marking his first trip to India in seven years. In his address, the Chinese president took a veiled swipe at US policies and urged the bloc’s members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Through a joint declaration, the two-day summit also forged a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” policies – all without naming Washington.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, noted that Beijing’s diplomatic blitz strengthened its hand ahead of the second US-China summit of the year.

“Xi’s visit to Egypt – a major Middle Eastern power – underscores China’s rising influence in the region,” he said.

“As Washington is currently entangled in conflict with Iran, this serves as a reminder to the US that it cannot overlook China’s regional clout when managing its bilateral ties with Beijing.”

Amid escalating conflicts in the Middle East, Xi used his first Cairo visit in a decade to urge the countries of the region to build a self-led security model and “take charge of their own future”.

Observers noted that the approach nudged the countries in the region away from Washington, without committing Beijing to a role as a replacement security guarantor.

US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that Xi would visit on September 24 and that they would have “a lot of good things to discuss”. Beijing has yet to confirm the trip, in line with its practice of leaving official travel announcements to the last minute.

Wu added that Beijing’s diplomatic whirlwind highlighted its focus on Asia and the Global South, showing its expanding reach as a global power and standing in sharp contrast to a US administration that has alienated traditional allies.

His view was echoed by Ali Wyne, International Crisis Group’s senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations.

As Trump undermined US alliances, Xi was building “China’s portfolio of transactional alignments”, Wyne said, although he added that Beijing was “unlikely to establish a coherent counterbalancing coalition”.

“Still, the Trump administration’s foreign policy enables Beijing to present itself as a more stabilising force than Washington.”

According to Wyne, while Xi would avoid upstaging or upbraiding his counterpart, he might enter the Washington summit far more confident than in May, buoyed by Trump prioritising their relationship over allegations of Chinese election interference and support for Iran.

Patricia Kim, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Brookings Institution, said Xi’s multiple tours showed that China had other important relationships and diplomatic options. They aimed to portray Beijing as “increasingly central to a more multipolar international order”, she said.

“The message Xi wants to project is that Beijing can engage Washington without making the US the centrepiece of its foreign policy.”

In Bishkek, Xi praised the SCO approach of peaceful coexistence “without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”, taking a veiled swipe at the US military alliance system.

Bloc leaders – representing Central Asian states, Iran, Russia, Pakistan, India and Belarus – condemned military strikes on Iran as international law violations and backed Tehran’s right to a peaceful nuclear programme, directly countering US demands for total nuclear abandonment.

Meanwhile, pressed by November’s midterm elections and the approaching summit with Beijing, Washington has also stepped up efforts to resolve the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

Following a phone call on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said, though not for the first time, that he thought his Russian counterpart wanted to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine.

The call came after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks with Putin on Saturday. Both sides have signalled optimism and that plans for next steps could be expected soon.

Witkoff and Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday for talks aimed at resuming Russia-Ukraine negotiations – their first visit to the Ukrainian capital after numerous trips to Moscow since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022.

While no breakthrough was announced, Witkoff said he was “confident there would be a good resolution”.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian, European and US officials would meet to continue talks, while reiterating his call for a trilateral meeting involving Russia and the US.

Zelensky also said he expected the war with Russia to continue into the winter.

On Wednesday, Trump addressed the Middle Eastern front where the US has been deeply embroiled since February. The war with Iran would end immediately after the midterms, he said, and hinted that negotiations “could possibly happen”.

Surging oil prices and broader inflation from the US-Israel war in Iran have plunged Trump’s approval ratings to new lows, stoking Republican fears of what the midterms may bring.

Though neither conflict has a clear end in sight, analysts say that Washington might need China’s cooperation to resolve them, giving Beijing a stronger hand ahead of the Xi-Trump talks.

According to Zhu Junwei, director of Chinese think tank Horizon Insights, Trump – unable to resolve the conflict in Iran – is pursuing alternative wins in North Korea and Ukraine to project a “can’t stop winning” narrative in a bid to distract voters and boost his political prospects.

“None of these crises can be resolved quickly. If Trump wants quick, tangible wins to boost his midterm prospects, he is likely to need China’s help,” she said.

“Even if he approaches this by applying pressure, it fundamentally comes down to needing Beijing’s cooperation.”

Trump has repeatedly signalled a desire to revive personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, saying he expected to meet him later this year after scaling back last month’s US-South Korea military drill, widely seen as a conciliatory gesture.

On Thursday, the South China Morning Post reported exclusively that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue.

Zhu also noted that calming the Ukraine and Middle East conflicts – even if impossible overnight – “ultimately benefits Beijing, regardless of its impact on US-China rivalry, as it significantly improves China’s external environment and creates new opportunities”.

Sun Yun, director of the China programme at US think tank the Stimson Centre, echoed this view, saying that China could help the US resolve both conflicts and describing Beijing’s role as a potential bargaining chip in broader US-China talks.

However, both Sun and Wyne of the International Crisis Group noted that Beijing was not the main driver behind Trump’s pre-summit rush to resolve both conflicts.

“While the Trump administration would indeed have more diplomatic bandwidth were it to freeze the Russia-Ukraine war and reach a fresh ceasefire with Iran, it has not prioritised China policy nearly as much as many observers had anticipated when Trump retook office,” Wyne said.

Even though Putin might view Trump as a more favourable interlocutor than his predecessor Joe Biden, Moscow “is unlikely to weaken its relationship” with China for a fragile US truce under Trump, knowing American leadership was likely to revert to a hostile stance towards Moscow, he added.

Even without major deliverables, the summit could still prove useful if it maintained a cordial rapport between the leaders and sustained a “tactical thaw”, Wyne stressed.

According to Kim from Brookings, the leaders’ meeting was “unlikely to produce a significantly expanded bilateral agenda or result in a fundamental reset” of ties. Instead, the focus remained on extending the trade detente and sustaining leader-level diplomacy as the main buffer against further deterioration, she said.

Zhu noted that while Trump aimed to stabilise ties with China, an overall hawkish US bipartisan consensus meant there was “still a long way to go” towards achieving “constructive strategic stability” – the framework introduced at the Beijing summit in May.

“A single summit cannot resolve every issue; if this meeting yields partial economic and trade agreements and temporarily manages differences, it should be viewed as a success.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why the Global South keeps its doors wide open to Russia
item.description:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.

Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.

Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin.

Fuel and energy

Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country.

It has forced the Russian government to import refined fuel from countries it has traditionally exported to, such as Belarus, Turkey and India.

At the same time, the Kremlin continues to push for the expansion of its energy exports. This includes finalising the contract to build the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which intends to deliver 50 billion cubic metres (1.77 trillion cubic feet) of natural gas annually from Russia to China via Mongolia.

Last week, Russia also signed a deal to establish a new strategic oil reserves hub in Vietnam.

Moscow is also expanding cooperation on nuclear power, which was part of the discussion agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Vietnam’s President To Lam (during his state visit to Russia), and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Deeper ties

The ongoing sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival and future development.

Two friendly interstate bodies, in which Russia plays core roles, are becoming especially important. The first is Brics, a group of 11 economies comprising Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

The Brics economies now account for about 40 per cent of global gross domestic product. Last year, mutual trade turnover between Brics member states exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time.

The second is the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. This is a political and security bloc spanning countries in Europe, Asia and the Indo-Pacific. According to Putin, Russia’s trade turnover with the SCO exceeded US$400 billion in 2025.

Overall, Asia accounted for 73.4 per cent of Russia’s trade turnover last year. It’s no surprise that Moscow’s trade links with Asia featured in almost every conversation in Bishkek, Vladivostok and Delhi.

Bypassing disruption

Despite its friendly ties with Iran, Russia and its clients aren’t immune from the ongoing disruption to transport and trade routes through the Middle East. To mitigate these risks, Russia is actively lobbying two relatively new transcontinental transit networks.

The first is the 7,200km (4,470-mile) combined rail-road-maritime International North-South Transport Corridor. This route connects Russia’s Baltic Sea ports with Mumbai in India, via the Caspian Sea and Iran.

Russia reportedly discussed this route with the Indian and Iranian delegations this month.

The second is the 5,600km (3,480-mile) maritime Northern Sea Route, which connects Asia’s ice-free ports with Russian and European ports as part of a maritime passage across the Arctic Ocean.

In August, Beijing launched commercial operations along this route for the first time.

Political signalling

Russia walked away from this month’s diplomatic blitz with some clear wins. In addition to securing US$7.7 billion worth of investments in Vladivostok, along with some lucrative deals with Vietnam, Putin could also claim some political success.

First, although challenging at times, Putin’s interactions with his counterparts showcased how Moscow’s relationship with major non-Western international players remains a geopolitical constant, even in the fifth year of the Ukraine war.

For leaders of emerging centres of global influence, whether India’s Modi, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto or Vietnam’s Lam, interacting with Russia forms part of their countries’ foreign policy approach based on the notion of “strategic autonomy”.

This sends a powerful signal to the United States and its allies, amid the latest round of high-level consultations involving the CIA and US Treasury chiefs and their Russian counterparts.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump sent his own personal envoys to Moscow and made a follow-up phone call to Putin.

Second, Russia and its core partners in Asia jointly signalled they would continue to maintain strategic partnership links. This includes the question of importing Russia’s fossil fuels, nuclear power and other goods, and exporting processed fuel back to Russia.

Fuel security is particularly relevant to the Russian authorities’ attempts to stabilise the domestic situation. The Kremlin is under pressure to mitigate the aftershocks of the escalating war with Ukraine amid coming parliamentary elections from Friday to Sunday.

Concerns persist

Still, many in the Global South remain concerned about the growing impact of what seems to be becoming a forever war in and over Ukraine.

The latest round of tit-for-tat attacks against merchant shipping in the Black Sea triggered fears of grain and wheat shortages.

In mid-November, China will host the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. This is tipped to be a possible venue for the first trilateral meeting between Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump.

Here, Moscow might feel increasing pressure to settle the war by political means from its partners. These countries don’t want to feel the effects of the sanctions war between the West and Russia, let alone be dragged into it.

Alexey D Muraviev is senior research fellow at the School of Arts and Humanities at Edith Cowan University. This article was first published by The Conversation.

item.title: [SCMP] As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
item.description:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.

That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing.

Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began.

The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push.

The cloud escape hatch

Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers.

“For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.”

To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year.

Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring.

Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data.

To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024.

However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing.

The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access.

“If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said.

Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners.

The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power.

The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”.

Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained.

“Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added.

Southeast Asia’s data centre boom

If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs.

Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda.

Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market.

Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry.

If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market

Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group

“If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries.

Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.”

The region also offers competitive energy economics.

In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining.

While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News.

Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep.

Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”.

The domestic bottleneck

For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale.

Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported.

The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only.

For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing.

The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities.

ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August.

“There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution.

Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter.

Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally.

Accelerating self-reliance

If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs.

Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity.

“Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products.

Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier.

Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year.

The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.

However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August.

Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang.

Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report.

That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank.

As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries
item.description:
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.

In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030.

The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.

In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030.

The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

He also focused on improving living standards and social well-being, announcing initiatives ranging from higher baby bonuses to encourage childbirth and increased healthcare spending to more subsidised housing and shorter waiting times for public flats.

“[China’s] 15th five-year plan, which outlines a blueprint for future national development and also places a heightened demand for Hong Kong’s better integration into and service of the overall national development, presents major opportunities and opens up new ground for the growth of our city,” Lee said in his speech to the Legislative Council.

“Hong Kong’s economic structure still leaves room for enhancement, the mission of transitioning to new growth drivers remains formidable, and deep-seated social problems still require speedy resolution.”

The five-year blueprint, a seven-part document described by Lee as “an action agenda” for Hong Kong’s medium- and long-term development, lists 105 indicators, including 22 major targets covering economic and innovation development, livelihoods, and environmental protection.

The major indicators are divided into 17 anticipatory goals and five binding targets, some of which would be affected by geopolitical uncertainties and other external factors.

“If the binding targets are not met at the end of the day, there is a need to be held accountable,” Lee said. “But we need to appreciate that some things may be out of our control, such as economic development. Some countries might suddenly change their policies.”

The anticipatory goals include 10 per cent annual increases in two key technology indicators: nearly doubling spending on innovation activities to 3 per cent from 1.63 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) over five years; and raising the economic share of value-added manufacturing to 5.5 per cent from 3.8 per cent.

Another anticipatory target is to increase by 4 to 5 per cent annually the number of companies whose parent firms are based outside Hong Kong.

Four of the five binding targets concern environmental protection. They include cutting carbon emissions per unit of GDP by 32.5 per cent and raising the share of zero-carbon energy in Hong Kong’s electricity fuel mix to 30 per cent from 25 per cent over the five-year period.

Goals for the Northern Metropolis, the massive undertaking near the Shenzhen border to build a 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) business, education and housing zone, include a binding target to raise the “spade-ready sites” available from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030, and an anticipatory target to increase the number of homes completed in the zone to 70,000 from the current 11,000.

On livelihoods, Lee pledged to raise the doctor-to-population ratio to 2.43 from 2.25 per 1,000 residents, and lower the risk of early deaths caused by chronic conditions to 6.9 per cent from 7.3 per cent.

Lee’s long-term blueprint dedicates a chapter to national security as a priority for the city’s success and prosperity, stressing that “a holistic approach” will be adopted to strengthen economic resilience by improving the city’s legal system and enforcement mechanisms.

The wide-ranging, traditional policy address that followed the announcement of the five-year plan was titled “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era, Driving Reform and Boosting Development, Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihood”.

The address, which was the last of Lee’s current term, set out priorities targeting five major areas of development opportunities, alongside 25 key livelihood initiatives.

Measures offering immediate benefits to residents include one-off cash incentives and subsidies.

While extending the HK$20,000 (US$2,549) newborn bonus for three years, Lee said the government would increase the amount for second and subsequent children to HK$30,000 and offer subsidies to employers providing an extra 10,000 full-time jobs to young people entering the workforce.

Expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis is a key highlight of the policy address, which matches the “dual-core planning” vision set out in the five-year plan that clusters innovation and technology (I&T) sectors near the northern border and places finance sectors south along Victoria Harbour.

Describing the northern development zone as “an important strategic vehicle” for integrating I&T and industry, Lee said selected strategic industries establishing a presence there would receive targeted tax breaks.

While developing three university towns that will span 1,000 hectares in the northern zone, the government will invite universities to build campuses in Hung Shui Kiu from this year. Authorities are also studying the feasibility of a southern extension of the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Western Rail Link to enhance connectivity.

The Northern Metropolis will seek to improve living conditions in space-starved Hong Kong, with its housing projects increasing the proportion of more spacious flats with an area of about 45 square metres (484 square feet) to 25 per cent from the original 20 per cent.

Both policy documents devoted significant space to consolidating Hong Kong’s role as an international financial centre under the broader “Four Centres, One Hub” strategy.

The strategy seeks to strengthen the city’s position as an international financial, maritime and trade centre, develop it into an international innovation and technology centre, and establish the city as a hub for “high-calibre talent”.

The chief executive said the city would introduce an auction system allowing banks to bid for short-term yuan liquidity to meet their short-term financing needs.

Lee said his administration would actively promote the use of the Chinese currency to settle government expenditure, for example purchasing fresh water from Guangdong, and expand the dim sum bond market, while the operator of the city’s stock and futures markets would launch an offshore renminbi bond index and introduce new products.

Following the official launch of Hong Kong’s central clearing and settlement system for gold earlier this year, the government is considering tapping into the Exchange Fund to buy more gold and participate in the spot and futures markets.

The policy address also outlined growth strategies for emerging sectors, including dispute resolution, international property and marine services.

A new task force on frontier technology will spearhead deeper research on aerospace, marine and quantum technologies.

Addressing housing issues that Beijing has often instructed Hong Kong to resolve, Lee said the aim was to reduce the waiting time for subsidised rental flats to 4.5 years from 4.8 years by 2027, and to bring it below four years after 2030.

The long-term plan envisages public rental housing accounting for 40 per cent of total supply, with subsidised sale flats and private homes each making up 30 per cent over the next 10 years.

Lee put a heavy emphasis on leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) in various policy domains, which will include establishing an “AI City Brain” system to strengthen responses to extreme weather events, major incidents and public order management. A new AI commissioner’s post will be created to tackle emerging challenges.

Lee told the media later that while AI boosted efficiency, it also created “operational and societal risks”, prompting his administration to introduce seven risk governance guidelines, with a particular focus on protecting students.

Lee expressed confidence that the targets would improve livelihoods, strengthen economic development and deepen Hong Kong’s integration into the national development agenda.

“I hope and I’m confident that in five years, for everyone, whether it’s their income or development, there will be an improvement,” he said.

“Our industries will be more diversified, education enhanced, [the city] more international, and we will be a highly technologically empowered Hong Kong.”

item.title: [SCMP] Shadow of Xi summit hangs over Trump’s high-stakes talks with Japan’s Takaichi
item.description:
When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi meets US President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, the leader casting the longest shadow over the meeting will not even be in the building.

Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday – two days after Takaichi meets the US leader on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. It will be Xi’s first state visit to the US in over 10 years.

Faced with an unpredictable American president eager for tangible results ahead of what could be a tough November midterm election, Japan is working to ensure its vital interests are not traded away at the Xi-Trump summit.
item.content:encoded:
When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi meets US President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, the leader casting the longest shadow over the meeting will not even be in the building.

Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday – two days after Takaichi meets the US leader on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. It will be Xi’s first state visit to the US in over 10 years.

Faced with an unpredictable American president eager for tangible results ahead of what could be a tough November midterm election, Japan is working to ensure its vital interests are not traded away at the Xi-Trump summit.

The Takaichi-Trump talks will unfold amid frosty ties between Tokyo and Beijing. Takaichi’s remarks last November that an attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan infuriated Beijing and sparked months of diplomatic freeze.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Experts said the timing of Takaichi’s meeting revealed Tokyo’s determination to prevent Washington from making concessions at the expense of Japan’s regional security and economic interests.

They added that Beijing’s rare earth export controls and Taiwan would be featured in the Trump-Takaichi talks, with the Japanese prime minister using the opportunity to reiterate Tokyo’s perspective to the US leader.

Beijing confirmed on Monday that Xi would make a three-day state visit to Washington from Wednesday to Friday - his third face-to-face meeting with Trump since the US president returned to office last year.

Ahead of a meeting with Xi in South Korea last October, Trump visited Tokyo for hours of direct discussions with Takaichi. She reciprocated the visit in March for bilateral talks at the White House.

This pattern reflects a deliberate strategy by Tokyo: maintaining personal rapport with Trump and securing assurances before Washington enters critical talks with Beijing, even as unpredictable US rhetoric continues to test allies’ coordination.

“Tokyo’s priority is to prevent a US-China stabilisation deal from coming at the expense of Japan’s economic security or regional deterrence,” said Kenichi Doi, senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Japan.

Japan would welcome more reliable flows of rare earths and other critical inputs, he added.

“Tokyo will also want Washington to treat China’s dual-use restrictions on Japan as an alliance-wide supply-chain issue, given their potential spillovers through Japanese production into US industries,” he said.

Doi said Takaichi was likely to seek confirmation of Washington’s commitment to peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, along with closer alignment on critical minerals, export controls and wider economic security.

Following Takaichi’s Taiwan comments, Beijing enforced strict dual-use export controls covering items destined for Japan, including critical minerals, rare earths and advanced tech.

The rare earth restrictions loom large in Tuesday’s discussions. China controls 90 per cent of the world’s processed rare earths and at least 60 per cent of rare earth extraction, giving it considerable leverage.

Asked on Monday whether rare earth exports to Japan would be addressed at the Xi-Trump summit, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that restrictions on dual-use items were a necessary step to curb Japan’s remilitarisation and nuclear ambitions.

Beijing has defended its restrictions as a direct countermeasure against Tokyo’s defence build-up.

“In her own words, Takaichi sees Taiwan’s security as inextricably linked to Japan’s own,” said Sean King, senior vice-president at New York-based business advisory firm Park Strategies, adding that the Japanese leader was “unnerved by” Trump’s continued delay of an arms sales package to Taiwan.

“She will surely be keeping a close eye on Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping to see if Trump again appears swayed,” he said, adding that Takaichi might worry the Diaoyu Islands, known in Japan as the Senkakus, could be next on the US president’s “reeducation list” if Trump were to start siding with Beijing on Taiwan. The Diaoyus are a group of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea claimed by Tokyo, Beijing and Taipei.

The South China Morning Post reported earlier that Washington was considering postponing the announcement of arms sales to Taiwan until the end of the year, pointing to a planned bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and Xi’s expected visit to Florida for the Group of 20 summit in December.

According to Doi, Tokyo’s worst-case outcome for the Xi-Trump summit would be if the US leader secures economic concessions from Beijing in exchange for shifting Washington’s position on the Taiwan Strait or technology controls “without sufficient coordination with its allies”.

The timing of the meetings raises the question of whether Trump intends to use the impending Xi summit to squeeze Tokyo for concessions on burden-sharing, base hosting costs or currency valuations.

However, analysts believe obvious discord between the US and its foremost Asian ally would undermine Trump’s own diplomatic leverage.

“Trump is transactional with Japan, but he has little incentive to manufacture a visible dispute with Tokyo two days before negotiating with Xi,” Doi said.

“Extracting marginal concessions now at the cost of displaying alliance friction would weaken, rather than strengthen, Washington’s hand with Beijing.”

Doi said Tuesday’s meeting between Trump and Takaichi would be more about showing policy alignment before Xi’s visit.

King agreed that Washington’s commercial posture towards Tokyo was relatively stable, noting that Japan remained the top foreign direct investor in the United States.

“The purpose of Tuesday’s talk is to remind everyone that Japan is America’s premier Asian ally and that mainland China is a geostrategic rival, and Japan is the US’ anchor in Asia, as it were,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia supports multilateralism, wary of US or China leadership: survey
item.description:
Southeast Asia remains comparatively confident in international cooperation even as scepticism grows over whether the United States or China should take a leading global role, a new survey has found.

Analysts said the findings reflected a long-standing regional preference for keeping strategic options open, particularly among smaller and middle powers wary of an international order dominated by either Washington or Beijing.

“Seeking Security and Opportunity in a Stormy World”, released this month by The Rockefeller Foundation, surveyed more than 35,000 people across 34 countries on their assessment of global affairs. Its Southeast Asian grouping covered Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asia remains comparatively confident in international cooperation even as scepticism grows over whether the United States or China should take a leading global role, a new survey has found.

Analysts said the findings reflected a long-standing regional preference for keeping strategic options open, particularly among smaller and middle powers wary of an international order dominated by either Washington or Beijing.

“Seeking Security and Opportunity in a Stormy World”, released this month by The Rockefeller Foundation, surveyed more than 35,000 people across 34 countries on their assessment of global affairs. Its Southeast Asian grouping covered Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore.

Southeast Asia was among the regions most positive about whether global cooperation was working effectively, scoring 63 per cent compared with 37 per cent for the US and Canada, 32 per cent for Oceania and 31 per cent for western Europe.

At the same time, the survey suggested limited global appetite for either Washington or Beijing assuming a leading role, with 39 per cent comfortable with the US doing so and 37 per cent saying the same of China.

Another 61 per cent supported countries working together to address global problems without either superpower taking the lead.

The combination pointed to “a more fragmented global order”, said Alejandro Reyes, a senior fellow at the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong.

“There is widespread recognition of both American and Chinese power, but much less willingness to accept either as the natural or dominant leader of the international system,” Reyes said.
